Fishers detonate a bomb every hour on one Indonesian coral reef

New Scientist August 14, 2026

Within just a 17-kilometre radius in one Indonesian archipelago, there is an explosion almost every hour as locals practise “bomb fishing”, destroying coral reefs and decimating marine life.

Over 483 days between May 2023 and September 2024, Ben Williams at University College London and his colleagues deployed an acoustic monitoring system at Spermonde Archipelago, south-west of Sulawesi, Indonesia.

Oceans are darkening all over the planet – what’s going on?

As well as being a global coral reef biodiversity hotspot, it is a location where fishers detonate explosives underwater, stunning and killing fish that can then be easily harvested.

Advertisement

“The sound of bomb fishing is so loud that if you’re on a dive it can shake you out of your skin,” says Williams. “You feel it more than you hear it. But if you put your head up on the surface, you likely won’t even see the boat responsible because the sound of bomb fishing travels such a huge distance underwater.”

The recording equipment sat at a depth of 17 metres and was able to detect explosions inside a radius of almost 17 kilometres. The team used AI to analyse their 3650 hours of raw audio. They recorded 3567 explosions, or just over 23 per day while the device was underwater.

Free newsletter

“We have shown the true extent of this practice in a known hotspot for the first time ever, which we hope will drive action to curb this destruction,” says Williams.

One of the biggest issues is that there is an illegal supply chain underpinning the bomb fishing, usually involving the sourcing of fertilisers and fuses or detonators, he says. “In other regions these may be stolen mining explosives or even military explosives.”

Once the fishers have the explosives, enforcement at sea is sparse. “It’s like Whac-A-Mole targeting the bomb fishers. The best approaches should tackle the illegal supply chain that gets the materials needed to make explosives to bomb fishers or sellers of these,” says Williams.

Bomb fishing is a problem across the tropics, and part of the solution is retraining locals in sustainable tourism and reef restoration, he says. “It’s been documented in 34 countries, from South America to the Mediterranean to the East Coast of Africa and South-East Asia.”

This El Niño will be the hottest by a huge margin

Rinaldi Gotama, who wasn’t part of the work, is currently studying at the University of Queensland, Australia, and has worked extensively with Indonesian non-governmental organisations in reefs targeted by bomb fishing. He says he wasn’t surprised at the scale of the problem.

“I expected the frequency to be high, but studies regarding bomb fishing are relatively scarce because it is notoriously difficult to quantify,” Gotama says.

He says the new method employed by the researchers might help combat the practice. “If this acoustic method could be replicated elsewhere, it could help with detecting and quantifying blast fishing and help identify hotspots of activity,” says Gotama.

“That could be valuable not only for ecological monitoring, but also for targeting enforcement and evaluating whether management interventions are actually reducing blast fishing.”

How bad is the UK drought and how long will it continue?

New Scientist August 14, 2026

Summer 2026 is likely to be the warmest on record in the UK, with repeated searing heatwaves and a severe drought affecting much of the country. In southern England in particular, the landscape is parched and crispy, rivers and reservoirs are running low, and trees are shedding their leaves in a stress response to the dry weather. Much of Europe is baking under similar conditions.

How much longer can we cope without rain? And how long will it take us to recover from such an unprecedented dry spell? With the help of experts from across water, agriculture and climate, we’ve answered your key questions below.

Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought conditions after the driest July in almost two centuries, when barely any rain fell in many places. The National Drought Group – which includes public bodies, agricultural and environmental organisations – has described the situation as an “exceptionally serious” flash drought, driven by a combination of very high temperatures and exceptionally low rainfall over recent weeks.

Advertisement

It is taking a severe toll on the landscape. Almost 250 wildfires have been reported in biodiversity hotspots this year, wetlands and peatlands are drying out, and trees are dying. Some 22 per cent of rivers are at exceptionally low levels, including the Avon, Wye, Ely Ouse and Exe.

“The almost completely dry July is exceptionally unusual and add to that the heatwaves, the soils have dried very quickly and river flows have dropped very fast,” says Glenn Watts at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology.

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

The dry, hot weather over July and August has rapidly depleted rivers, reservoirs and underground aquifers, despite the wet winter England just experienced. Reservoir levels in England have fallen to 69 per cent – 11.6 per cent lower than what would be expected for this time of year. Reservoir storage in the country fell 16 per cent in July, the greatest reduction in raw storage for at least 30 years, the UK government said this week.

It is a sign of the impact of climate change, which is expected to bring drier, hotter summers to the UK. This year shows that even a wet winter isn’t enough to carry the UK through an extremely hot, dry summer. “Currently the situation is that we’re just simply using too much water,” says Kevin Grecksch at the University of Oxford. “We’re not replenishing at the same speed as we’re using water.”

But great progress has been made in improving water storage, infrastructure and the industry’s response to drought in recent years, says Kevin Collins at the Open University. This means the water industry is better equipped to deal with drought than it was in 1976, even though the weather has been hotter and drier for a longer period than 50 years ago. “It’s more severe than 1976 in terms of heatwaves and repetition of heatwaves, but the status of the water-supply system is currently not as bad as it was in 1976,” he says.

Free newsletter

You may have noticed the crunch of dry leaves underfoot in recent weeks. That’s a sign stressed trees are going through a “false autumn”, where they shed their leaves and even branches in an effort to keep their main stem alive. Some will not make it through – the 2022 heatwave killed 400 trees at Kew Gardens in London. Younger trees are at greater risk, as newly planted trees need 50 litres of water per week during the summer months for the first three years after planting.

Meanwhile, low river levels are causing algal blooms in rivers, and hard, dry soils make it impossible for animals such as badgers and hedgehogs to dig for food. Fierce wildfires have swept through nature reserves, destroying habitats and killing wildlife.

Unfortunately, this is the third drought in five years for England, and ecosystems are already stressed and weakened by these previous events. That makes it more difficult for them to recover from this extreme summer.

The intense heat of this week will give way to cooler temperatures next week, according to the Met Office, the UK’s national weather service. Although temperatures are expected to be closer to average for this time of year, whether rain will fall in the areas under the most stress is far from certain. Forecasters have struggled this year to accurately forecast rain, with wet weather often failing to materialise.

Even if rain showers do arrive next week, it is unlikely to be enough to alleviate the drought, the Met Office said in a blog post this week. There’s also the not insignificant risk of a dry, hot September, with long-term forecasts currently favouring drier weather.

Extreme heat is now making cities unlivable. How can we survive it?

Water companies will prioritise maintaining household water supplies above all else, but other sectors, such as agriculture or commercial businesses, are likely to face increasingly tight restrictions over the coming weeks if the drought continues.

Hosepipe bans – known as temporary use bans – are already in place across much of the country and can reduce consumption by 5 to 10 per cent. At least one water company – Southern Water – has applied to the government for a drought order. That would give it powers to introduce a non-essential use ban that restricts certain commercial activities such as car washing, window cleaning and watering commercial premises. Other water companies have signalled they will follow suit if the situation doesn’t improve in the next few weeks. Water companies can also apply to take more water from rivers and aquifers to maintain supply, but this threatens wildlife and habitats.

The next step up is an emergency drought order, which needs to be approved by the environment secretary. This would allow water companies to impose rota cuts on household and commercial customers, as happened in 1976 when mains water to households was curtailed and standpipes were installed in streets.

However, this is highly unlikely to happen this year, says Collins, as water companies would deploy all other possible measures first. “Public water supply is always the priority, no matter what happens,” he says.

Farmers are already warning that yields of some crops will be significantly lower than normal this summer because of the drought. Wheat yields are expected to be down 14 per cent compared with the average, and potato yields are expected to be 10 to 15 per cent lower than average. Meanwhile, harvests of fruits such as apples are also expected to be lower than usual, and the fruit smaller in size. The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a think tank, estimates it could be the worst harvest on record for UK farmers, with drought-related yield losses potentially costing arable farmers £390 million in lost revenue.

The situation is made worse by the fact that much of Europe is also sweltering under hot, dry conditions, meaning food production across the continent is also likely to fall this year. Together, that is likely to push food prices up for consumers into the autumn, particularly for fruit.

Farmers in England are struggling to adapt to heat and drought extremes because the weather is still so changeable, says Matthew Paul at Rothamsted Research. “We’re not like the Mediterranean, where you get predictably hot, dry summers every year,” he says. Paul’s research is focused on breeding crops and developing treatments to boost yields in both wet and dry conditions. “The solution isn’t to breed drought-tolerant crops that only do well under droughts,” he says.

Is the climate change food crisis even worse than we imagined?

Over the longer term, England needs to get better at storing water from its wet winters to tide it over during the summer months. This means building new reservoirs – a costly, time-consuming endeavour – and expanding water-transfer schemes to transport water from wet regions to dry ones. Even more radical plans are being explored, from building desalination plants to artificially injecting more water into underground aquifers during winter months.

The Environment Agency predicts there could be a shortfall of 5 billion litres per day in water supply across England by 2050 if more isn’t done to limit demand and increase supply.

In the eyes of the public, a few days of rain is enough for the drought to be over. But it takes landscapes and wildlife far longer to recover from such an extreme dry spell. The flash drought that developed last year across England only ended in autumn when weeks of above-average rainfall arrived.

Hydrologists will be watching closely for a wet autumn and winter this year, which will help to recharge rivers and groundwater ahead of next summer. A strong El Niño now underway in the Pacific Ocean could increase the chances of a wetter start to winter for the UK, although El Niño’s influence on UK weather is indirect and difficult to predict.

However, a dry winter could leave the UK vulnerable. “A dry winter would make us worried about next spring and summer,” says Watts. That would put the country in a vulnerable position and raise the threat of emergency drought orders being introduced.

Monsoon-driven wildfires may have shaped human evolution

New Scientist August 14, 2026

Wet climatic spells didn’t quench wildfires in East Africa’s Turkana basin 1.75 million years ago. Instead, they fuelled them. That’s what chemical traces from ancient plants in the region seem to suggest, and this pattern could have shaped our hominin ancestors’ evolution, including the use of fire and tools.

Rich in hominin fossils and archaeological finds, the Turkana basin – sometimes dubbed the Cradle of Humankind – has long been considered important for understanding the lives of our early ancestors. These include Homo erectus, a species that appeared about 2 million years ago and that is regarded as one of our earliest recognisably human ancestors.

The first truly complex stone tools were found here, too, in layers dating back to around 1.76 million years ago. Compared with earlier tools, these “Acheulean” tools were more advanced, and included refined multi-purpose hand axes, useful for both butchery and plant processing. The Acheulean technology then persisted for the next 1.5 million years.

Advertisement

The 85-million-year timeline of human evolution

One idea is that ancient hominins evolved the greater cognitive flexibility required to produce Acheulean tools – and to begin controlling fire – in response to dramatic environmental swings and rapidly changing ecosystems. But although previous studies have found evidence in favour of this “variability selection hypothesis”, establishing exactly what kinds of shifting environmental conditions may have driven these cognitive and technological advances has proved challenging.

Now, Rachel Lupien at Aarhus University, Denmark, and her team think they may have an answer. They analysed chemical signatures in sediments that formed in the Turkana basin over a 21,000-year period, roughly 1.75 million years ago. With the information, they could reconstruct rainfall, vegetation and wildfire patterns when the earliest Acheulean tools were in use.

“Because these three powerful climate and ecosystem indicators are all from the same sample, we could directly look at how their relationships vary through time with no guesswork,” says Lupien.

An incredible Denisovan skull is upending the story of human evolution

The chemical signatures came from ancient leaf waxes and plant combustion, revealing how the nature of the vegetation shifted from woody to grassy conditions, and how wildfire intensity changed across time.

They found that the landscape was predominantly forested with limited wildfires for the first 5000 years of the study interval. It then became far more variable for the next 5000 years, fluctuating between very dry grasslands with occasional wildfires, perhaps caused by lightning strikes, and wetter forested conditions with far fewer fires. But during the final, longer period of the study interval, something surprising happened: rainfall increased significantly to produce monsoon conditions – and the number of wildfires rose, too.

“We find that higher precipitation leads to more vegetation growth, which allows fires to burn because of the additional biomass,” explains Lupien. Meanwhile, more fires limited vegetation expansion, which created a feedback loop. “What we can say from our data is that if humans were taking advantage of fire in Turkana, it would have been during these… wet intervals when monsoons were magnified.”

Subscriber-only newsletter

“Here we’re now beginning to see the definite evidence that bushfires were there in their world,” says John Gowlett at the University of Liverpool, UK, who wasn’t involved in the analysis. It wouldn’t be surprising if ancient hominins then experimented with using those fires to improve their access to resources, he says.

For instance, frequent natural fires would have increased hominin opportunities for ‘fire foraging’: gathering up animals or plants that had been killed and cooked in the flames. It would also have allowed hominins to experiment with taking burning branches from natural wildfires and feeding them to keep fires burning longer, so they could cook food for themselves.

“It is far easier to keep a fire going than it is to start one,” says Matt Grove, a study co-author at the University of Liverpool, UK. “In this way, hominins could have started to reap the benefits of fire long before they were able to create it.”

New evidence reveals that Arabia was not a mere stopover for ancestral humans leaving Africa, but a lush homeland where they flourished and evolved

A study published this year presented evidence of this type of fire use between 1.07 million and 1.79 million years ago at South Africa’s Wonderwerk Cave. Tentative evidence of fire use in Turkana dates back to around 1.5 million years ago.

The appearance of Acheulean stone tools during this interval may be further evidence of behavioural changes linked to the extremely variable environments in which ancient hominins evolved. Rick Potts at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington DC, who pioneered the variability selection hypothesis in the 1990s, thinks a link is plausible.

“This is the first paper I’ve encountered to illustrate the emergence of the Acheulean as a response to ecological variability and the process of variability selection,” he says. “Episodic and intense natural fires offer a novel contribution.”

Quaternary Science Reviews DOI: 10.1016/j. gr.2026.05.014

Why do people ask so few questions in conversation?

New Scientist August 14, 2026

I was at a friend’s birthday party recently when I found myself sitting next to a writer I didn’t know. Oh good, I thought optimistically, we might be able to bond over the joys and pains of the job. Two hours later, I knew the ins and outs of the surrealist novel he was writing, but he found out very little about me, since he didn’t ask a single question in return.

I am sure this will be familiar to many readers, so I was delighted to come across some new work on “interpersonal curiosity” by Niobe Way, a professor of applied psychology at New York University. She suggests that, from a young age, Western patriarchal culture subtly discourages us from demonstrating an interest in others – an idea reinforced by masculine stereotypes. Fortunately, she has plenty of suggestions for ways to cultivate it in ourselves and our children.

How to sparkle in conversation with strangers

Way tells me that she was inspired by her personal experience of moving to Shanghai for a few months with her young children in 2007. It was, she says, “a transformative experience”. When she returned to the US, however, she tried to talk to her friends about the amazing time that she’d had, with little success. “No one, literally nobody, asked me questions about it,” she says. “And I remember saying, what is going on with people’s curiosity?”

Advertisement

Nearly 20 years later, she is finally answering that question. Previous research on curiosity, she says, had mostly focused on intellectual interests in the physical, material and natural world, while largely neglecting to measure people’s inquisitiveness about others’ lives and its consequences.

As a developmental psychologist, Way has so far focused her efforts on children and adolescents. She and her colleagues asked 389 school students aged 11-13 to describe the two questions that they would most like to ask their closest friend, teacher and primary caregivers. They received a wide variety of responses. Some of the participants reported having no questions at all, while others opted for simple information-seeking (such as “When is dinner?” or “What is the point of this work?”). Those who wished to probe others’ personal lives and relationships, however, had better friendships and greater overall wellbeing.

Free newsletter

Such findings are perhaps unsurprising: supportive relationships are known to be central to our health and happiness, and asking others questions about their lives is surely one of the best ways to build those bonds. “It really is the secret sauce of all human connection,” says Way.

The big question, then, is why we don’t do it more often. Way suggests that we have been conditioned to think that it is rude to pry into others’ lives, and the rise of individualism means that we also simply care less about the people around us. In their study of adolescent students, however, Way and her colleagues found that boys were about twice as likely to report having “no questions” than girls – suggesting that gender roles may play a large part.

Earlier this year, Way published a paper that tackled this topic head-on. To measure their adherence to masculine stereotypes, each adolescent was asked to rate their agreement with statements such as “I do not let it show to my friends when my feelings are hurt” and “It is necessary for me to fight others in order to gain respect.” As hypothesised, the team found that these scores were inversely correlated with interpersonal curiosity, meaning that the more someone endorsed macho values, the less likely they were to say they enjoyed hearing others’ stories. And this, in turn, seemed to have a big influence on the quality of their friendships, measured by things like the amount of free time they spent with their closest friend and the amount of social support they received from them.

If you struggle with small talk or find it hard to express yourself, research by psychologist Alison Wood Brooks and others will help you master the art of conversation

You may imagine that this affected only the boys – and the connection was indeed much stronger for those who identified as male. Although some girls have started to associate the tough-guy image with success, and internalised the associated behaviour, this didn’t seem to be so closely linked to interpersonal curiosity, which independently predicted their relationship quality.

Sexist assumptions about interpersonal curiosity may even explain why it has been understudied in science. “We think that interpersonal curiosity is feminine, and we don’t value what we’ve deemed feminine,” says Way, whose book Rebels with a Cause: Reimagining boys, ourselves and our culture explores these themes. “But this ‘soft’ side is essential for our social species.”

Can we ever overcome this cultural conditioning? Way argues that children are born to be interpersonally curious, and that innate interest can be reawakened with the right education. To do so, she designed the Listening with Curiosity Project, a 26-lesson curriculum for adolescent students in New York Public Schools. It includes advice on asking open-ended questions and techniques to encourage people to open up about their experiences with greater nuance and detail – with plenty of opportunity for practice. The early evidence suggests it works: by the end of the curriculum, the students showed greater curiosity and increased friendship quality, with boys showing the biggest gains.

The brain processes voices differently depending on the volume of the speaker and if the listener is focused on them

Way thinks that plenty of adults could also benefit from a bit of practice. You might start out with someone you know, by asking them about their favourite childhood memory, a topic that most people enjoy discussing. You can then use this opportunity to show your genuine interest in what they say through lots of follow-up questions.

You could even try it at a party, she suggests. Simply explain that you’ve been reading about the benefits of asking deep questions, then pick a topic to begin with.

You may feel shy about getting started, but Way reassures me that it will be far more rewarding than you expect. When she encourages her students to try the exercise, they almost all take pleasure in the experience. “We are starving to be asked real questions,” she says. “Just do it.”

David Robson’s latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life. If you have a question that you would like answered in his column, please send him a message at davidrobson. me/contact

A stormy end to the weekend is in store for parts of the country with heavy rain, potentially severe gales, colder temperatures and widespread frosts forecast.

MetService has issued a heavy rain watch for the Wairoa District and strong wind watches for Taranaki, Wellington, the Marlborough Sounds and the Kaikōura Coast.

A low northeast of the country is directing an east to southeast flow onto the North Island today, before moving east on Sunday, allowing strong southerlies to spread across the country.

Wairoa District is under a heavy rain watch for the 24 hours from 3am tomorrow, with periods of heavy rain forecast and rainfall amounts potentially approaching warning criteria.

MetService said there was a moderate chance the watch would be upgraded to a warning.

Strong winds are also expected across parts of central New Zealand tomorrow.

Taranaki north of Hāwera and west of Whangamōmona is under a strong wind watch from 6am to 6pm tomorrow, with southeast winds potentially approaching severe gale in exposed places, mainly north of the mountain.

Wellington, the Marlborough Sounds and the Kaikōura Coast about and north of Clarence are under a strong wind watch from midnight tonight until midday tomorrow.

South to southeast winds may approach severe gale in exposed places.

Both wind watches have a moderate chance of being upgraded to warnings.

MetService meteorologist Devlin Lynden told the Herald the weather would start wet today before temperatures take a sharp dip.

“The big thing is it starts off wet and then is cold,” he said.

While heavy rain warnings have been lifted for eastern parts of the country, the North Island is expected to continue to see showers throughout today and tomorrow.

“There’s a low pressure sitting just north of the country at the moment and that is set to move eastward and in behind it a cold front moves up the South Island through Saturday and then into Sunday.”

Falling temperatures, particularly overnight, will accompany the system as it moves northwards.

“It looks like temperatures will really take a noticeable dip for the South Island, with many of those eastern areas really only getting highs in the single digits.”

Widespread frosts are forecast for tomorrow morning in Christchurch, Ashburton, Timaru, and Dunedin, as well as Twizel, Alexandra, Wanaka, and Queenstown.

The front will bring highs in the low teens to the upper part of the country tomorrow morning, dropping from this week’s earlier averages.

“We’ll see those cold temperatures and rain really push up through the North Island on Sunday,” Lynden said.

The coldest conditions will arrive overnight, with frosts expected to spread across central parts of the North Island on Monday.

Hamilton, Tokoroa, Rotorua, Taupō, and Taumarunui are among the areas forecast to wake up to frosty conditions.

While more settled weather will spread across many parts of the country heading into the working week, cold southerlies will keep temperatures low.

“The South Island continues clear, again it will be cold, perhaps some cloud about Southland and some of those eastern areas,” Lynden said.

“Temperatures are expected to stay low with fine spells for many areas but again perhaps some cloud pushing into the likes of Wellington, Wairarapa, and some of those eastern areas.”

Marina out, market square in: The changing face of Kaiapoi’s regeneration project

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Six years ago, a bold vision was promised for a North Canterbury earthquake red-zone site – a Kaiapoi riverside development with a marina at its heart.

The marina has since been abandoned and replaced by plans for a covered market square precinct, with the project repeatedly delayed by the challenges of developing the site.

And today, there is still no guarantee it will happen – the council has yet to decide whether it will sell the publicly owned land.

Senior journalist Anna Leask reports.

The 2.9ha site sits in the heart of Kaiapoi, beside the river and just east of the town’s main retail centre.

It was once home to residential housing before being red-zoned following the Canterbury earthquakes and acquired by Waimakariri District Council for future regeneration.

The site was later identified for mixed-use development through the Waimakariri Residential Red Zone Recovery Plan and Kaiapoi Town Centre Plan, with the vision of creating a vibrant new destination in the heart of the town.

In 2020, the council put the land to the market, inviting developers to pitch ideas that would help make Kaiapoi “New Zealand’s best river town”.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

Five proposals were received, and in 2021 a proposal from William Hill Consulting was selected, promising a mixed-use riverside development with a marina as a centrepiece.

A memorandum of understanding was signed between the council and developer later that year, formalising their relationship as the project moved into detailed due diligence, feasibility and planning.

But the MOU did not commit the council to sell the land – a distinction that remains crucial six years later.

In June 2023, the developer advised the marina component was not viable and an alternative proposal was put forward.

Documents provided to the Herald under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act outline why the marina was abandoned. The developer cited uncertainty over stopbank requirements, major engineering and approval hurdles, geotechnical and construction challenges, financial feasibility and opposition from Ngāi Tūāhuriri.

Technical reports commissioned during the feasibility process, including hydraulic flushing, topographical and geotechnical studies, supported those concerns. Preliminary discussions with Environment Canterbury, council engineers and Ngāi Tūāhuriri Rūnanga also highlighted significant challenges.

In September 2023, the council resolved to continue working with the developer after the marina concept was abandoned and, in its place, explore a proposal linking public amenities such as a market square with the stopbanks and existing town centre businesses.

The marina-centred development has since evolved into a proposal built around a covered market square, which the developer is pitching as a new community and riverside destination for Kaiapoi.

The council and developer subsequently amended their memorandum of understanding and continued working through an updated outline plan for the project.

In June 2024, the council adopted a further updated plan, giving the developer greater flexibility around the sequencing of its work while retaining milestones that ultimately had to be met.

Then, on June 2 this year, the council received its most recent update and considered several outstanding matters, including public spaces and community outcomes.

Documents provided to the Herald show councillors noted that “substantial work remained” before a final go/no-go decision on selling the land could be considered.

Staff then provided further direction to the developer, which continued design, feasibility and assessment work intended to inform a future council decision on whether to enter into a sale and purchase agreement.

A resource consent application was also progressing as the developer refined its plans.

But consent does not guarantee the project will go ahead – and the council has repeatedly stressed that the consenting process is separate from any decision about whether to sell the land.

“It is … important to note that the resource consent process is separate from any decision regarding the sale or divestment of the land. Progress in one process does not determine the outcome of the other,” said the summary document.

“The council has not yet decided whether it will/will not enter into arrangements regarding the South MUBA land with the developer. Any future decision will be based on whether the final proposal is considered suitable, is deliverable, aligns with the council’s strategic objectives and community expectations, and delivers appropriate value and outcomes for Kaiapoi and the wider district.

“This proposal is large and complex, especially considering land constraints, and investigations over recent years have led to the evolution of the development concept.”

The document said extensions and changes to the project plan “have been granted with good intent”.

“The council and developer are both seeking a positive outcome for Kaiapoi – one that will bring vibrancy and energy to the town centre and align with the aspirations of the Red Zone Recovery plan,” it said.

“A key objective for the council in approving any future proposal is that it supports and complements existing businesses and activities, providing confidence to existing property owners and businesses to invest further into the continuing post-earthquake development and success of the Kaiapoi town centre.”

William Hill Consulting commercial manager Mike Luck said he was “pleased” with the progress his team had made on the “significant” project.

“We are big believers in Kaiapoi,” he told the Herald.

“From the outset, we knew that transforming a former residential red zone site into a vibrant mixed-use destination would be a complex and long-term undertaking.

“There’s a lot to a proposal like this … Over time our understanding of the site has developed, and the proposal has evolved. Some elements of the original concept, including the marina, proved impractical due to significant engineering, geotechnical and flood-protection considerations.

“Rather than compromise the long-term success of the development, we have worked with the council to reshape the concept into one that better responds to the opportunities and constraints of the site.”

Luck said a “considerable amount of effort” had gone into the various redesigns to ensure it accommodated the council’s “requirements”.

“Our view is that these changes have strengthened the proposal and reinforced our commitment to delivering a development that is resilient, sustainable and integrated with the existing town centre and river environment,” he said.

“We remain excited by the opportunity to develop one of the most important regeneration sites in Kaiapoi. We believe this development has the potential to further enhance Kaiapoi’s already vibrant riverside attraction for people to live, work, shop and spend time in the town. We are particularly excited about bringing the Kaiapoi Market Square precinct to life.”

Luck acknowledged the square was worlds away from the original marina proposal – but he described it as “the heart of the development”.

“We are proposing an approximately 900 square metre covered canopy, designed as a community hub and all-weather destination,” he explained.

“The space has been carefully planned to accommodate community gatherings, markets, food vendors, seasonal events, live entertainment and public celebrations, creating a vibrant focal point where residents and visitors can come together throughout the year.”

Luck said the end goal was to deliver a site that “reflects the community’s aspirations, complements the unique character of Kaiapoi and provides lasting economic and social benefits for the wider district”.

“Success, for us, will be seeing this former red zone land transformed into a thriving central riverside precinct that future generations can enjoy and one that further enhances Kaiapoi’s reputation as one of New Zealand’s most attractive riverside towns,” he said.

Waimakariri Mayor Dan Gordon was also “pleased” with the project’s progress and was comfortable with the length of time it had taken so far.

“Projects of this scale and complexity often take longer than people would expect, particularly when they involve public land and significant community interest,” he said.

“The council has a responsibility to do the homework and carry out the necessary due diligence before making a major decision on behalf of the community. This project has also evolved over time as the developer responded to land and water constraints, and we’ve had to carefully assess those changes every step of the way.

“There’s still work to do, but we’re continuing to focus on achieving the best possible outcome for Kaiapoi and the wider district.”

Gordon said the site was “very significant” and he made no apologies for how long the design process took.

He was also clear that the development would not go ahead until he was sure it was the best option for the community.

“It’s a key piece of land in the heart of Kaiapoi, and both the Kaiapoi Town Centre Plan and Red Zone Recovery Plan recognise its potential to support the town’s long-term growth and revitalisation,” he said.

“Getting this site right is important for the future of the town centre and the council will only consider selling this land if we’re satisfied the project delivers real value and strong outcomes for Kaiapoi and the wider Waimakariri district.”

While Gordon was not making any formal promises about the future of the land, he was confident a successful development was in sight.

“We still have work to do and some important decisions ahead of us, but I believe we have an opportunity to create something that delivers lasting benefits for Kaiapoi,” he said.

“I’d like to see a high-quality development that brings people into the town centre, adds activity and vibrancy, and creates a place that residents can be proud of. Ultimately, it needs to reflect the community aspirations set out in the Kaiapoi Town Centre Plan and Red Zone Recovery Plan and contribute positively to the town’s future.

“A successful development could help strengthen the town centre, attract investment, create jobs, increase activity in the area, and provide new spaces and opportunities for businesses, residents and visitors. Most importantly, it can strengthen Kaiapoi’s identity as a thriving, attractive river town and give people even more reasons to live, work, visit and invest here.”

Gordon understood the community was “keen to see progress” but said council would not be rushed into a final decision on the development.

“The council has a responsibility to carefully consider all aspects of a proposal before making decisions about public land,” he said.

“We need to be confident that any development is deliverable, aligns with community expectations, and delivers the right outcomes over the long term. I’d rather take the time to get this right than rush a decision we’ll live with for decades.

“There are still assessments and processes underway, and councillors will need sufficient information before making any decision – including more clarity on resource consenting, for example. Councillors will decide when we’ve worked through the outstanding issues and have the information we need to make a confident, well-informed call.”

Gordon hoped that in the next five to 10 years the currently unusable site would become “a genuine community asset” that attracted people to the town centre, supported local business and gave residents “something they can be proud of”.

“I want future generations to look at the site and see an example of thoughtful regeneration that has delivered ongoing and lasting benefits for Kaiapoi and the wider Waimakariri district,” he said.

Despite the lengthy process the project still appears to have the backing of the community.

“Following the earthquakes, the community consistently expressed a desire to see the red-zone land used in a way that would create vibrancy, attract visitors and reconnect people with the river. While the original marina-centred proposal proved unfeasible due to the engineering, environmental and financial challenges involved, it is positive to see the vision evolve rather than stall altogether,” siad Enterprise North Canterbury business support manager Miles Dalton.

“We are supportive of the current market square-led proposal. A covered market precinct has the potential to create a unique destination for Kaiapoi, provide opportunities for small and emerging businesses, and further strengthen the town’s appeal as a place to visit, live and invest.”

Dalton said the project could also deliver substantial benefits for the wider town centre.

“Increased visitor numbers would create additional foot traffic for existing retailers, hospitality operators and service businesses, while also encouraging people to spend more time in Kaiapoi,” he said.

“Developments that complement rather than compete with the town centre are important, and this proposal has the potential to do exactly that.

“In terms of timing, everyone involved in post-earthquake recovery has learned that worthwhile projects often take longer than originally anticipated. While we would welcome certainty and progress whenever decisions are made, it is more important that the right outcome is achieved than a rushed one. If delivered successfully, this development has the potential to be a lasting asset for Kaiapoi, North Canterbury and the wider Canterbury region.”

The Kaiapoi-Tuahiwi Community Board also backed the development – but wanted to action on the site soon.

“The board is supportive of this project as it is the final part of the post-earthquake recovery which has transformed Kaiapoi,” said board chair Jackie Watson.

“So the board is also disappointed at the lack of progress.”

2020: After receiving several development approaches for the site, the council commenced a Request for Concept Proposals (RCP) process to test the market and identify potential development opportunities.

2021: A proposal from William Hill Consulting Limited was accepted, which included a marina component, as the preferred concept to progress to a more detailed due diligence, feasibility and viability assessment stage.

2023: The developer advised the council that it could no longer deliver the marina component of the proposal and wished to proceed with an alternative concept. Council later accepted an updated plan which recognised the change in concept.

2025: The developer applied for resource consent, noting while “key tasks” remained incomplete, it wanted to progress the plan “concurrently with the resource consent process”.

2026: Developer still undertaking design, feasibility and assessment work. The council provided “direction on issues relating to public spaces and community outcomes”, noting that substantial work remained before a final go/no-go decision to sell the land could be considered. The resource consent application is ongoing.

Diver David Casey sentenced for illegally gathering crayfish for Queenstown tourism experience

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

David Casey gathered crayfish as part of The Helicopter Line's heli crayfish experience. Photo / Supplied

A luxury helicopter and crayfish-gathering experience was marketed to tourists as showcasing “amazing fresh produce of New Zealand”.

But it has now led to Invercargill diver David Casey being fined $3750 for illegally gathering crayfish for a Queenstown helicopter company and a hotel when neither party held a permit.

According to the summary of facts, in May 2022 Casey was engaged by The Helicopter Line (THL) to provide diving services as part of its collaborative heli-crayfish experience with The Rees Hotel.

The experiences involved customers being flown from Queenstown to remote locations in Fiordland and Milford. In a promotional video by THL, it said while customers waited on a remote West Coast beach, a diver would be sent to “go and get your lunch”.

Upon landing, Casey would dive and take the maximum recreational limit of six crayfish, entertain the customers with facts about crayfish, allow them to take photos, then put the crayfish in a pod outside the helicopter.

“The diver will go in and get fresh crayfish, so it’s really about showcasing that amazing fresh produce of New Zealand,” the promotional video says.

The crayfish were then provided to The Rees Hotel for its dining service. Casey was paid $800 by THL each time.

THL charged for its services to the hotel at a cost of between $2541.50 and $4650.

Under the Fisheries Act 1996, any seafood used as part of a commercial business must be sourced under a valid commercial permit.

But during the relevant time, neither THL nor Casey had a permit or exemption to take crayfish for a commercial purpose.

In July 2022, THL provided a marketing heli-crayfish experience for a group of three people from The Rees Hotel at a cost of $2541.50.

The cost included Casey’s taking of the crayfish.

The chief executive of The Rees Hotel, Mark Rose, was also on the trip.

Upon returning to the hangar, the crayfish were removed from the helicopter’s external pod and placed in a chilly bin owned by THL.

The chilly bin was then given to Rose and the crayfish were used as part of a meal for eight hotel guests.

In a text exchange with the hotel’s agent, Casey replied to an image of the crayfish meal and said: “Can’t get any fresher than that.”

Fisheries New Zealand became aware of the activity in 2022 and warned the hotel it needed a permit. When this was not done, an investigation began and the Ministry for Primary Industries brought a prosecution.

It also brought charges against THL and The Rees Hotel.

The starting point for the charge against Casey was a $5000 fine.

Contact the Open Justice team

Yesterday, he appeared in Queenstown District Court via audio-visual link from Invercargill District Court for sentencing.

Judge Ali’imuamua Sandra Alofivae gave Casey a 15% discount for his early guilty plea.

“You knew what you were doing was wrong.

“I know you have a young family and work long hours and you’re doing your best to get by,” she said.

She also granted a 10% discount for personal circumstances.

That brought the fine down to $3750 which could be paid in increments.

In July 2025, The Rees Hotel was fined $22,000 for illegally selling recreationally caught crayfish and failing to keep proper records.

Company chief executive Mark Rose was discharged without conviction, while THL is still before the courts.

Brianna McIlraith is a Queenstown-based reporter for Open Justice covering courts in the lower South Island. She has been a journalist since 2018 and has had a strong interest in business and financial journalism.

Blood on the floor: Best and worst leadership coups and the ones that backfired

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

As Prime Ministers and other political leaders have found, the success or failure of a leadership coup isn't always obvious immediately.

Judgments on the success or failure of a leadership coup are sometimes best made with the benefit of time, suggests senior political correspondent Audrey Young, who has covered many of them over 30 years.

The least successful attempted coup in the past 30 years was the one against Helen Clark as Labour leader in 1996.

It failed to get rid of Clark and she went on to become the most successful Labour Prime Minister of the modern era and the second longest-serving Labour Prime Minister in history.

In that regard, it could be described as successfully unsuccessful.

Jenny Shipley’s coup to get rid of Jim Bolger in late 1997 was one of the most technically successful coups, having been hatched in complete secrecy while Bolger was overseas and requiring her supporters to put their names in writing. Maurice Williamson recounted on Newstalk ZB this week that he had to fax his support for Shipley to Wellington. Luckily, he faxed it to the right place or the cover for the “Te Puke Bypass” as the coup was code-named might have been blown.

But the political chaos that ensued for the two years following the coup was as great if not greater than those that it preceded. It led to instability and the Government was dumped at the 1999 election, for Clark’s Government.

After the unsuccessful attempt to muscle Clark out of the leadership, she had another three years of preparation.

On that morning of May 28, 1996, she famously prepared for a delegation of five MPs – Michael Cullen, Phil Goff, Jim Sutton, Annette King, Koro Wetere – who sought an appointment with her before a regular caucus meeting on a Tuesday at Parliament.

Anticipating that they would be putting pressure on her to step aside as leader, with polls as low as 15% with four months to go to the election, she quickly roped in five “witnesses” to the meeting, her former press secretary Mike Munro recounts in his recent book Ringside.

They were Clark loyalists David Caygill, Jonathan Hunt, Trevor Mallard, Steve Maharey and Judith Tizard. Clark stared down the visitors and told them they could move a leadership motion in her at caucus that day, but the motion never eventuated.

While it was never stated who should replace her, Cullen, in his memoir Labour Saving, says the only viable candidate at that point had been Mike Moore – the embittered former Labour leader whom Clark had rolled in a coup shortly after the 1993 election.

It was an unusual attempt to unseat the leadership in that there was no subterfuge, besides fairly consistent white-anting by Moore. It was a civilised invitation from senior MPs more in sorrow than in anger. And there was safety in numbers. Retribution would have been difficult.

Clark decided to draw the plotters closer to her orbit, assisted by the voluntary retirement of Caygill, her loyal deputy and finance spokesman. He was replaced by Cullen, who wrote in his book: ”Thus began a 12-and-a-half-year partnership of stability and mutual respect between Helen and me which saw us win three elections on the trot, something that Labour had not done since 1943.”

With the distance of time, it could easily be argued that the unsuccessful attempt to remove Helen Clark ultimately contributed to a successful Government, and the successful coup of Jenny Shipley’s failed in terms of improving National’s fortunes.

Perhaps the most successful nascent coups of the past 30 years were the ones against Don Brash as National leader in 2006 and against Andrew Little as Labour leader in 2017 because neither of them are remembered for being coups.

They weren’t coups in the classical sense of a vote being taken. But they were both resignations tendered with at least the possibility of a vote of no-confidence being taken against them.

Brash resigned in November and was replaced by John Key, who went on to win three elections and lead New Zealand as Prime Minister for eight years.

And after Grant Robertson and Chris Hipkins persuaded Little that he did not have the support of the caucus to continue in 2017, he resigned 54 days before the election in favour of Jacinda Ardern, who secured a role for Labour in Government for the next six years.

The turning point was when Labour’s Māori caucus, which had staunchly supported Little remaining, backed an offer to Kelvin Davis of being Ardern’s deputy.

Winston Peters was the kingmaker at the 2017 election, and some of us believe his New Zealand First party would have gone with Labour whether Little or Ardern were leader.

So long as the overall numbers added up, Labour gaining less support under Little would likely have meant an even stronger New Zealand First relative to a bigger party.

While Labour’s share of the vote increased under Ardern, the total combined vote for Labour, New Zealand First and the Greens was reshuffled rather than increasing substantially.

The initial sinking of support for Labour was a direct result of the speech by Greens co-leader Metiria Turei admitting to historical benefit fraud.

Such was the pile-on against Turei that Labour-left voters initially threw their support behind her and the Green Party, at the expense of Labour.

Nobody anticipated that a speech by Turei at the Green Party AGM about welfare would have resulted in Jacinda Ardern taking the leadership of Labour. But it did and, ironically in the circumstances, before Turei finally resigned, Ardern ruled her out as a minister in any Government she led.

The inept attempted coup against Prime Minister Christopher Luxon this week will obviously be classed as a failure because Luxon is still there and, in the short-term at least, is stronger than he was before the attempt.

Broader historical judgments about it should be reserved.

If, for argument’s sake, National’s polling plummeted to the mid-20s over two months on the back of disunity, and Luxon fell on his sword, the role of the failed coup might be rewritten.

More so if Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop or Erica Stanford took over at the last minute and led a recovery back to Government.

In another scenario, if Luxon’s personal ratings and party polling improved in the wake of what might be seen as a display of decisive leadership in dealing with the attempted coup, and he led National to a second term, the role of the failed coup would be seen in a different context.

Luxon sacked Chris Penk from Cabinet within hours of the emergency caucus on his leadership and Penk announced his retirement from politics within hours of his sacking.

It is debatable whether Penk, a popular MP, needed to retire – and to have done so swiftly was not particularly wise.

Perhaps he feared there would be moves to remove him as a candidate for Kaipara ki Mahurangi and/or remove him from the party – although party president Sylvia Wood tells me there was no thought given to either of those scenarios.

MPs have been punished for a lot less. Chris Carter was suspended from caucus and expelled from Labour in 2010 after being revealed as the person sending anonymous letters to the press gallery criticising Goff and suggesting others could do better. He was reinstated to the party in 2018.

Expulsion has not always been a punishment for disloyalty.

Maurice Williamson was suspended in July 2003 for publicly criticising leader Bill English, who had led the party to a disastrous election result the previous year.

I well remember covering the party’s annual conference at the Hotel Grand Chancellor in Christchurch and Williamson holding an entertaining stand-up with media in the foyer, comparing the party under English to the Titanic.

Williamson: “I’m yelling: Will somebody tell the orchestra to shut up? Will everybody get up on deck and man the lifeboats.”

After Don Brash took over the National leadership in October 2003, he brokered a deal with the board to end the suspension. It involved Williamson writing to the board with expressions of contrition.

Brash took the leadership from English after a novel sort of coup run in part by political operative Matthew Hooton, who is now editor-in-chief of The Post. It was like no other coup before it because his challenge was announced by public declaration at a press conference at the Tamaki Yacht Club.

Despite claims by some that it was inept, because there had been a lot of humming and haa-ing about whether to challenge, the result suggests it was highly successful.

On the basis of votes promised, English was confident he would win. But rumours emerged that when the secret vote was counted, the vote was tied, and that one of the whips who was a scrutineer decided to change his vote to Brash to break the deadlock, knowing that a tied vote would be as damaging for English as a loss.

Brash won and then came within a whisker of toppling the Labour Government at the 2005 election. But party insiders reported that while Brash’s leadership looked like a rough ride from the outside, it was worse on the inside, and that he would be given only one shot at leading the Government, not another in 2008.

He was given the dignity to step down in 2006, to be replaced by John Key, but if he hadn’t resigned, he would have been ousted. Key won in 2008 and Labour was back in Opposition with Helen Clark anointing Phil Goff as her successor. No contest was held but the pressures built up, particularly in Labour’s second term in Opposition, after David Shearer replaced Phil Goff.

One of the most unusual long-running coups took place within Labour, with the party’s ruling New Zealand Council and former president Moira Coatsworth having a big role in replacing Shearer with David Cunliffe.

Shearer had beaten Cunliffe in the caucus vote in 2011, after Goff stepped down. The New Zealand Council, many of whom supported Cunliffe, played a big role in supporting constitutional rule changes that removed the sole right of caucus to elect leaders. It gave the unions and members a vote as well.

Under pressure from poor performance, Shearer stepped down a year out from the 2014 election and Cunliffe was elected under the new rules. But pointedly, Cunliffe did not win the caucus vote.

Key presided over a great period of stability for National. The next National coup did not happen until 2020, in Opposition, when Todd Muller challenged Simon Bridges.

The vote on Bridges’ leadership was called quickly, not unlike the vote Luxon called this week with a day’s notice. Hooton, a commentator at the time and supporter of Muller, said Bridges had made a fatal error in calling the vote and that Muller’s supporters would have lost their nerve if Bridges hadn’t called the vote.

Former party president Michelle Boag thought it was a mistake to have called a vote so quickly. She thought that if it had been timed for the following week, more contenders other than Muller would have joined the contest and Bridges might have survived.

The leadership challenge was initially successful but what may have looked like sweet success for critics of Bridges turned to disaster.

Muller lasted only 53 days before having a mental breakdown and being forced to resign. Judith Collins reluctantly replaced him.

And a year after her poor election result, and with divisions still rife in the caucus, rumours of an impending coup by Bridges drove her to overplay her hand. She issued a late-night statement demoting Bridges for an apparently bad-taste joke he had made five years earlier, and for which he apologised at the time. It was an inexplicable action and the last straw for a leader who was fast losing support.

The caucus moved a no-confidence in her the next morning with no alternative stated. It was enough to get rid of her.

Over time, she rehabilitated herself in both the Opposition and as a respected minister in the current Government. She retired earlier this year to become President of the Law Commission.

Chris Penk was given most of her former portfolios.

After Collins’ demise as leader in 2021, the next step was to elect a new leadership team, the main choices being to give Bridges a second chance, or to elect someone who had been there only a year, namely Christopher Luxon.

He united the party in Opposition but has not been as successful as Prime Minister, having now survived two confidence votes in his leadership in four months.

Luxon leadership coup: Why surviving the confidence vote is only a reprieve – Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Chris Penk’s military career – officer of the watch on HMNZS Te Kaha and a submariner in the Australian Navy – ought to have steeled him for the darker arts of politics.

Particularly, equipping him with the strategic nous on how to launch an attack with military precision.

But the chain of command, if it ever existed, broke before the target could be annihilated.

Former Act MP and lawyer Stephen Franks put it this way: “I suspect Chris Penk was encouraged to ‘go over the top’ first by colleagues vowing to be right behind him, only to find himself effectively unaccompanied as he forged into no man’s land.

“I know what it feels like to look around to find your allies and backers cowering anonymously in the trenches or even standing beside your common opponent, pointing you out for the artillery,” he wrote on X.

Franks is right on the money.

It is fatuous to believe Penk’s initiative was a solo kamikaze raid and that perceptive journalists such as the Herald’s Thomas Coughlan could write up such a storm to provoke the Prime Minister into calling yet another vote of confidence in his leadership without a great deal of priming right across Parliament.

Luxon survived the coup hands down.

His praetorian guard of Cabinet ministers Mark Mitchell, Louise Upston, Todd McClay and Paul Goldsmith circled the wagons effectively.

Mitchell is the key operator here. He comes across as an affable political teddy bear but anyone who has operated as a major security contractor in Iraq knows their way around how to protect and ensure the survival of a high-value asset when crossing a battlefield.

The second confidence vote in four months is, however, a warning sign.

Luxon survived because National MPs ultimately concluded that changing leaders 87 days before an election was more dangerous than sticking with him.

Smart call.

The coup has again exposed internal divisions.

Advice to top-ranking ministers Chris Bishop and Erica Stanford – learn how to dissemble and fast.

Photos of the pair bracketing Luxon on Wednesday at his Banquet Hall “press conference” were unconvincing. Bishop with his sideways glance looking credulously at the Prime Minister and Stanford poker-faced.

Talk at several business-related events in Auckland this week varied between “a change of National’s leadership would have been galvanising” to “why can’t they put their own egos aside and focus on the election?”

Business expects better leadership.

More references to Luxon having the “full support” of his colleagues just remind voters of the problem.

And here’s another thing: Luxon needs to make it absolutely clear that coalition partners can disagree, but Cabinet cannot freelance.

That does not mean humiliating New Zealand First leader Winston Peters nor Act leader David Seymour, both of whom have ably served as his Deputy Prime Minister within the coalition Government.

For instance, the problem isn’t that Peters disagrees with Luxon. That’s inevitable under MMP.

The problem is when voters cannot tell which statement represents Government policy. He cannot simply sack Peters without potentially detonating the coalition.

But he can establish protocols around foreign policy: what is Government policy, what is party policy, and what is an individual minister expressing as personal political opinion.

Luxon’s proposal for another referendum on MMP appears to have surprised National colleagues and provoked an immediate reaction from Peters.

If Luxon’s strategic objective is to retain the coalition, campaigning against the electoral system that makes coalition government possible is an extraordinary distraction. It looks like a Prime Minister blaming the system for his difficulty managing the people elected under it.

It may be too late to bring Seymour and Peters into a private “no surprises” pact where they agree no public surprises on major Government policy, no public undermining of another coalition leader or minister and where disputes are settled privately before they become media events.

The existing coalition agreements already recognise that the Government consists of National, Act and New Zealand First. The missing ingredient is political discipline.

The Prime Minister now has 12 weeks to change the narrative from: can Luxon survive? to what has the Government actually achieved and what will it achieve if the coalition returns for a second term?

That means a ruthlessly narrow campaign: economic recovery, infrastructure, productivity, investment, energy security, law and order, health and cost of living.

Every day spent discussing coups, MMP, “numpties”, coalition tensions or leadership succession is a day the Opposition gets to define the election.

For the Prime Minister the hardest lessons to swallow are on his operating style.

The recent troubles have been about judgment.

The MMP announcement was unexpected. The comments about business leaders caused another backlash. The coalition relationships have repeatedly become public. And now there have been two leadership challenges.

That means fewer spontaneous interventions and considerably more consultation before major announcements.

In business, a CEO can win by being decisive. In coalition politics, decisiveness without consultation can look like arrogance.

The bigger strategic point Luxon should understand is what happened on August 12 was a reprieve, not a victory. The MPs who didn’t roll him have effectively said: we don’t want to change horses three months before an election.

They have not necessarily said: we have complete confidence that Christopher Luxon is the leader who can win it.

The paradox is that the best way for Luxon to demonstrate that he has survived the coup is to stop behaving like a Prime Minister who has something to prove.
