From the battlefield to the ballot: NZSAS veteran Josh Jacobsen stands for Green Party

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

Former NZSAS lance corporal Josh Jacobsen - now a Green Party candidate - pictured in Afghanistan and (inset) receiving the NZ Gallantry Medal from Governor General, Sir Jerry Mateparae, in 2014.

Josh Jacobsen served with elite fighting force the NZSAS during the Afghanistan war, placing him close to Operation Burnham and the 2011 raid in which Lance Corporal Leon Smith was killed. And now he’s standing for the Green Party. David Fisher reports.

Meet the Green Party Candidate for North Shore. Also meet Lance Corporal J, recipient of the NZ Gallantry Medal.

And meet the NZSAS soldier who ran into a battlefield to try to save his mate, Lance Corporal Leon Smith, who died in Afghanistan on September 28, 2011.

Josh Jacobsen, 40, knew he had a tough sell when he went through the Green Party selection process. Wearing a navy blue suit and light blue shirt, he tells the Herald: “I knew I didn’t look like a lot of Green Party MPs”.

It seemed best to hit that upfront. He says he told them: “I have the face, bearing and background of an AI-generated right-wing voter.”

Then he laid out the vision that led to his selection as a candidate - placed at 25 on the party list.

It’s far enough down the list that Jacobsen is unlikely to need to surrender his day job as a software engineer to enter Parliament in November.

But if he does, he could be the first New Zealand MP to have fought for New Zealand since the World War II generation.

Either way, Jacobsen is intent on further raising the Green Party vote – from 6.6% in 2017 to 8.3% in 2020 and 11.7% in 2023 – in a National Party stronghold.

Born in Whakatāne, Jacobsen spent part of his childhood in Glenfield before his parents – both teachers, although his dad retrained as an engineer – moved the family to Papua New Guinea when he was 7. They lived near Madang for six years, where he alternated between correspondence and local schooling and grew up around the physical remnants of World War II.

Returning to New Zealand for high school in Dunedin was a culture shock. School never fitted easily and, with a long-held ambition to join the military, Jacobsen went to a recruiting office at 16.

“One of the things that really appealed to me was service. How are you going to serve your country?”

He wanted the Army and, eventually, the NZSAS, but knew better than to announce that. “I said I wanted to be a carpenter. You don’t want to walk into recruiting and say, ‘I want to be in the SAS’.”

The Army was not recruiting carpenters or riflemen. Then Jacobsen noticed a photograph of a Navy diver on the wall.

“I want to be a diver,” he told the recruiter.

He was too young for that trade, so he joined the Navy through logistics, boarding a Hercules that collected recruits around the country before delivering them to Auckland and the Devonport naval base.

“That was when the yelling started.”

In the years following, Jacobsen turned 18 and did the NZ Defence Force diving course and deployed with the frigate, HMNZS Te Kaha.

At age 20, he attempted selection for the NZSAS – the notoriously gruelling 10-day process designed to test candidates physically, mentally and socially under sustained stress.

Amid endurance tests and long marches carrying heavy loads, food is restricted and sleep reduced as candidates approach the final stages that include a long navigation march. “The whole idea is to leave you alone with the voices in your head and see what those voices say.”

Jacobsen was caught short with land navigation skills – a core infantry rather than sailor’s skill. With Navy mentor support, he returned a year later and passed.

Jacobsen first went to Afghanistan in 2010. “As a soldier, we wanted to be deployed. We wanted to go and put into action the skills we had been taught. And I think everyone who joins wants to help people. You want to serve your country.”

Jacobsen is clearly uncomfortable speaking about himself, and particularly about his time in the NZSAS. The elite regiment has – as a core tenet – the embrace of humility.

Jacobsen recalls one of the NZSAS training staff gathering soldiers one evening and saying: “If you are looking for glory, you are in the wrong place. No one will ever know what you’ve done. When the moment of celebration comes and the party’s being thrown, you’ll come and take your cake and then you’ll go and eat it in the dark.”

Politics can encourage the exact opposite approach. This causes Jacobsen intense discomfort. “This isn’t about me and this isn’t about talking up myself or what I’ve done. I’m here because I want to see Green kaupapa, Green values, make it into policy to enrich the lives of everyone who lives in this country. The last thing I want to be doing is talking about myself.”

Jacobsen is reluctant to speak in detail about his service in Afghanistan. Elements can be discerned in the recent book, Keep Calm - We Are Coming, in which historian lawyer Rob Crosby details four selected missions in the war-torn country.

Jacobsen’s second deployment to Afghanistan took place in the latter half of 2011, during which the Regiment lost two of its members. The deployment consisted of around 40 people, including support staff.

The first casualty was Corporal Douglas Grant at the British Council battle in Kabul. In his book, Crosby describes Jacobsen among four soldiers who fought through heavy fire to help create an extraction route, then took part in the rescue of three British civilians trapped inside the compound.

During the operation, Jacobsen and two others shielded the civilians with their bodies as they moved them to safety. Returning to the building, the soldiers were metres away when an insurgent detonated a suicide vest. The blast injured several men and left Jacobsen concussed.

Leon Smith was among those who ran to help. Six weeks later, their positions were reversed, with a tragic outcome.

Sparse detail is available about the firefight in which Smith was killed. The regiment, along with the Afghan Crisis Response Unit (CRU), was approaching a compound in Wardak province, west of Kabul.

Jacobsen recalls Smith having gone forward with the CRU team the NZSAS was mentoring, while he was a little further back with another unit of Afghan soldiers. “And then I heard gunfire – a lot of it. And then I heard, ‘man down’.”

Jacobsen recognised the voice in his earpiece and knew who that soldier was partnered with. He knew it was Smith who had been hit.

Jacobsen was one of three medics and the closest one to Smith. He was later awarded the NZ Gallantry Medal as “Lance Corporal J” for what followed.

The medal citation records how he “dashed across the open ground firing in the direction of the insurgents as he ran”.

Jacobsen: “I knew [the gunfire] was coming and where it was coming from. But my mate needed a hand.

“I could see Leon lying by the doorway. I moved down, grabbed him and dragged him out of the way.”

Having recovered Smith from the worst of the danger, Jacobsen moved through the life-saving steps drilled into troopers in training. “I’m trying to talk to him, let him know I was there and he was going to be alright.”

While doing so, he’s calling for support. Smith was lifted to a stretcher and then to a helicopter. And then Jacobsen turned back to the fight. “You’ve still got a job to do.” Part of that job, as the citation records, was treating a wounded insurgent.

It was later, back at the NZSAS base, that the impact began to register. The urgency of the fight had passed, Smith had died and the surviving troopers were back together.

Jacobsen remembers looking at another soldier and the two embracing. “At that point, you start to feel the pain.”

The possibility of losing someone was always there, he says, but so was the bond between them. “I knew if I needed help, these guys will run through bullets for me.”

Jacobsen applied to officer cadet school after returning from Afghanistan but also considered taking a break. It turned out to be easier to do so by disengaging from the military.

He planned to join again but time passed, he finished his degree in defence studies then travelled. He spent time studying at a university in the United States where he met his wife – whom he has asked the Herald not to name – then in South America and Africa where he embraced learning languages, scratching an itch that began with Pashto in Kabul.

When his wife moved to Jordan, Jacobsen followed. The Syrian war was approaching its height. Jacobsen’s experience landed him work with the United Nations, including roles that took him inside Gaza around the time military action by Israel saw thousands killed and a humanitarian crisis that stretched into 2015 and beyond.

Gaza was incredibly affecting. It was an experience, like Afghanistan, that asked the question: “How do we avoid getting here in the first place?”

On return to New Zealand in 2016, Jacobsen rejoined the Naval reserve and considered returning fulltime. “I’d been out of it for a long time and I was starting to think more about how do I make a difference long term.”

When visiting other countries, Jacobsen would study their histories to better understand the world he was entering. He realised he didn’t have the same grasp on New Zealand’s history.

“A lot of our history is pretty f***ed. People say, ‘what radicalised you’. It was reading. There are some problems here – how do I get involved?

“I really believe we all need a purpose. We all have things to contribute. The worst thing you can say to someone is ‘you’re not needed, you’re not useful’.”

Jacobsen popped up in 2019, involved in a petition – after the March 15 terror attack in Christchurch – seeking a ban of semi-automatic weapons. He knew weapons well and, with friends “on both sides” of the debate, felt he could use his background and experience to better inform it.

There was also the inquiry into Operation Burnham, the 2010 raid in Afghanistan that was the focus of allegations in the book Hit & Run. It alleged the raid was revenge for Kiwi troops killed in Bamiyan and alleged NZSAS actions killed civilians, including a child, and that NZDF covered up what had happened.

Jacobsen’s hesitancy to discuss his service with the NZSAS means he will not acknowledge being part of the raid.

The Green Party pushed strongly for the inquiry at the time. While Jacobsen won’t be drawn on details, he says there will be no future surprises for the Greens: “I was upfront with everybody through the process.”

The inquiry report offered no criticism to the soldiers on the ground over the incident, finding five civilians, including a child, were killed by a United States Apache helicopter gunship with faulty sights.

It did expose bungling in command that led to multiple Ministers of Defence being misinformed over the civilian deaths. As Jacobsen puts it: “It acknowledged that the actions of the people on the ground was in keeping with what New Zealanders would expect of the Defence Force.” That, he says, is good for New Zealand to see.

For Jacobsen, the return to New Zealand and personal connection to political issues became an awakening, of sorts. “As I engaged with the history of New Zealand, I looked at the political world as it is in New Zealand and thought, here’s what I believe and the Green Party is the place I see those values expressed.”

There was a strong appeal in the Green Party stance on Palestine. “That’s brave and that’s principled and that’s what I want for our political leaders. That tipped me from voting for the Greens to joining the Greens.”

Having joined the party, Jacobsen looked for work and became co-chair of the North Shore electorate in which he lives, and then a candidate.

He will talk local issues – protecting the Hauraki Gulf and the need for improved access to ferry services to relieve the Lake Rd crawl of 22,000 vehicles a day – and big picture policy. He’s a fan of ground-up economic reform, and is enthusiastic about workers’ co-operatives and union membership.

“Coming back to New Zealand, I thought, I see the New Zealand I grew up in and I see the New Zealand that shaped me and I think we’re losing that.”

Neo-liberal economics, as Jacobsen describes the past 40 years of New Zealand’s direction, erodes the ties that bind the nation together.

“If you make money, you can be less reliant on other people around you. The problem with that is it then becomes about buying someone else’s service rather than that service being given through the ties of mutual obligation.”

He spoke earlier about how his grandad, fresh from Norway, built the family home in Glenfield. He worked with others to do so, and then helped others build their own homes.

Jacobsen says he has a strong policy interest in defence which includes the pay and conditions of military personnel and others in service roles, such as firefighters and police.

“We look at firefighters and what they’re going through at the moment. They’re fighting for decent pay and conditions. They’re fighting to be looked after by the country in recognition of what they’ve given.”

He entered the military, he says, to serve New Zealand. Politicians are in the same role, he says, “to serve all New Zealanders”. Part of that service, which he considers missing, is accountability.

“Now we look around [and we see] record numbers of businesses going under, record homelessness, record number of children living in poverty.

“I think everyone deserves a good shot at life, regardless of where you’re born, who your parents are, what your start was. You deserve the chance to live life and live out your potential.”

The aspect of politics Jacobsen is finding he has embraced is talking to people. That’s how he started learning Pashto in Afghanistan, and other languages as he travelled.

And as people talk, they work each other out and begin to understand each other’s issues and perspectives.

To the people of North Shore, he says: “Come have a yarn.” He’s happy to talk about anything.

Well, almost anything.

David Fisher is based in Northland and has worked as a journalist for more than 30 years, winning multiple journalism awards including being twice named Reporter of the Year and being selected as one of a small number of Wolfson Press Fellows to Wolfson College, Cambridge. He first joined the Herald in 2004.

Hastings Rottweiler attack: ‘I’m going to die here’

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

Sophie Greer and her 10-month-old cavoodle Lottie were attacked by a Rottweiler while walking in the new reserve across from the dog park in Pākōwhai Rd, Hastings.

WARNING: This article contains a distressing image further down the story.

A Hastings woman who felt the teeth of a roaming Rottweiler sink into her thought she was going to die when she saw a second dog approaching.

Sophie Greer was walking her family dog, 10-month-old cavoodle Lottie, on a reserve opposite the Pākōwhai Regional Park on Friday, July 24, about 9.40am when an unrestrained dog with no owner in sight approached them.

Lottie was on the lead, and Greer said she turned and let her sniff the dog.

Greer, a nurse, said the dog immediately began trying to “dominate” Lottie, so she went to pick her up.

“The dog started jumping up at me, attempting to get to Lottie.”

Greer felt her hand get bitten.

“I was screaming for help and yelling, ‘Your dog’s biting me’.”

The dog reared onto its hind legs on her right side, so she turned her back to it. It then moved to her left and grabbed the back of her arm.

“I felt those teeth sink into my upper arm, and I was like, oh my God, it’s just broken my arm.

“At the next jump it got Lottie’s tail and yanked her. I went down too because I knew, if I let her go, she’d be mauled. She’s only like 7 or 8kg max.”

Greer, still holding Lottie, managed to get to her knees.

“Then the dog grabbed Lottie’s back leg, and that’s when he just tore her.”

She said she spotted a man coming towards her at the same time as she saw another unrestrained Rottweiler approaching.

“He was on his way, but he was only walking.

“Then I was like, oh my God, he’s got another Rottweiler with him. I’m going to die here.

“I’m getting mauled, and if this other dog joins in, and there’s no one else around and this owner does not look like he cares.”

As the owner got closer, he started yelling at the dog to “get off,” but he didn’t get physically involved, she said.

The owner apologised to her as she got to her feet.

“I told him I needed help, but he just walked away over the hill and disappeared.”

She was left alone with bites to her hand and the back of her arm, holding Lottie, who had a tear from her groin to halfway along her stomach and puncture wounds to her leg.

She called her husband, telling him to pick up Lottie and take her to a vet.

“I didn’t really know what to do about myself, but my husband told me to call an ambulance so I could describe where I was.”

Her left upper arm had a deep wound that needed stitches, but she said the injury to her hand, although more superficial, was the most painful. She was also covered in bruises.

Lottie had 17 stitches to a T-bone-shaped wound. The treatment cost about $2000, with a further $400 in ongoing costs expected.

Considering her injuries, Lottie was doing well, Greer said.

If she could talk to the Rottweiler owner, she would ask him to “do the right thing” and hand his dog to the authorities.

“You know your dog is dangerous.

“It’s just a matter of time until this happens again.

“It’s frightening to think this could happen to a child or an elderly person. I’m a 38-year-old woman who could fight.”

She did not think she could face going back to the reserve or the Pākōwhai Regional Park again.

She reported the incident to Hastings District Council and police.

The council said Animal Control contacted Greer on the day of the attack to check on her welfare and took a victim statement from her three days later.

“Animal Control ranged the area and looked for any businesses with CCTV cameras covering the road.

“Police were contacted to advise them of the Animal Control investigation, which is continuing.”

Council regulatory solutions manager John Payne said the Animal Control team responded to reports across the district, but officers could not patrol every street around the clock.

“We understand people can become frustrated when they see a roaming dog, but Animal Control can’t be everywhere 24 hours a day.

“We rely on the community to report incidents promptly and provide good information so our officers have the best chance of locating the dog.”

The end of winter and early spring was a common time for dogs to roam, particularly around lambing time, nd owners needed to be vigilant, he said.

Even dogs that were usually well-behaved could become a danger if allowed to roam.

“A dog that’s allowed to run free is going to behave in line with its instincts – to hunt and chase. That’s why it’s so important to keep dogs properly restrained.”

The Rottweiler owner had not been found at the time of publication.

LDR is local body journalism co-funded by RNZ and NZ On Air.

$2b Mill Rd: See all 287 Auckland properties being bought by taxpayers for project now on ice

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

The ability to gift paywall-free articles is a subscriber only benefit. See more offers by clicking the button below.

Reminder, this is a Premium article and requires a subscription to read.

Auckland’s multibillion-dollar four-lane Mill Rd highway could be on the rocks — but the Government has been moving to buy land faster than ever. Search the Herald’s exclusive map to see the status of 287 properties - those bought in full, those partially bought and those in the Government’s sights.

It’s been talked about for two decades, has no start date, no money for construction and, according to some commentators, was as good as cancelled by the Government last month.

But moves to take land for South Auckland’s four-lane Mill Rd highway have accelerated this year, the Herald can reveal – uprooting families and throwing lives into turmoil for those whose homes are in the project’s path.

Almost half the 287 properties required for the project’s first stage received formal paperwork in 2026, land records show.

That included 95 private owners getting notice the Crown wants at least some of their land, and 56 compensation deals being signed.

The Crown has snapped up at least 14 whole properties – home and land – direct from owners since June last year, after doing just two deals in the previous four years, according to public records.

Government planners said 68 of the 73 full blocks of land needed had now been taken into Crown control, and $131 million had been spent buying property since mid-2020.

Despite the recent rush, the Government last month cast uncertainty over when – and perhaps if – building work on the road would start.

“As funding becomes available, these projects can progress to construction,” Transport Minister Chris Bishop said on July 9 about Mill Rd stage 1, without indicating when the cash might be put up.

Labour said Bishop’s comments meant Mill Rd and other Roads of National Significance were now on a “wishlist” rather than a firm timeline.

The Herald’s political editor opined that the delayed road was “as good as cancelled”.

Meanwhile, scores of families have been moved out, others are still negotiating, and tenants say they don’t know when they will be told to leave.

South Auckland councillor Daniel Newman said the Mill and Redoubt Rd families had lived in a “state of miserable uncertainty for years”, and it was “beyond depressing” to again be waiting on a road with no start date.

Redoubt Rd homeowner Taro Joy said he’d lost his tenants during negotiations with property agents for the NZ Transport Agency (NZTA).

He’d been hopeful of hearing back on a final price from the agency over the strip of land it wants to take from his property.

Then the Government deferred the road again, and the phone line has gone quiet – heaping more uncertainty on him, he said.

Proposed as an alternate 21.5km, four-lane highway, starting at Manukau and running parallel to the traffic-jammed Southern Motorway, the project has been on the drawing board since at least 2008.

Now the Herald’s exclusive interactive map can help you make sense of where it’s at after almost two decades.

Red on the map is land already owned by the Crown – 68 properties, most purchased years ago by Auckland Transport for the project and later transferred to the Crown.

Orange shows properties where public records indicate a deal done for a strip of land – like a piece of driveway – but the owner is staying put.

Pink blocks are properties where the Crown has given notice to the owners, but the records don’t yet show if the full block or just a piece of it is required by the Government.

You can also look at the map’s legend, or click on an individual property to see its current status.

The National Party campaigned at the last election on beginning to build a number of what it called Roads of National Significance, within its first term in power.

That included the first stage of the Mill Rd highway.

It said the project would cut traffic congestion on the route by 30%, reduce deaths and injuries from crashes, and support 120,000 people moving into the growing area of South Auckland.

Last year, it committed $91m to finishing design work on the first stage.

Then last month, the Government back-pedalled, admitting its build programme had been ambitious. Mill Rd was caught in the reshuffle.

The project’s first stage was classified as being in a “pre-implementation” phase.

That involved “route protection” with “focused property acquisition” and detailed design works.

But construction would only begin when funding was available, while the second and third stages of the project would be “continuing more slowly”.

Bishop said the announcement provided certainty and financial responsibility.

“This pipeline demonstrates that we have struck the right balance with our ambitious and responsible transport programme,” he said, citing rising construction costs.

Herald political editor Thomas Coughlan, however, said the announcement meant the road was cancelled again.

July’s announcement is the latest lurch in a prolonged cycle of promise and postponement for the road – spanning multiple governments.

The Manukau City Council first sketched the route as early as 2008, telling owners construction was “at least 10 years away”.

By 2013, the project’s first stage had a $246m price tag.

Contact senior reporter Ben Leahy

In 2016, Auckland Transport won planning approval for the first stage, about four years after the Crown had bought the first homes for the project.

National promised $1 billion towards the project and ran into the 2017 election vowing to build it.

After taking control of the Government, Labour mocked National’s unfunded roading promises as “ghost roads” – then funded Mill Rd anyway: earmarking $1.35b in 2020, for a 2022 construction start date.

A year later they scrapped it amid ballooning costs.

In opposition, National MP Simeon Brown called Labour’s scaled-back rethink “dithering” – before taking over the Transport Ministry in the new coalition Government, which arrived promising to get building.

Now estimated costs for Mill Rd’s first stage have risen to between $1.75b and $2.05b.

By April last year, Bishop had taken over the Transport Ministry and announced $91m for project design work, saying construction could begin “as early as mid-2026” – and that by 2031, drivers on the corridor would enjoy “25% faster journey times”.

High on Redoubt Rd hill with a view to Rangitoto, Taro Joy’s home sits in a “beautiful place”.

He bought in 2017 and lived there for years, before moving to Australia.

It’s now split into three units.

But the strip of land the Government wants has led to empty rooms and a nine-month fight over the price, rather than a steady home and income, Joy told the Herald.

The upstairs tenants left within a fortnight of the Crown’s notice arriving last year.

The flat has been vacant since.

He said the Crown first offered a price based on what he called old information that didn’t take into account the new units.

He pushed back, insisting a valuer visit in person, but claims that took six weeks.

The back-and-forth had dragged the negotiation out nine months, he said. “Every step I’ve had to fight.”

Joy feared that even if a deal to buy his land was struck, further delays and construction might stretch on for a further 10 to 15 years.

“It’s come to a point where this has just gotten to ridiculous proportions, and I can’t move on.”

The Herald spoke to other owners in negotiations for a buyout, or who had lost a home, but didn’t want to talk on the record.

One family bought on a side street off Redoubt Rd and later found out their home was in the project’s path.

They responded by demolishing their own house and rebuilding a new one further back on their section.

It’s meant they could remain on the land, with the Crown taking the front strip of their block while the neighbouring homes have been bought out.

It was incredibly stressful, they told the Herald.

With the NZTA now a major landlord along the route, renters are also affected.

One tenant said he told his daughter to sell her chooks because the family don’t know when they will be ordered out and need to be ready.

Despite the uncertainty, nearly everyone the Herald spoke to agreed the new roadway should be built.

Councillor Newman said the Mill Rd corridor was “vital” because the adjacent Southern Motorway was so jammed at peak hour it was a “car park”.

Newman said the jams added up to lost economic productivity and the Government needed to “get on and do it”.

An NZTA spokeswoman said stage one of the project was in the pre-implementation phase, with work continuing on design, consenting and supporting activities.

“We will provide directly affected landowners further updates when these are available.“

She said the agency acknowledged a notice could “create uncertainty for affected property owners”.

“However, a designation does not prevent people from continuing to own, use, buy or sell their property.”

Missing war medals: Napier family heirlooms found after near 20-year mystery

New Zealand Herald August 14, 2026

Joan Patten holds a picture of her uncle Leonard Clarence Shepherd and his war medals she found after a near 20-year search. Photo / Jack Riddell

A Napier woman thought she’d never see her uncle’s war medals again.

Nearly 20 years later, a museum tip led her to a British auction house, and sure enough, she’d found the trail that would lead her to them.

Joan Patten grew up with her uncle’s war medals on her grandmother’s mantelpiece in Levin.

The medals belonged to Leonard Clarence Shepherd, a World War II pilot with No 218 (Gold Coast) Squadron, Royal Air Force.

On December 17, 1942, Shepherd and his six crew were shot down between Texel Island and the Netherlands mainland. None survived.

Patten had traced the route of her uncle’s final flight in what she believes was a Short Sterling bomber, one of the first heavy four-engine bombers.

“They didn’t stand a chance in those bombers from what I can tell,” she said of the crash.

For his war effort, Shepherd’s family were posthumously sent a War Medal, an Air Crew Europe Star, the Defence Medal, the 1939-45 Star and the New Zealand Memorial Cross.

After Patten’s grandmother died, Shepherd’s medals went to her father, who kept them in a drawer.

In 2005, Joan and her husband, John Patten, were about to take an overseas trip for several years.

Before they left, Joan’s father asked if she would visit Shepherd’s grave in Bergen op Zoom, an area in the southwest of the Netherlands, and if she could look after the medals after his death.

Two weeks after Joan left New Zealand, her father died.

She returned for the funeral and was offered the medals but refused, concerned about taking them on her travels, though she wanted to care for them when she returned to New Zealand.

However, when Joan and John returned in 2007, the medals were gone.

“We just had no clues where they were,” she said.

When Joan Patten’s mother died a few years later, the family cleared out her home but found no sign of Shepherd’s medals.

“It always was in the back of my mind that they must be somewhere,” Patten said.

When one of Patten’s sisters died in 2024, John was looking through photos when he found a picture of the medals.

Joan suspected the medals had gone to a collector.

“Everybody was telling me I haven’t got a hope in a snowball’s chance of finding them.”

She went to multiple Returned and Services Associations (RSAs), police, and her local MP, none of whom could help.

“I thought I’d have one more go,” she said.

She got in touch with Linda Fletcher at the Levin RSA, who said she’d try to help with the search.

Several weeks later, Joan and John were with friends at a winery when Fletcher rang.

She had traced the medals by cross-referencing official service history to Noonens Mayfair, a London auction house where they had been sold five weeks earlier.

“Sounds very posh, doesn’t it?” Joan said.

Patten reached out to the auctioneers, explaining her situation and asking if the buyer could be approached to buy the medals back.

Two weeks later, the auction house emailed her to say she could buy the medals back. “I couldn’t believe it.”

Contact Jack Riddell

On Monday, July 21, the family heirloom Joan Patten had spent nearly 20 years trying to find arrived at her home.

She said she felt relief holding the medals in her hands.

The medals arenow on display in her home, and she said she looked forward to wearing them to the Taradale RSA next Anzac Day.

She hoped her story would inspire others to find their family’s missing medals.

“Keep searching,” she said.

The last time Patten visited Shepherd’s grave in 2023, she told him the medals had gone missing under her watch.

Since then, she has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s and isn’t sure if she’ll get back to Bergen op Zoom to tell him they are safe with her.

“It’ll be up to someone else.”

Jack Riddell is a multimedia journalist with Hawke’s Bay Today and has worked in radio and media in Britain, Germany, and New Zealand.

Before he was Anthony Bourdain, he was a ‘young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking’

Sydney Morning Herald August 15, 2026

Dominic Sessa stars in Tony, a film about the making of the man and myth that was Anthony Bourdain.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In Sydney, in Melbourne, in Boston and New York, haloed murals of “Saint Tony” – the beloved chef, writer and TV personality Anthony Bourdain – pay tribute to his rebellious spirit and moral integrity. On Instagram and Reddit threads, fans cite his quotes like ancient scriptures that hold the meaning of life: “Your body is not a temple, it’s an amusement park. Enjoy the ride.”

After his tragic death in June 2018, aged 61, Bourdain’s mythical pull has only intensified. It’s amusing then that, in the face of such reverence, A24’s new film Tony beckons cinemagoers with an unsuspecting whisper: You love Anthony Bourdain? Come, let us tell you the story about when he was a young piece of crap.

Dominic Sessa laughs mischievously at my summation. Before making the film, he couldn’t have picked Bourdain in a police lineup, anyway.

“I know he means something important to so many people, but for me, I wasn’t a huge fan. He didn’t exist in my life the way he does for millions of people. And that was the reason I felt comfortable doing it,” says Sessa of taking on the role of a man who, even from the beyond, remains a daily household fixture in reruns of his hit TV series, No Reservations and Parts Unknown.

Tony is a film that could be subtitled “Bourdain: The Incel Years”. It takes the early chapters of Bourdain’s bestselling 2000 book Kitchen Confidential – mainly his evocative telling of absconding at 19 to Provincetown, off Cape Cod, where his kitchen journey began – and crafts an affecting coming-of-age tale.

When we first meet Sessa’s Bourdain, he’s bloviating to college literary professors about his plans to update Orwell’s Down and Out in Paris and London. He stalks bars with a pair of nunchucks in his pants, hitting on sorority girls and bartenders with uncomfortable desperation. Painfully insecure, he lies and lies and lies. With the notch turned up slightly, he’d be Rick from The Young Ones.

You’d imagine this was an odd invention from writer-director Matt Johnson (in Johnson’s hands, even Bourdain’s infamous oyster awakening gets twisted towards shame), if it wasn’t all there in Bourdain’s own writing. From the beginning of his public profile, Bourdain never hid his demons and was quick to self-scrutiny. An “insider’s edition” of Kitchen Confidential, released in 2013 and featuring scribbled footnotes from the author, finds Bourdain furiously taking the piss out of sentences he’d written just over a decade before, fed up by a tone he now saw as pompous and self-important.

The film revels in that disposition – the man on the way to the man – taking as its starting gun a quote from the same book where Bourdain summed up his own youthful (un)appeal. “I was a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive, and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking.”

In a culture struggling to salvage young men from the clutches of toxic masculinity, it’s a loaded launch. After #MeToo, Bourdain apologised for how Kitchen Confidential – full as it was with fighting and f—ing, as much as food – might have contributed to the era’s “boys will be boys” permissiveness.

But in the film, he’s still a young scrub in search of a role model, latching onto mentors both bad (Leo Woodall’s drug-abusing, womanising line cook Sal) and good (Antonio Banderas’ wizened, zen-like Chef). For Sessa, this was the appropriate entry point.

“I can’t relate to the Bourdain everyone knows, this guy who is writing novels and working in kitchens in a professional sense, but I can relate to being an impressionable young person with pessimistic views on the world and a sense of entitlement. I know what that feels like,” he says.

“For the first time in his life, he saw like, ‘Wow, I can live my life this way? I can party and drink and do drugs and have sex and also make incredible food at the same time?’ It was in that excitement, at that moment of being opened up to this, where this person was formed.”

Sessa is speaking over Zoom from high above the Los Angeles skyline, in the office headquarters of film distribution darling, A24. The sun is beaming in LA, but with his mussy hair and sunken eyes – a ’70s character actor out of time – Sessa looks exhausted. Deep into the film’s press campaign, he’s been answering the same inane questions about his cooking skills for days. Well, he’s not getting a reprieve from me. How are his cooking skills now?

“About the same,” he says. “I mean, I can shuck an oyster and I can sauté some vegetables. I know how to make a paella now, thanks to Antonio Banderas. Not an incredibly difficult thing, but it feels good. And I know how to hold a knife a little bit better, which is encouraging.”

At 23, Sessa is only marginally older than Bourdain was when he took up the dishwashing job that set the path to his life in food. Born in New Jersey to a teacher mother and a father who worked in payroll (his father died when Sessa was 14), in tenth grade he earned a scholarship to the elite boarding school Deerfield Academy in Massachusetts to play ice hockey. When he broke his femur before his first season, he shifted his interest towards drama classes. He was still at school when he landed his first professional role in Alexander Payne’s The Holdovers, where he held his own against prime Paul Giamatti.

“In the same way that Tony is in the movie, I’ve felt myself role-playing some sort of version of myself that I thought I had to be in order to be respected,” says Sessa. “When I was in high school, I put a lot of pressure on myself to seem smart and capable. But it wasn’t until I started acting that I was like, ‘Oh, I actually could be good at this in real life, not just in my head.’

“That’s sort of the moment that Bourdain is having in this movie. For so much of it he’s telling people, ‘I’m good at writing, I’m going to be the next great American novelist’, but he has nothing to show for it. And then he has this experience working in a kitchen where he actually does something and gets better at it. He learns how to make a Lobster Thermidor! I think that’s pretty relatable for people. When you’re able to work with integrity and honesty, it changes your life. It happened for me and it happened for Bourdain, and I hope it encourages people to participate in voluntary hardships.”

Before Tony started shooting, Sessa did a brief placement in a Brooklyn bistro to learn the kitchen environment. Much of the film’s authenticity, however, comes from the cast’s rakish camaraderie.

“We didn’t have that much time [filming], but when we were in Provincetown that’s where we really bonded,” Sessa recalls. “Leo would do barbecues. He had a really cool house that he rented in Cape Cod with a backyard and a grill, so every weekend we would just go to his place and have a barbecue, drink some beers, enjoy the summer.”

The film’s other star is Provincetown, those seaside streets where Bourdain walked and worked. In Kitchen Confidential, Bourdain wrote about the town evocatively as a Portuguese fishing community turned “pirate colony”, a home to burnouts, stoners, hippies and freaks. Sessa says there are still people living in the community who remembered Bourdain, and were eager to share their smallest interactions with him.

“A few of the restaurants he worked at are still there and operating. The pizza shop in the movie, Spiritus Pizza, the same family owns that place and they all remember him because he used to sleep above that place during the summers,” says Sessa.

“Another is a restaurant called Ciro and Sal’s, owned by the Luster Brothers. These guys are younger than Bourdain but they worked with him when he was the same age as me, early 20s, working in the kitchen, washing dishes, trying to cook. They told us endless stories. But, I mean, a lot of the stuff we couldn’t really utilise because it was too graphic,” Sessa adds with a laugh. As ever, Bourdain’s spirit lives on.

Tony is in cinemas from August 20.

John Howard neutralised Pauline Hanson 30 years ago. What’s changed since then?

Sydney Morning Herald August 15, 2026

The recent surge in One Nation’s support has echoes of its original 1990s political insurgency – but there are reasons why its vote might hold up this time.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Who are we becoming as a nation? The question of our political identity as voters had a simple answer before Pauline Hanson finally cracked the populist code in 2026, after almost three decades on the electoral fringe.

Before this year, Australia’s democracy was defined by the absence of extremism. Liberal prime ministers sat consistently to the centre-left of their Conservative and Republican peers in Britain and the US, while Labor’s were to the centre-right of British Labour and less ideological than the US Democrats.

The flipside of our gold coin of moderation was the leaders and parties that Australians rejected. The Liberals lost winnable elections when they imported American agendas, to deregulate the workplace or to wind back Medicare, as John Howard learnt twice, from opposition in 1987 and in the defeat of his government in 2007. Labor failed when it tried to redistribute income, most recently under Bill Shorten in 2019.

Our system of compulsory preferential voting had reinforced our egalitarian and obedient national temperament by pulling the major parties towards the centre while creating a barrier to entry to those on the hard right.

So what changed this year to elevate One Nation above the Coalition and up to level-pegging with Labor in the national opinion polls? How did One Nation suddenly break out of its Queensland-centred political identity to seize its first House of Representatives seat at the byelection for Farrer, in southern NSW, and come within a single win of claiming the formal opposition from the Liberals in South Australia, the state traditionally considered one of our most socially progressive?

All this before the Victorian showdown in November, where the polls, if they are to be believed, point to the first three-way contest since the early years of federation when the establishment side of politics was represented by two competing Liberal parties, the Protectionists and the Free Traders, while the trade union-backed Labor was the rising political force on the left.

Understanding Hanson’s late career surge, and the implications for both our politics and our sense of self as a nation, starts with a reminder of her role as an electoral wrecking ball in the late 1990s, when she threatened Howard’s first-term Coalition government. For Howard, Hanson was an accident waiting to happen. Liberal Party pollster and strategist Mark Textor explained it to me long after her insurgency had passed into political history: “Why did Hanson flatfoot Howard? Because Howard, after attacking Paul Keating from the right, was being attacked from the right.”

Hanson had caught the anti-incumbent wave that wiped out the Keating Labor government in 1996. Preselected by the Liberal Party to run for the safe Labor seat of Oxley, south-west of Brisbane, she had her endorsement withdrawn after she ignored repeated warnings to tone down her comments to the media. She said, among other things, that the government had created racism “by looking after Aborigines too much”. Howard said her removal from the Liberal team proved that his party would “govern for all Australians”.

Howard assumed the seat was unwinnable, so the gesture was aimed more at seats, like his own Sydney electorate of Bennelong, which were diverse and socially progressive. Hanson, though, won regardless. While she sat in parliament as an independent, she posed no obvious threat to Howard’s landslide majority. The Coalition held 94 of the 148 seats in the Parliament. But that changed from the moment Hanson launched her One Nation party in 1997.

Hanson drew her initial support mainly from Coalition voters in regional Queensland and NSW. Then-PM Howard thought he could retrieve those votes through the distribution of preferences, so he treated her supporters as his own. But that approach risked the Liberal Party’s standing in the cities. Many of his colleagues, including then-treasurer Peter Costello and then-foreign affairs minister Alexander Downer, had urged him to denounce Hanson from the outset.

Howard’s great fortune as prime minister was seeing the Coalition lose the Queensland state election in June 1998. That campaign served as a crash test for his plan to treat Hanson as a fellow political traveller, with the Liberals and Nationals placing One Nation ahead of Labor on their how-to-vote cards.

The Queensland state parliament was particularly vulnerable to a hostile takeover. The main parties were tied at 44 seats each, with the sole independent, Liz Cunningham, providing her support to the Coalition led by the Nationals’ Rob Borbidge. Hanson was not a candidate at the state election, but she was treated like visiting royalty as she toured the state. Her anti-establishment message inspired Queenslanders to cast a system-shaking protest vote. Her One Nation party claimed 11 seats, five from the Nationals and six from the Peter Beattie-led Labor opposition.

Hanson’s 11 seats would have held the balance of power if the Liberal vote hadn’t collapsed. The Liberals, the junior partner in the Coalition, lost six seats to Labor: four in Brisbane and one in each of the coastal cities of Cairns and Townsville. This left Labor with the same number as it started, 44. The Nationals lost a further seat to the independent Peter Wellington, reducing the Coalition total to just 32. It was Wellington who provided the vote that made Beattie premier.

When Howard and his advisers processed the Queensland result, they confronted a stark political choice between the blue-collar males who had abandoned Labor at the 1996 federal election and the traditional Liberal middle-class base. Should they continue to chase the battlers in the regions as they swung from Labor to the Coalition and ultimately to One Nation, or double back to the suburbs? By chance, there were two unresolved policy questions that sat between the two constituencies. Howard’s 10-point plan to restrict native title following the High Court’s Wik decision remained stalled in the Senate. He could follow up on his threat of a double-dissolution election and run a culture-war campaign with race at its heart, or he could run a tax reform campaign centred on a 10 per cent goods and services tax.

The question answered itself. A race-based campaign would elevate Hanson to equal status with Howard and risk a repeat of the Queensland catastrophe. The GST would cut her out of the debate.

Textor said the goal was to “repolarise” the electorate into a traditional left-versus-right contest on the economy. “We had to refocus the agenda on an economic agenda, not Hanson’s fragmented social agenda. You couldn’t just do that by having a normal economic plan. You had to have what the movie-makers would call ‘a bit of tension’ in there.

“And that was the intuition of John Howard. He said [the GST] gave his pollster a heart attack, and it certainly did for a while. But it had enough tension to take the [focus] off Pauline Hanson’s social debate and move the tension into an economic debate, which was much safer territory for Howard given that he was a former treasurer and knew the stuff intimately.”

Howard reached back to the examples of Bob Hawke and Paul Keating to save his first-term government. By showing both sides of the budget – the national interest sacrifice represented by the GST and the reform bonus of personal tax cuts – Howard gave voters the respect they had grown accustomed to under the previous Labor government. Textor said: “What we decided to do was not sell the detail of the policy but sell the fact that the policy represented true leadership, which was reflecting the best part of the Keating years and the Hawke years.”

At the 1998 election, Kim Beazley’s Labor opposition needed to pick up 26 seats to form majority government. It fell just eight seats short of that improbable target, claiming 17 from the Coalition as well as Oxley from Hanson. The third-party vote was 20.4 per cent, then the largest of the postwar era. One Nation accounted for almost half of that – 8.4 per cent – but it was left without a seat in the House of Representatives. Hanson had moved from Oxley to contest the new seat of Blair, west of Brisbane. She recorded the highest primary vote – 36 per cent – but the Liberal candidate, Cameron Thompson, overtook her with preferences from the Labor and National parties. The One Nation Senate vote was a fraction higher at 9 per cent, but it delivered just one senator in Queensland. The Australian Democrats had 8.5 per cent of the vote but won four spots, giving them the balance of power in the upper house. That was the difference placing One Nation last on how-to-vote cards had made to the Parliament: Hanson became a one-term MP and her party had no leverage in the Senate.

The unique circumstances of the 2001 election cut Hanson out of the debate again, even though this campaign was fought on her preferred ground of immigration. Howard’s so-called Pacific Solution, which prevented asylum seekers from landing in Australia, restored the government’s electoral support after a difficult start to the year. The Tampa episode on its own may not have been sufficient to ensure the government’s re-election with an increased majority. But in confluence with the September 11 attacks on the US and the deployment of Australian troops to Afghanistan, it allowed Howard to use border protection to repolarise the electorate to the Coalition’s advantage.

Hanson complained that Howard had pinched her ideas, but he had no reason to engage in this argument. Voters tend to rally around the incumbent when they perceive an external threat. After the election, Howard told me that “we have seen off our Le Pen”, referring to Jean-Marie Le Pen, founder of France’s far-right National Front party.

Hanson’s return to the political stage in 2016, as a senator, was wedged between two populist earthquakes: the British vote to leave the European Union and Donald Trump’s election as US president. If there was a Brexit-style backlash brewing against immigration, Hanson would have reflected it in her party’s vote. But One Nation’s constituency in 2016 was half the size of its previous peak. The primary vote in the Senate was 4.3 per cent, compared to 9 per cent in 1998.

In fact, the 2016 federal election made history in the other direction, because this was the first to be decided by New Australia, at the cultural tipping point when those born overseas or with one migrant parent were about to claim the majority of the population. Chinese Australians were “without a doubt” the difference between majority and minority government for Malcolm Turnbull, according to Paul Erickson, who was the ALP’s assistant national secretary for the 2016 campaign. Labor lost the Chinese-Australian vote again in 2019, a crucial and under-reported factor in Scott Morrison’s “miracle” election win.

Nothing in Pauline Hanson’s first nine years as a senator between 2016 and 2025 hinted at what was to come in her 10th. The clue, instead, was in her party’s foundation – because there is a remarkable symmetry in One Nation’s resurgence in South Australia in March this year with its stunning debut at the Queensland state election of 1998.

The primary vote for One Nation was almost identical: 22.9 per cent in SA in 2026 and 22.7 per cent in Queensland in 1998. The difference was the SA vote broke more cleanly for the incumbent Labor Party along the city-country divide. Peter Malinauskas’ government picked up five seats from the Liberals in Adelaide and lost none the other way to secure a second-term landslide, with 34 of the 47 seats in the SA parliament. The key to this victory was the capital: Labor won 32 of Adelaide’s 33 seats, but just two of the 14 in the rest of the state. The Liberals lost a further six seats outside Adelaide: three to One Nation and three to independents. This left the Liberals with just five seats. One Nation won four seats in total, one from an independent, while independents also finished with four seats.

The result mirrored Labor’s federal triumph last year, when Anthony Albanese’s government won 94 of the 150 seats in the Parliament. Sixty-four of those seats were in the capital cities, based on the boundaries used in the Australian Electoral Commission’s results maps. The Liberals, by contrast, were reduced to just six capital city seats: three in the whitest parts of Sydney and one each in Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth.

The Liberal Party’s review into the 2025 election contained a telling admission that nothing had been learnt from the autopsy of their previous defeat. “Our observations about the election results are consistent with those made after the 2022 federal election; foremost, that the Liberal Party continues to lose support to key voter demographics and in metropolitan Australia.”

The party’s standing with young people, women and multicultural Australians remained concerning, with the “multicultural problem appear[ing] to outweigh the gender problem”. The party’s “capacity to thoughtlessly offend groups, including the Chinese” cost them seats in Melbourne and Sydney that they should have saved. Repeating a finding from 2022, the review said: “It is undeniably true that no party in Australia can expect to win government without holding a substantial share of metropolitan seats.” That lesson applies equally to One Nation.

History repeats, first as the GST, then as negative gearing. Howard had ruled out a GST before the 1996 election, declaring it would “never, ever” be Liberal policy again after the John Hewson-led opposition had lost the so-called unloseable election in 1993. Albanese made the equivalent commitment to preserve the negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions for property investors during his successful 2022 and 2025 campaigns, after voters had twice rejected Labor’s plan to scrap them in 2016 and 2019. Where Howard asked the electorate for permission to bring the GST back from the policy grave, the Albanese government’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax will be old news at the next election, which is due in 2028.

The tax reforms introduced in Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ May budget and passed into law before Parliament went on its winter break are aimed predominantly at urban voters – another echo of Howard’s GST. The difference is that the Liberals are not a serious part of the three-way contest, while One Nation continues to cannibalise the Coalition base in the regions. Echoing Howard, Albanese and Chalmers want to repolarise the electorate into a centre-left versus hard-right contest on the economy.

The thinking, which has been detailed to me by a number of Labor sources, is that the step-up in One Nation’s support comes from two distinct sections of the electorate. The first, which Labor has no realistic prospect of competing for, are former Coalition voters in the regions who no longer believe their old team can win the next election. The second are Labor voters in the outer suburbs and provincial centres who see Hanson as a convenient means to smash the system.

On the evidence so far in 2026, Australia is creating a multi-party system with Labor as the establishment party in the cities in competition with the Greens to its progressive left and the teals to its small-l liberal right, and One Nation as the regional insurgent in competition with the Liberals, Nationals and independents to its left.

This is the paradox of Hanson’s late career surge. She hasn’t suddenly joined the mainstream. Rather, she is exploiting the collapse of the two-party system, mainly at the expense of the Liberal and National parties. The nation at large is more diverse, and more urbanised than it was 30 years ago. Hanson is relevant today only because the party of Robert Menzies, Malcolm Fraser and John Howard has forgotten the secret of its postwar success that built an electoral bridge between city and country.

This is an adapted extract from Three Shocks by George Megalogenis (Penguin Random House), out on August 18.

Liane Moriarty’s new book is nearly here – but first, she wants women to read these three sentences

Sydney Morning Herald August 15, 2026

The latest novel by the queen of “domestic noir” revisits her most captivating characters a decade later – but Australia’s most successful living author has something else on her mind.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

I have arranged to meet Liane Moriarty at the Mosman library. This sounds straightforward, but when I arrive – miraculously 20 minutes early – my phone tells me I’m actually at the Barry O’Keefe Library. Barry O’Keefe?! Have I given the world-famous, 25-million-copy-selling author the wrong library name? Is she standing, at this moment, outside some other council building, cursing my name? Alas, even if she is, there’s nothing I can do about it. Her publishing PR is in Italy, and no journalist gets access to the mobile number of a 25-million-copy-selling megastar.

I scuttle up the nearest concrete ramp to the door, which – wave of relief – is labelled Mosman Library, while on the left is a plaque to Barry O’Keefe, who was, it turns out, a long-time mayor of Mosman (and, it seems, an energetic donor of water features to the municipality). Inside, with 15 minutes to spare, it suddenly seems like a good idea to apply for a library card. I’ve just completed the online form when I spot Liane Moriarty beyond the entry doors, sitting on a low wall. She is three minutes early. I listen to the nice librarian’s mercifully brief explanation about using the returns slot, then rush back down the ramp.

“This ramp!” says Liane Moriarty. She appears exactly as she did 10 years ago, when I first interviewed her, before the publication of Truly Madly Guilty, her seventh adult novel: pale skin, blue eyes, lovely voice. As has always been the case, there’s no hint in her appearance of Moriarty’s capacity to command the forces of novelistic evil. The central tension of all Moriarty stories is their balance between hidden horror – domestic violence, abuse, even murder – and the sunny, funny minutiae of ordinary, middle-class life. But in person, the sunniness prevails – a proof that art does not always imitate life.

Today, she’s wearing a greeny-turquoise dress and a black cardigan, a small sapphire pendant around her neck. Her fair hair is still, as it was a decade ago, reassuringly non-blow-dried, and she’s wearing flat black pumps. “I came here for an event years ago and I had heels on,” she says as we head back up towards Barry’s plaque. “And I couldn’t get up this ramp: the slope was too steep. The publicist had to grab my hands and pull me.” She holds her arms out like a mountaineer, roped to a rescuer on the slopes of Everest.

The mountain analogy is a good one for Liane Moriarty, because her literary career has been a process of scaling peak after peak – a whole mountain range of success – that no other Australian novelist has ever reached. She is the only fiction writer from this country to debut at number one on The New York Times bestseller list – not to mention the only one to have three novels reach number one on this same list, and the only one to have three books on it simultaneously. All 11 of her novels have been optioned for the screen, as has a 2026 short story called The Price of Honey. Four have been made into streaming series.

Financially, she has also been wildly successful. She is acknowledged as Australia’s highest-earning living novelist: her books alone have made her, by conservative estimates, more than $50 million, and her screen earnings have netted an unknown number of millions more. The first time I met her she’d just bought a beautiful home in Pymble in northern Sydney; now she reportedly lives in Mosman, in an extraordinary-sounding house with panoramic views of Balmoral beach, a koi pool and, according to the sales figure in 2023, a $19 million-plus price tag.

A good portion of this house was probably paid for by the most successful of her works, both on screen and on the page: the smash hit Big Little Lies, about a handful of school mums grappling with kids and partners, as well as domestic violence and murder, on Sydney’s northern beaches. The two-series HBO production, set in California, starred Nicole Kidman, Reese Witherspoon, Laura Dern and Meryl Streep – and, for that matter, Alexander Skarsgård, Shailene Woodley, Adam Scott and Zoë Kravitz: a line-up of star power that illustrates Moriarty’s ability to create entire ensemble casts of star-worthy characters. Series one of Big Little Lies won eight Emmys and was among the most successful limited-run prestige dramas of the decade.

Now she’s done it again. Big Little Truths is the sequel to Big Little Lies. Published in Australia on August 25, it will also return as a third series for HBO, with Nicole Kidman and Reese Witherspoon as executive producers. Ten years have passed, and the same school mums are now heading perilously into their 50s; their kids, meanwhile, are teenagers, captivating and terrifying in equal measure. There’s high-school angst, a history project, a severed finger. Most of all, there’s Moriarty’s lovely authorial voice, funny and kind, subversive and dark.

This voice hasn’t changed in the past decade, and neither, it seems, has Moriarty. The first time we met, I was surprised by her modesty, her genuine lack of interest in being a famous person. Since then, she’s entered a whole new league of publishing power and success, but here at the library, none of that is evident. She’s only mildly interested in finding Moriarty in the “M” section of Fiction (copies of Nine Perfect Strangers, Apples Never Fall and The Last Anniversary) and totally unconcerned that none of her children’s book series (written under the name L. M. Moriarty) appear on the shelves at all.

They’ve probably been borrowed, I suggest.

“Or perhaps they don’t stock them,” she says, matter-of-factly.

I tell her I’ve just got myself a library card. “Really?” she says. Now she looks genuinely pleased, even excited. “What a good idea. Let’s find you some books.”

The first recorded sighting of Liane Moriarty writing a book was by her mother, Diane Moriarty. “I remember when Liane was eight, she was sitting on the front steps and Bernie [Liane’s late father] said, ‘What are you doing?’ ” she recalls. “And Liane looked up at him and said, ‘I’m writing a story.’ She had a tiny little notebook in her hand, and a pencil.”

Diane credits Bernie – a surveyor specialising in aerial photography – with providing the crucial early elements for literary success: a wildly enthusiastic readership, plus an excellent royalties deal. “Bernie was so excited,” she remembers. “He was beside himself. He leapt up and flew for his camera. He said, ‘If I buy you an exercise book, would you fill it with a whole story? I will pay you a dollar for it and that means I’m commissioning you. That’s a big word for you.’ ”

Liane remembered the word and fulfilled the commission, as she has fulfilled every one since. “Liane hits every deadline,” says her US editor Amy Einhorn. “And I mean every deadline.” And that exercise book – featuring a sweeping saga about The Joneses, now lost to posterity – was the first step on her road to stardom.

Right from the beginning, she was happy in many literary genres. As well as her novels, when she was in second grade, she wrote a fictional play with 30-odd roles in it: one for each member of her class. Every single child turned up at her house after school to play their part. “I think what the kids these days would say is that she had Big Sister Energy,” says Jaclyn Moriarty (second-oldest among the Moriarty siblings). “She had this kind of vivaciousness; this sense of being thrilled by the possibility of life, that was completely infectious.”

There was, it seems, no limit to her powers. “When she was 10 and I was 8, she invented a boyfriend named Monty Carlo,” Jaclyn recalls. “She would climb out of the window at nighttime to go and meet him. She made him a complete, comprehensive, complex character: he was pretty swashbuckling for a 10-year-old. And I remember thinking, ‘Could this be real? I mean, Monte Carlo is the same name as the biscuit. But that could just be a coincidence.’ ”

Liane is the eldest of six Moriarty children – five girls and a boy – and their collective childhood sounds like a storybook itself: siblings as far as the eye could see; 40-odd foster babies cared for by Diane Moriarty; a dad who returned from overseas work assignments with wild tales of near-aeronautical death. The Moriartys had no TV, and every day was packed with stories – spoken, written, performed – for anyone who would listen.

“I remember our family dinners,” says Katrina Harrington (third-oldest sister). “Everybody sat down, everyone talked – ‘What have we got to share? What’s something funny? Who can get a word in?’ Then cups of tea, everyone still chatting, kids cleaning up while Mum and Dad stayed at the table talking. I remember being in year 12 and hating the fact I had to leave to go and study.”

No wonder 50 per cent of those children became professional novelists. Three sisters, three novelists, one superstar. How does that play out? “I’ve definitely felt added pressure, and professional envy,” says Nicola Moriarty, youngest sibling, who is the bestselling author of seven novels (and the original Nicola Berry in Liane’s kids’ books: 25-year-old Liane created the character as a 10th birthday present). “On the one hand, there are readers who will draw the direct comparison between us – that can be really hard. But conversely, I don’t like it if somebody tells me, ‘Oh, I like your writing better.’ Then I feel quite protective: ‘What do you mean? That’s my sister!’ ”

“When people ask me if I’m jealous I get confused,” says Jaclyn Moriarty (bestselling and award-winning author of 19 novels). “Because I think, ‘Liane wrote those books – I couldn’t write those books.’ Writing only works if you’re true to yourself: I can only write what’s right for me. And also –” she laughs, “I make my living as a writer, and I’m published all over the world, and that is beyond my wildest dreams. It would be absurd for me to go around being bitter.”

Jaclyn was actually the first published author in the family: it was her initial book deal that galvanised Liane. “I was in my [marketing director’s] office, with my shoulder pads, in North Ryde, thinking I was pretty good, and [Jaci] rang,” Liane explained to me when we first met. “I was excited for her … [But there was also] the other feeling – sheer rage! No, no [not really]. But definitely disappointment with myself, that I hadn’t done it and she had.” Three years and a master’s in creative writing later, Liane published her first novel, Three Wishes – about, of all things, three sisters. Since then, her own novels (including Big Little Truths) take the family total to 37. “Every book on the top shelf of my bookshelf is a Moriarty,” says Diane Moriarty. “Every time I walk by it, I go crazy with pride.”

To be honest, I was a bit worried about taking Liane Moriarty to a library. What if she was bored? What if she was mobbed? In fact, the opposite occurs: she seems totally at home among the books and the grey carpet squares and the community events pin-up boards; and no one so much as glances in her direction. You could get a library card, too, I suggest as she combs the shelves. She shakes her head. “I get sent so many books from publishers,” she says apologetically. “I just wouldn’t get the chance to read them.” She looks around almost wistfully. “I was trying to think of some anecdotes to tell you about this library,” she says. “And I remembered that when I was really young I lived near here, and I came in once when I was heartbroken, and borrowed every single book by Elizabeth Berg. I read them one by one, and by the time I’d finished them, my heart was healed.”

There are no Elizabeth Berg books on the shelves today, but Moriarty oversees my choice of Frances Whiting and Bonnie Garmus. Both these women are bestselling authors – though not quite in Moriarty’s league, of course. “Well, it’s very hard to think of anyone who is in her league,” points out Fiona Inglis, her agent. “She now has 53 translation territories, which I’m sure is some kind of record.”

Moriarty’s success, says Inglis, has forged a new path for female authors both in Australia and overseas. “Liane kind of invented ‘domestic noir’,” she remarks, “and there are now a lot of people writing in that space. It’s aspirational: ‘If she can do it, we can do it.’” Young female authors, she goes on, are now being seen by editors who might previously have dismissed them. “I shamelessly spruik the fact that I represent her,” Inglis says. “And she’s such a big name, publishers go, ‘Oh, you represent Liane. Maybe it’s worth having a look.’ ”

That being said, “being super famous doesn’t come naturally to Liane. She finds it awkward to have the light shining on her. But she does know what she wants. She’s never strident, she’s just firm.” When she was writing the (unpublished) novella the showrunners used as a basis for the second season of Big Little Lies, Inglis discovered that Moriarty had changed one of the character’s names to Mary Louise, and made her English. “And I said, ‘Oh my god, you’re so clever, you’re going to be able to get Judi Dench or Helen Mirren to do that role!’ And Liane said, ‘No. I’ve called her Mary Louise because that’s Meryl Streep’s real name. That’s who I want.’” And that, of course, is who she got.

These opposing qualities – profound confidence, modest diffidence – seem contradictory, but of course they’re not: it’s possible to be both self-assured and also genuinely humble. “Oh yes,” says Jaclyn. “She’s very low-key. But she’s also brilliant at giving advice. I mean that in the best possible way. She doesn’t just do that thing you’re supposed to do of listening and nodding and waiting for the person to figure out their own answer. She listens very kindly, and then she says, ‘OK. This is what you should do.’ ”

Today, en route to lunch, she asks me carefully all about my life. This is rare enough in an interview subject – usually, of course, the questions go all the other way – but then she tells me decidedly that I should 1) write a book, 2) on the (genius) subject of x, 3) with the (brilliant) title of y. Then we arrive at the cafe, and she hesitates about the extravagance of ordering a green juice to go with her soup.

Speaking of food, she admits that the meals on her upcoming book tour have been worrying her. Or rather, the lack of meals. “The publishing PR is trying to get me hotels with 24-hour room service,” she says apologetically. “It’s so embarrassing, but often you’re doing an event at night, and you come back to the room afterwards, and you just want dinner.” At one breakfast event, all the guests were sitting at tables and the authors had to move every five minutes and repeat a little spiel about their books, “as if we were selling Tupperware. The guests were eating their croissants, having a lovely time, and we got nothing. I became quite hysterical. I thought, ‘I cannot tell another person how I got the idea for this book.’ ”

She got the idea for Big Little Truths, as it happens, when she was thinking about an entirely different novel, set in a high school, and then suddenly thought, “Oh. I could give this story to my women.” By “my women”, of course, she means the sextet of stars in Big Little Lies. But in Big Little Truths, the new stars are their high-school-aged kids.

In real life, Moriarty’s own children are also now in high school. She met her husband, Adam, when she was 37, and they had their son and daughter, George and Anna, via IVF. He runs the house, she writes the books – slowly at first, struggling to face the horror of the blank page. Some days, she admits, “I can’t even bring myself to open the document.” She’s tried programs that turn off her internet; podcasts about meditating (“I nod along, I think a lot of profound thoughts; I totally believe in it”); even – Jaclyn’s suggestion – a sticker chart. “I think, in the end, I’m always trying to write the way I wrote when I was a little girl,” she concludes, “when it was as easy as riding my bike: ‘Now I ride my bike, now I write a story.’ Just entertaining myself. Just having fun.”

The pleasure – and pain – of childhood still feels close to Moriarty: her writing about children of all ages has always been filled with love. “She totally adores kids,” agrees one of her old friends, Marisa Colonna, who met her 35 years ago. “I think she would have loved to have twins or triplets: I just told her my niece is pregnant with twins and she was like, ‘I’m so jealous!’ ”

“I miss little kids desperately,” Moriarty agrees. “And babies. Where are the babies? I am so ready for grandchildren. My children are 15, 16, so they say to me, ‘That’s so inappropriate. You can’t put that pressure on us for, like, at least 10 years.’ ”

All of Moriarty’s novels are, in some form, a reflection of herself. “Liane in person is exactly like she is in her books,” says Colonna. “The tone, the funniness, the subject matter. Reading one is just like sitting down with her for a three-hour lunch.”

“You can see her deep observation of everyday life in every novel,” says Claire Craig, her Australian editor, “her deep interest in people. It’s always such a joy when an author says what we’re thinking or feeling or experiencing in our own lives. And she does it again and again.”

Take the parents’ WhatsApp group in Big Little Truths:

″ ‘Let’s keep it clean folks, this is a pubic forum.’

‘HA HA HA HA HA HA’

‘PUBLIC forum!!’ ”

No one will ever convince me that doesn’t come from real life. “Well, I did tell her about a parents’ WhatsApp group,” laughs Colonna. “And she did say, ‘Oh my god, that’s gold.’ ”

Big Little Truths is, as much as anything else, a multi-stranded tapestry of midlife in all its dubious glory. There are ageing parents and perimenopause; frozen shoulders and fried pelvic floors. There’s even a cancer diagnosis. And that, too, is true to life.

Liane Moriarty had breast cancer for the first time in 2021. She later recalled the experience in an essay for The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. For days after her biopsy, she wrote, she couldn’t look at her children “without a whooshing sensation of vertigo. By the time my GP calls to say she’s very sorry but it’s not good news, I am wild with panic.”

“I sort of regretted writing that piece afterwards,” she says now. “I think it just felt … too personal? Too something.” She shakes her head. She was diagnosed earlier this year for the second time. And she’s willing to mention the recurrence publicly now, “in case it reminds anyone to get their mammogram. Even if something’s already happened.” She leans forward. “Don’t think, ‘Oh, that’s happened to me, and now it’s done.’ ”

In her own case, the second go-round has involved none of the discombobulation she described so beautifully in her essay. “They’ve caught it very early …” She stops and thinks. “I’m not … it’s more that I’ve realised I’m just going to have to think of this as something like paying your taxes; some kind of an administrative thing. So it’s annoying, but it’s nothing I need to feel frightened of.” She looks at me firmly. “I don’t want it to be a big ‘Liane Battles Cancer’ thing.”

So, without making it into a big Liane Battles Cancer thing, let it be said that she has had surgery and will soon have three weeks of radiation. “Then I’ll recover a bit and then I’ll be off on the Australian tour [for Big Little Truths].” That and her various other publicity commitments will last most of the rest of the year. “And then I’m going away with a group of old friends,” says Moriarty: “for our 60th birthdays.”

Turning 60, she says, holds no fears at all. “I’m always interested in people at different ages.” She leans forward. “Actually, I used to have this thing that I would see this particular type of woman at my events who was really cool; just really had it together – a good sense of humour about the world.” She grins. “I thought I was going to be like that in my 50s, but it was not like that: I’ve been still sweaty and anxious in my 50s. But I think in my 60s, it’s all going to come together. Colourful glasses, interesting scarves, beautiful shoes. They all have handmade shoes that look like they could walk in them, but they’re also fashionable. And they also have sparkly eyes. And they look at me like, ‘Oh darling, it’s all fine. Just calm down.’” She sits back, hands on the table, looking pleased. “I think it’s going to happen.”

So can we expect, in another 10 years, to see Celeste and Madeline – or some other Moriarty characters as yet unknown – at 60, drinking their flat whites and getting their hips replaced while battling whatever zeitgeist terrors the 2030s hold? “I think so,” says Moriarty, smiling again. “I like the idea of my characters getting older along with me.”

Moriarty’s characters – and, one suspects, many of her readers – are not all so serene about growing old. But it’s some comfort, at least, to imagine another Moriarty novel in the library when we do.
