Jason Arday, professor at centre of Cambridge plagiarism row, found dead

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 21:50:41 GMT

Academic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on Friday

Jason Arday, the academic who resigned last week as a professor at the University of Cambridge, has been found dead at his home in south London.

The Metropolitan police said officers were called to Arday’s address by the London ambulance service after 3pm on Friday.

A spokesperson for the Met said: “A 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s central south command unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.”

The body was believed to be that of Arday. At this stage, police are understood not to believe anyone else was involved in the death.

London ambulance service was the first emergency service at the scene. The person discovered inside the home was found unresponsive.

Arday’s family said in a statement: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.

“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.

“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.

“We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.”

The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends of Jason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.

“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”

Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest-ever black professor. But he resigned last week after accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.

In a statement announcing his resignation, Arday said: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at the University of Cambridge and Jesus College.

“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”

Arday said he had been driven to resign because the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.

Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said in a statement: “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”

Durham University, where Arday worked between 2019 and 2021, said: “We are shocked and terribly sad to learn of the death of Jason Arday.

“He is remembered at Durham as a kind and warm person who actively sought to promote opportunities for PhD students. We want to express our deepest sympathy to his family who are in our thoughts.”

Arday’s rise to a prestigious professorial chair was remarkable. Arday said he had been nonverbal until the age of 11, requiring extensive speech and language therapy, as well as being illiterate until 18.

That life story contributed to him being made a torchbearer for the 2012 London Olympics flame.

After leaving school, Arday went on to further study before completing a doctorate in education at Liverpool John Moores University in 2015. That was followed by a string of academic posts culminating in a professorship at the University of Glasgow and a professorial chair at Cambridge.

Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. But he denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University earlier this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.

But other elements of his life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running.

He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.

However those claims meant little in the world of academia. After initially defending Arday as the victim of a smear campaign, as further questions arose about his academic career, the university began to temper its support.

On 5 August Cambridge announced it would hold an internal inquiry after it said it received “new information” about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, as well as what it described as “a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct”. Jesus College, of which he was a member, said it would also hold an inquiry.

But while Cambridge said Arday would remain in post and continue to receive support, Arday immediately announced his resignation.

At the end of last week Glasgow University said it would also investigate Arday’s academic credentials.

The controversy has stirred considerable anger within Cambridge’s academic community, both between Arday’s supporters and those who said the university had erred in appointing him to such a prestigious position.

After resisting calls from senior staff for an independent inquiry, earlier this week Prentice backed down, saying she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case”. She described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour.

Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, was published this week in the US by an imprint of Simon & Schuster, with UK publication scheduled for later this month. Simon & Schuster has been contacted for comment.

Trump threatens to declare strait of Hormuz ‘territory of the United States’

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 21:38:17 GMT

Seriousness of remark made in New York on Friday, and whether it signaled new policy ​position, not clear

Donald Trump has threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States” as his administration struggles to conclude the war with Iran.

During a speech at a police academy on Long Island, New York, on Friday, the US president said he would “pretty soon” designate the waterway – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – a US territory.

The comment came as peace talks with Iran remain at an impasse following failed negotiations, with Tehran refusing to reopen the strait, which has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.

Almost six months into the war, there is little indication that negotiations will soon yield peace, as Iranian officials continue to defy Trump’s demands. The US has been blockading Iranian shipping and ⁠ports in recent months in an effort to pile economic pressure on Tehran.

“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said on Friday. “Essentially, that’s what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.”

The seriousness of Trump’s remark, and whether it signaled a new policy ​position for his administration, was not immediately clear.

Responding on X, formerly Twitter, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said Tehran would not ⁠be intimidated by threats, ​or ‌a show ‌of force, by ‌the US – and added that the strait of Hormuz ​would only ​be opened, ​or ‌closed, under Iran’s ​authority.

Earlier this week, the president claimed that the US had “total control” over the strait and said “I think we will keep it” on Truth Social, despite the waterway being an internationally navigable strait bordered by Iran and Oman.

Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, forcing working Americans to pay significantly more at the pump.

Nevertheless, on Friday, Trump said that Americans who have had to “pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” should remember that they are “doing it so that a very evil country cannot have a – really, it’s the No 1 state sponsor of terror in the world – we don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon.

“When you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK, I mean, it’s not. I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing,” he added.

Over the past six months, the Trump administration has repeatedly claimed victory in the war, saying Iran’s regime has been pleading for a deal.

Tehran has remained steadfast in its demands, saying as recently as last Saturday that it will not reopen the strait of Hormuz unless the US “corrects its behavior”, “completely compensate[s]” Iran for war damage, lifts sanctions and “unconditionally” releases frozen assets.

‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situation

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 21:30:38 GMT

Manager’s deal expires at end of the new season

‘They don’t have to worry … I want to be here’

Mikel Arteta has said he is relaxed about his Arsenal contract expiring at the end of the new season and believes his side will need to be better than last year to defend their title successfully.

The Premier League champions will face Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff on Sunday and are heavy favourites to win back-to-back league titles for the first time since the 1930s. The departure of Pep Guardiola from their traditional rivals City means Arteta is now the Premier League’s longest-serving manager, with the Spaniard having joined in December 2019.

He signed a three-year contract extension in September 2024 after Arsenal finished as runners-up to City and had been expected to agree a new deal over the summer that would make him one of the highest-paid managers in the world. Arteta acknowledged on Friday that his priorities have been elsewhere this summer as he attempts to strengthen his squad before the new season but reassured supporters that he is fully committed to the club.

“They don’t have to worry about any of that, because I want to be here. I am extremely happy. I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and when we have the possibility, we will resolve that. And that’s it,” he said.

Asked if he expects talks over a new contract to continue after the transfer window, Arteta added: “There is always another priority, I think. And that’s the way we have been treating it, I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue. I think because my will, certainly, is to be here and I am very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That is why everyone is doing things in a really organic way.”

Arsenal have opened negotiations with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber, while they are still in the market for another attacker if they can offload Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. After missing out on Vinícius Júnior when the Brazil forward opted to sign a new deal with Real Madrid, Arteta defended Arsenal’s strategy this summer and is hoping that they can still add to their squad.

“I am really happy with the squad, the players that I have and I am really happy with the ambition of the club. There is zero question about that. We have shown that in the manner we have tried to act,” he said.

“But I think we need to do it our own way. We have super strengths and we have other areas we need to be very conscious [of] because we don’t have the elements or the structure that other clubs have. We need to do it our way. We are always on it that way and we will do what we believe is the right thing to do. To have the best possibility to compete in every competition that’s for sure.”

Raúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against Blackburn

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 21:21:18 GMT

Raúl Jiménez marked his return to Wolves with the stoppage-time equaliser that saved them from an embarrassing start to their return to the Championship.

The Mexico striker, who scored against England during the World Cup finals, retained his composure to convert a penalty given for handball by Rayan Alebiosu that would have had VAR questioning whether the defender was in the area when Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross struck his arm. Thankfully for Wolves, the video assistant referee is no longer their problem. Jiménez, who had bought scarves for all supporters in the South Bank in gratitude for their response to welcoming him home, tucked away his first goal in this second spell for the club he graced during their recent heyday.

All that’s gold does not glisten. Wolves may have reverted to a richer sheen of their traditional colour on their return to the Championship after nine years in the Premier League, but that does not mean the gloom of relegation ends there. Cesar Peixoto’s new era in the league got off to a disappointing start as they were fortunate to gain a point off unfancied Blackburn Rovers and their former West Bromwich Albion manager Tony Mowbray.

Goals from Sean McLoughlin and Andri Gudjohnsen allowed Blackburn to provide Wolves with a reality check after Marshall Munetsi had given them an early lead. Confidence is a fragile commodity and, after their decision to replace Rob Edwards with a manager with no experience of English football, the Wolves board know that their supporters’ patience is thin. Leading Gil Vicente to sixth place in the Portuguese first division does not make Peixoto a guaranteed winner.

Molineux was awash with fading golden sunlight and rising optimism at kick-off. A summer that started with such a surprising managerial departure is promising to end with renewed faith in the team’s direction of travel, if the early noises are anything to go by.

While Wolves had organised a stash of Starbars for the head coach’s corner of the away dressing room, in honour of Tony Mowbray’s legendary love of chocolate, the returning Wolves striker Jiménez had gifted a scarf for every supporter in the South Bank. But it was the Blackburn defence who were most giving in the early stages as they split generously to allow Marshall Munetsi a clean run through onto Fer López’s sumptuous pass. The left-footed finish from the Zimbabwean, himself coming back to Molineux after a loan at Paris FC, compounded the feelgood factor buzzing around the ground.

Cesar Peixoto has promised to bring a front-footed high press to Wolves, since he replaced Rob Edwards as head coach, and this has been effective in pre-season and against Port Vale in the Carabao Cup. But it also leaves gaps on transition. Blackburn, who finished 20th last season and have not done so much in the transfer market to suggest they should aim higher this term, got behind Wolves on several occasions. It was no great surprise therefore when, from another superb right-wing cross from Ryoya Morishita, Sean McLoughlin, timing his run off André to perfection, headed beyond Dan Bentley to equalise.

Some of Wolves’ best business so far this summer has been bringing players back to Molineux. While Jiménez started the night on the bench, after a late start to pre-season following his impressive World Cup for Mexico, López was the classiest player on view. Back from a loan spell at Celta Vigo, he has been invited to make the No 10 position his own, and the Spaniard so nearly regained Wolves the lead only to curl his shot just wide.

Receiving Kieran Trippier’s prompt, Mateus Mané also swerved a shot just over as Wolves finished the half on the up.

Blackburn continued to benefit from Wolves’ soft centre however. Oladapo Afolayan’s shot needed tipping over by Bentley before the right winger again got space down Wolves left – where David Møller Wolfe, the Norway left-back, was in for the injured Hugo Bueno – to cross for Andri Gudjohnsen to get in front of his man and turn in Rovers’ second goal.

By the hour mark, the South Bank were swirling their Jiménez scarves above their heads and chanting ‘Si Senor’ in honour of the veteran striker who was such an esteemed figure here at Molineux for five of the club’s best years in modern times. He was the pivotal attacking player during Nuno Espírito Santo’s reign when Wolves reached the latter stages of the FA Cup and the Europa League. The scene was set for the Mexican. Could he deliver?

Jiménez struck one free-kick into the wall, before laying an astute pass back for Tommy Doyle, though his fellow substitute could only hammer the ball over the bar after appearing to handle. It was interesting that Tripper was withdrawn, and Peixoto’s game plan was being questioned when two youngsters, in Pedro Lima and Tawanda Chirewa, were thrown on into a rejigged 4-4-2 for the final 10 minutes.

Audrey Werro holds off Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson to win European 800m gold

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 21:16:38 GMT

Swiss runner sets 1:54.81sec championship best

Femke Broeders-Bol secures bronze in 1:55.54

The 800m European women’s final we all hoped for delivered as Switzerland’s Audrey Werro led from the front to win a classic for the ages. But it was a close run thing as Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson pushed her all the way to take silver.

However, Werro proved too strong as she came through in a championship record 1:54.81sec. Just behind her was Hodgkinson, who ran 1:55.01 to take silver. Femke Broeders-Bol took bronze in 1:55.54.

“I am really happy with this medal after a crazy 24 hours,” said Werro, who beat Hodgkinson by about three metres. “It was a great race,” said the British runner. “I am sure there will be many more battles ahead. But I think I would have been happier with gold.”

Hodgkinson was attempting to complete a European Championship hat-trick after golds in 2022 and 2024.

As those in the press box discussed their likely 1-2-3s beforehand, there were coherent advocates for all six potential permutations. But cracking the enigma code was easier than getting agreement on what would happen when the big three of Hodgkinson, Werro and Broeders-Bol met for the first time.

Naturally Hodgkinson had plenty of supporters. She was the Paris Olympic champion, after all. And she was on home turf. In the winter she had also broken the world indoor record and then won the world indoor title in March.

But that was before her fateful meeting with Werro in Stockholm in June, where she had suffered a shock – and comprehensive – defeat. Werro was considered the favourite by the bookies. Especially as she had run the third, fourth and ninth fastest times in history since June. The only doubt? How would a cut on her knee from a heavy fall in the semi-finals affect her?

And then there was the giant curveball: Broeders-Bol, the double world 400m hurdles champion whose 49.17sec personal best for 400m is an indoor world record, who was running in her first 800m championship final.

Sebastian Coe, the president of World Athletics, first suggested to Broeders-Bol that she was a natural 80om runner a few years ago. Her first instinct was to recoil in horror. Her second was to avoid Coe for years. It was only after the Dutch athlete won the world 400m hurdles title again last year that she decided to give it a whirl.

It made for a highly anticipated final, with the three fastest women in the world this year lining up together. And it certainly didn’t disappoint.

Earlier in the night, Norway’s Karsten Warholm ran a championship record to storm to gold in the men’s 400m hurdles. The world record-holder’s time of 46.63sec was some performance on a windy night and a slow Alexander Stadium track. The victory was his fourth European title at the event. Germany’s Emil Agyekum was more than a second back in silver, while Turkey’s Ismail Nezir took bronze.

Nadia Battocletti added the European 10,000m title to her 5,000m crown with a devastating 28-second sprint over the final 200m. That took the Italian to victory in 31:41.20, four seconds clear of Maureen Koster of the Netherlands, with Belgium’s Jana Van Lent winning bronze. Britain’s Megan Keith ran bravely from the front but she emptied out with two laps to go and finished eighth.

There was little joy either for Katarina Johnson-Thompson in the women’s heptathlon. The 33-year-old won bronze in the world championships last year but was clearly hampered by a calf niggle that led to her missing the Commonwealth Games, ending day one in 16th place.

Johnson-Thompson started poorly and her time in the 100m hurdles of 14 seconds flat was her slowest ever in a major championship. And while things picked up with a 1.83m clearance in the high jump, she was already behind where she needed to be.

Sadly Johnson-Thompson’s performance was to get no better. A shot put of 12.79m was also below par and she could run only 24.46sec in the 200m, the final event of day one.

That left her on just 3644 points – and a long way behind the leader Adrianna Sulek-Schubert of Poland on 3968, with Sofie Dokter of the Netherlands and Kate O’Connor of Ireland close behind her.

In the men’s 200m, Britain’s Zharnel Hughes had to settle for silver behind Germany’s Owen Ansah, who powered to victory in 19.95sec. Hughes had a time of 20.16sec, while there was a rare dead heat for bronze between Italy’s Eseosa Fostine Desalu and Switzerland’s Timothé Mumenthaler, who both ran 20.26.

However, Ansah’s gold medal was instantly controversial given that last week Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency recommended that Ansah should receive a four-year suspension over a possible anti-doping violation. The German authorities claim that is because Ansah missed a test in July. Ansah disputes this. But the case continues.

‘I shot Mr Thompson’: Luigi Mangione describes his planning and the killing of health insurance CEO

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 20:29:40 GMT

It was a dramatic twist to the federal case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare’s Brian Thompson – but state charges are still pending

When Luigi Mangione stepped into a Manhattan federal courtroom shortly after 11am on Friday, his demeanor was less debonair than at other recent court proceedings.

The 28-year-old, wearing tan jail scrubs instead of natty menswear, walked with hands behind his back and ankles shackled en route to the defense table. Mangione sat and then studied a piece of paper alongside his attorney.

This morning’s proceeding would mark a dramatic twist in Mangione’s legal saga. Mangione, who faces federal and state cases in UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson’s 4 December 2024 killing, had long maintained a not-guilty stance.

But this hearing would change that with one simple sentence.

“On the morning of December 4, 2024, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he said.

He added: “I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

The killing of Thompson – gunned down on a Manhattan street – shocked the US and triggered a manhunt that ended with Mangione’s arrest in a Pennsylvania fast-food restaurant. But it also sparked an outpouring of public anger and rage at the actions of the US’s widely reviled for-profit healthcare industry.

Many assumed that as Mangione went on trial, so perhaps would an entire industry, as the defense might seek to explain his actions. But the guilty plea – in the federal case against him at least – has ended that prospect.

Much of the emotional proceeding, which saw both members of Thompson’s family and some Mangione supporters crying in the gallery, involved Judge Margaret Garnett engaging in the standard questioning judges use to determine whether someone is capable of admitting guilt.

Was Mangione ever treated or hospitalized for any kind of mental illness? Was he under the care of a doctor or mental health professional? Had he been treated for any sort of addiction?

Mangione answered “no” to all these questions.

Garnett asked whether he had taken anything in the last two days and Mangione said yes: trazodone, “for sleeping”.

Garnett then queried Mangione on whether anyone had made any promises – or threats – to induce him into pleading guilty. He said no.

Then came the moment many observers had long waited for: Mangione would have to describe what happened, in his own words, potentially shedding light on the grisly slaying.

Mangione said that “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back, navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others”, he learned that UnitedHealthcare would hold its annual investor conference on 4 December 2024.

The specific location wasn’t publicly disclosed, Mangione said, so “I then researched the event online”.

“I observed that the annual conference of America’s largest healthcare organization with the stated mission to make health – excuse me – with the stated mission to make the health system work better for everyone, would be attended by company executives, the board of directors and hundreds of investors, not doctors, nurses and patients,” Mangione said.

Mangione then told the court that in November of that year, he traveled into Manhattan and engaged in subterfuge to get more information.

“I then emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership posing as an investor at a firm managing over $50bn in assets and requesting information about the conference,” he said. “Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour.”

Mangione said that he used a 3D printer to forge part of a firearm and affix it with a silencer and magazine.

“My travel to New York and email to UnitedHealthcare was with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson,” he said.

Both prosecutors and Mangione’s lawyers, under Garnett’s questioning, said they believed there was “sufficient factual evidence” for a plea.

“Mr Mangione, how do you now plead to counts one and two of the indictment?” Garnett said, referring to the federal stalking charges against him.

“Guilty,” Mangione said plainly, bringing an end to the prospect of a federal trial against him and throwing his state case into potential disarray.

After the proceeding wrapped, dozens of journalists convened outside the federal courthouse in downtown Manhattan.

“There can be no celebrity in assassination,” prosecutor Jamie McDonald said afterwards, adding that Mangione had “attempted to send a public message through violence”.

Mangione’s team announced that they filed paperwork to dismiss the separate state case, which is due to start in September, and in which he faces murder charges. They argued that he could not be charged in Manhattan state court because of New York’s own double-jeopardy law.

However, Manhattan prosecutors said their case wasn’t over, saying: “We are prepared to litigate the defense motions” and the team “remains committed to seeking justice for Mr Thompson and his family”.

So the Mangione saga is still not over. Not yet.

It came as no surprise that almost a year of pent-up emotion exploded from Iga Swiatek the moment she slotted her final backhand winner to clinch the Canadian Open title by defeating Elena Rybakina in two clean sets on Thursday night.

As she screamed towards her team members on her corner of the court, pointed to her head and furiously pumped her fist, though, it was the tenor of Swiatek’s emotion that made her reaction noteworthy: she was angry. Her anger, she explained later, stemmed from the doubtful, disapproving voices she has heard throughout these difficult periods, most of it coming from viewers and the media alike in Poland.

“After I won, I kind of let myself feel it [anger] a little bit because there are plenty of things that athletes, not only athletes, all the people have to struggle with,” she said. “Sometimes we need to fight things that we shouldn’t.”

Considering her generational achievements, Swiatek is one of the most famous people in Poland, and certainly one of the country’s most famous athletes. Her fame has reached a point where she rarely ventures outside when in her home country, only really going to her friends’ apartments or inviting them to hers, to avoid being watched. Last year, Swiatek explained how she had to negotiate with paparazzi after they took photos of her apartment building.

“I can accept it when it’s like at work or when I’m going to practise and everything, but for example, like when it’s close to my home or when I’m having just a walk with a friend or with a family member I’d rather them not doing that, because it’s my time off,” she said. “I had an incident, actually, after Miami, when I was home, when paparazzi followed me almost to my apartment. But I stopped them, and I said: ‘OK, tomorrow I’m going to practise. You can make photos of me when I go there, but this is off limits.’ So also they kind of understand sometimes. And I think I understand what their job is about, and we can have a nice, even cooperation if they want to be supportive.”

While fame is something that Swiatek has had to accept, the additional scrutiny that comes with her status is what she refuses to tolerate. Practically every tennis player receives some level of social media abuse, hate and threats, one of the many pressing issues in the sport, but the criticism Swiatek receives is distinct because of the amount that comes from home. Every result and decision is the subject of intense public scrutiny, something that has increased during her more difficult past two years on tour, and they have further complicated her attempts to rediscover her confidence. One of the biggest points of contention has been her relationship with her team, with ample focus on the role of her psychologist, Daria Abramowicz. Asked why so much negativity comes from home, which should be a safe space, Swiatek shrugs: “That’s an interesting question, I think, for a sociologist or someone, because honestly, it’s not only in Poland, but in Great Britain as well, in different countries, for different sports, not only for individual athletes.

“There is unfair judgment from different parts coming to us, and we need to handle it. For sure, last month I faced it, my team faced it. My goal was for it to not interrupt my process and define who I am. Being sure about my decisions, not letting this disrupt anything and focus on growing because it’s just the world that we live in. It shouldn’t be like that so I took yesterday’s opportunity to just talk about it a little bit more even if it helps one person, or one young athlete knows that we all try to do something with it, maybe it will help a little bit.”

This is a significant moment for Swiatek, her first title in 11 months and after so much enthusiasm about their partnership, her first alongside her new coach Francisco Roig. Such are the demands of this gruelling sport she had no time at all to savour it. Swiatek closed out her 6-2, 6-3 win over Rybakina at about 7.30pm and her press duties ended around 10pm on Thursday.

By midday on Friday, she had packed her bags, taken a private jet to Cincinnati, provided by the tournament, and was addressing the media before her title defence in Ohio. “It’s intense, but it’s OK,” said Swiatek. “I’ll find my time to appreciate what happened and to be grateful about it, for sure. Because without it, it doesn’t make sense to keep going. You need to get a taste of these moments and remember them.”

Cheryl Hall obituary

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 18:53:19 GMT

Actor who played Shirley Johnson in the sitcom Citizen Smith, and whose dozens of other roles included EastEnders, Doctor Who and The Bill

Cheryl Hall, who has died aged 76, was an actor best known for her roles in 1970s sitcoms. As Shirley Johnson in Citizen Smith, she was the girlfriend of Wolfie, the would-be revolutionary leading the Tooting Popular Front with the battle cry “power to the people”.

Wolfie Smith, played by Hall’s then husband, the actor Robert Lindsay, and his small “army” of self-styled urban guerrillas, are simply inept, concocting plans such as stealing a Scorpion tank in order to mount an attack on the House of Commons, only to discover that parliament is in recess.

Nevertheless, Shirley supports her boyfriend’s ideals while wishing they could settle down together in something resembling her parents’ middle-class lifestyle. Her father, initially played by Artro Morris, and then by Peter Vaughan, is less damning of Wolfie’s Marxist revolutionary politics than of his unemployed status and unkempt hair.

The sitcom, beginning in 1977, was written by John Sullivan shortly before he created Derek “Del Boy” Trotter, another south London antihero, in Only Fools and Horses. Citizen Smith ran for four series, finishing in 1980, but Hall left at the end of the second run in 1979, reportedly frustrated at her character’s lack of comic dialogue.

Although it did not help Hall’s career, Sullivan later admitted that she was right to be dissatisfied with her Citizen Smith role, and went on to prove he could write comedy for female characters with Just Good Friends (1983-86).

Hall’s departure also coincided with the end of her marriage, and she and Lindsay divorced in 1980. Later, in a 2022 interview with Zoe Williams in the Guardian, Lindsay said it was a result of his obsession with achieving success. “That single-mindedness broke up my first marriage,” he said.

Hall was born in Whitechapel, east London, to Lilian (nee Cole), a civil servant at the Royal Courts of Justice, and George Hall, a woodworker and market trader. She was brought up in Bethnal Green and attended Coborn school for girls, Bow, where she appeared in school plays.

While studying at the Corona Theatre School in London, she worked as a cleaner to supplement her grant. One day, she glanced up from her work and saw Stewart Granger, the British Hollywood film star, looking down at her. “Starstruck is the only way to describe how I felt,” she recalled. “But, when he heard that I was a drama student, he made me some tea and spent the rest of the afternoon talking about acting.”

Her early stage appearances included the role of Helen, a schoolgirl, in a 1971 revival of Barry Reckord’s groundbreaking drama Skyvvers, set in a London comprehensive, at the Royal Court’s Theatre Upstairs.

She was already in demand on television by then. Between 1968 and 1971, she appeared as a jobseeker in the ITV schools series You and the World. Then came roles in both dramas and comedies, from Special Branch (in 1969) and On the Buses (in 1971) to Callan (two parts, in 1970 and 1972), Sykes (in 1972) and Albert (also 1972), in which she played Doreen Bissel, the fiancee of Rodney Bewes’s factory worker of the title.

Hall lost out to Katy Manning for the part of the Doctor Who companion Jo Grant, alongside Jon Pertwee, but the programme’s producer, Barry Letts, gave her a guest role as Shirna, the assistant to a travelling showman, who rescues Jo in the 1973 adventure Carnival of Monsters. A year later, in the prison drama Within These Walls, Hall played an inmate in the drugs unit.

Back in sitcoms, she played Sid James’s secretary in 1974 episodes of Bless This House, then Kathleen, the girlfriend of a shy plumber, Shorty Mepstead (David Jason), who lives with his mother, in both series of Lucky Feller (1975-76). As Shorty’s girlfriend, she also has eyes for his elder, more worldly-wise, brother, Randolph (Peter Armitage ), and at one stage fears she is pregnant by him.

Hall’s other roles, in a television career in which she clocked up almost 100 parts in 40 years, included Mrs Jackson in the children’s foster home series Dodger, Bonzo & the Rest (1985); a short run in EastEnders (1988) as Christine, who provided a safe house to Den Watts (Leslie Grantham) – and was seduced by him – when he was on the run from the police; and seven different characters in The Bill (between 1984 and 2007).

Although she kept busy, starring roles remained elusive and Hall was able to focus on her interest in local politics. In 1993, she ousted a sitting Conservative on Kent county council to give Labour its first win in the Ramsgate South ward. She eventually became leader of the party’s group, in opposition, on the council.

At the 1997 election she stood as a parliamentary candidate for Canterbury. Although she gained 31% of the vote, the Conservative MP retained the seat. She lost her county council seat in 2001 and, from 2010, spent much of her retirement in Greece.

Before her marriage to Lindsay (1974-80), Hall was in a three-year relationship with the actor Robin Askwith. In 1985, she married Robert Potter; they divorced four years later. She is survived by their sons, Benjamin and Joshua.

Cheryl Georgette Hall, actor, born 23 July 1950; died 9 August 2026

Burnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisis

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 18:51:11 GMT

Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2 to emissions in UK, say green campaigners

Andy Burnham has been criticised for moving to cut electric vehicle (EV) sales targets and accept North Sea drilling at a time of devastating wildfires caused by the climate emergency.

The prime minister for the first time acknowledged on Friday that the climate crisis was behind hundreds of wildfires that have ripped across the parts of the UK.

The scale of the disaster has prompted the government to bring in the military, ban the sale of disposable barbecues and activate the national alert system to issue safety advice to people across England and Wales in areas at risk on Friday night.

However, Burnham was also accused of failing to take the push for net zero seriously enough, as the government took steps towards watering down EV targets on the same day.

The government on Friday launched a consultation on cutting the target for new EVs to as little as 50% of all new cars in 2030, down from 80% under existing rules, in proposals that could add millions of tonnes a year to the UK’s carbon dioxide emissions.

The consultation will include several options, including leaving the headline target unchanged, or cutting it to 70%, 60% or 50%.

In a video from the West Midlands, where homes have been destroyed and dozens of people injured, Burnham appeared to acknowledge the seriousness of the climate crisis. “We cannot accept this as the new normal,” he said. “This isn’t happening in isolation.

“Much of England and Wales is in drought and we are in another period of extreme heat. Farmers are watching crops fail and firefighters have faced hundreds of wildfires in a matter of weeks. This is what climate change looks like, here and now.”

But in a broadcast interview, he also defended his “pragmatic” approach on extracting oil and gas from the North Sea. His government will shortly have to decide whether to allow new drilling at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, with a consultation on the former closing on Monday.

Environmental groups have said permitting extraction at the fields should be inconceivable after five heatwaves this summer, with Greenpeace saying it was a “Rubicon that he must not cross”.

The decision to consider weakening one of the UK’s key climate policies on EVs was announced hours after the country recorded its hottest day of the year so far – and the fifth hottest ever – after five heatwaves that scientists have said are almost certainly worsened by global heating caused by carbon emissions.

Fire services said 19 homes were destroyed, 200 hectares (500 acres) burnt and dozens of people sent to hospital in the West Midlands, the UK’s traditional automotive centre, in grassfires that may have been worsened by drought.

Speaking from Stourbridge, Burnham said it was necessary to bring in a temporary ban on disposable barbecues from Friday, asking retailers to withdraw them from sale.

“Please think about the situation we are in,” he said. “Britain is a tinderbox right now. Setting a fire in any outdoor setting is a risk to people’s homes and other people’s lives.”

The prime minister also revealed he planned to commission firefighting planes to combat the spread of wildfires and appointed a new fire minister, as he made the case that country had to “face up” to the “changing climate”.

Environmental groups largely welcomed Burnham’s words on the climate after 50 organisations earlier criticised him in a letter for failing to mention it following a Cobra meeting on the heatwave earlier this week.

Hannah Martin, the co-director of Green New Deal Rising which coordinated Friday’s letter, said: “Finally Andy Burnham has said the words ‘climate change’ as prime minister and acknowledged the cause of the wildfires, drought and extreme heat that is raging across the country. Now he needs to put policies in place to deal with the scale of the crisis.

“That means saying no to new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea … it also means ramping up new investment in renewable energy and climate jobs, doubling down on insulating homes and improving public transport, and making sure our homes, hospitals, schools and emergency services are properly equipped to deal with extreme weather caused by climate change.”

Sam Keely from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank also urged Burnham not to row back on the government’s commitment for the rollout of electric vehicles. Keely said: “At the same time as the prime minister was speaking, the government launched its consultation on watering down the zero emissions vehicle mandate.

“Getting more EVs on the road is one of the single most important policies for cutting UK emissions and will also insulate more British motorists from paying more at the petrol pump as a result of volatile oil prices, saving billions of pounds on the British driving bill.”

Electric car sales have soared by 29% in the UK this year, but the automotive industry has said the sales targets, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, are putting too much pressure on manufacturers.

They say the mandate forces them to sell electric cars at discounts and have threatened job losses or even UK factory closures if the rules do not change.

The government said it needed the targets to “remain pro-business and grounded in the real world”.

Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, said: “It’s right we keep targets under review to ensure they’re practical and back British industry. The end goal hasn’t changed – but we need to take business with us on the journey.”

The changes are strongly opposed by climate campaigners and by the electric car charging industry, which has plans to spend billions of pounds to install charge points across the country.

The switch to EVs is expected to be the single biggest contributor to cutting UK carbon pollution in the next decade, according to the government’s Climate Change Committee.

Under the existing rules, carmakers need to sell an increasing proportion of pure electric cars every year or face fines. The targets tighten from 33% this year to 80% in 2030. The sale of new petrol and diesel cars is then to be banned from 2035.

Ami McCarthy, the Greenpeace UK head of politics, said weakening the rules would be “a wrong turn for drivers, energy security, our climate and the economy”.

She added: “Both the Iran war and this summer’s extreme weather have shown once again why we’re better off cutting our dependence on fossil fuels.

“This mandate is one of the most powerful policies we have to bring down planet-heating emissions, which is the only way to stop more deadly heatwaves in future.

“Burnham can’t fulfil his promise of tackling the cost of living crisis and reindustrialising Britain without the green economy. So why put on the brakes now?”

It would be the second time that Labour has watered down the targets after it last year added loopholes called “flexibilities” to the original rules. The loopholes allowed more plug-in hybrid EVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, to count towards the mandate, as well as permitting carmakers to catch up with more battery car sales in later years.

Extending the flexibilities to 2034 will also be considered in the consultation, which will run until 23 October. Van sales targets are also likely to be changed.

The most extreme change proposed, cutting the headline rate to 50%, could reduce electric car sales by as much as 5.8m, according to analysis by the ECIU. It added that the changes would make the 2035 ban much harder to achieve, with some carmakers already lobbying for it to be delayed.

Colin Walker, the ECIU head of transport, said: “Proposing to water down the UK’s biggest climate policy the day after temperatures hit 38C, and a summer of heat and drought that risks the UK having its worst ever harvest, may seem strange to the increasing number of people concerned by images of homes on fire, and the security and affordability of the food we eat.”

Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders lobby group, said: “The automotive industry is fully committed to a zero-emission future, investing billions in new technologies, products and incentives.

“However, with the ZEV mandate conceived under vastly different conditions, this welcome review is a timely opportunity to adjust the transition so it works for all.”

Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 18:00:34 GMT

Ultimatum issued hours before plan was scrapped

European Football Clubs demanded Infantino back down

Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.

In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’s Club World Cup.

The letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantino shelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE) in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.

Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter asked Fifa to confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that the tie-in had, “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.

A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.

Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.

EFC’s letter also raised the continuing delay, first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.

“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”

It is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution, although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.

Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty, EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.

The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body, the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.

One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.

Israel’s defence minister wants to transfer law enforcement powers for Israelis in the occupied West Bank over to the police, a plan that Palestine’s vice-president described as a “flagrant violation of international law” and step towards full Israeli annexation.

Israel Katz announced that he had ordered the military to draw up plans for the handover of responsibility for policing Israeli settlers amid domestic and international criticism of the army’s failure to tackle militants besieging three Palestinian families.

The Palestinian vice-president, Hussein al-Sheikh, called for international intervention to enforce international law and stop a move that would “entrench the illegitimate annexation of Palestinian land”.

Katz unveiled his plan as a settler siege in the Palestinian village of Qusra entered its sixth day. The Israeli army has proved unable or unwilling to remove the group of militants trying to drive out Palestinian residents through a campaign of terror.

Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli human rights lawyer, said a transfer of law enforcement powers could constitute a major step towards formal annexation.

“The military can delegate enforcement but not responsibility [of the law],” Sfard said. “If they want to create a normative legal framework that absolves the army from responsibility and transfers it to police, that would be another brick, a very major one, of annexation.”

However, Israel could also legally expand police powers in the occupied West Bank under the current occupation framework, he added, and the lack of detail in Katz’s statement indicated it may have been driven more by politics than clear policy.

“This is a cowardly statement made by a minister of defence who is under scrutiny, because the army that reached Syria, Iran and Lebanon and annihilated Gaza cannot evacuate a few Jewish terrorists that invaded a Palestinian home in an area under occupation for six decades.”

There has been a surge in attacks on Palestinians and construction of new settlements across the occupied West Bank, as extremists backed by the most far-right government in Israel’s history intensify a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of national elections set for October.

On Thursday Katz celebrated the re-establishment of a settlement evacuated by Israel in 2005, under then-prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan.

“Here, this is the land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Katz said at the ceremony in Ganim, where two dozen prefabricated homes have already been installed, and the hillside is being levelled to make space for more.

On the road that leads to the settlement the army had levelled Palestinian property and used piles of rubble to block access roads for Palestinian communities.

On Friday the commander of Israeli forces for the occupied West Bank, Gen Avi Bluth, made a second visit to Qusra. Two days earlier he told Palestinians the army would remove the settlers, but soldiers retreated from confrontation with the group.

Instead they forced one of the Palestinian families out of their home, saying they needed it as a base for the unsuccessful military operation against the settlers.

One of the homes is owned by a US citizen, and US ambassador Mike Huckabee described the Israelis besieging it as terrorists, and said he had requested the Israeli police and army act to remove them.

Huckabee, who supports the settlement movement’s vision of establishing a “Greater Israel” on land seized from Palestinians and neighbouring countries, said the militants in Qusra represent a “very small minority” of the settler movement.

State and settler violence has driven a surge in displacement of Palestinian communities in the past three years.

Since October 2023, Israel has forcibly displaced 64 entire Palestinian communities and parts of 15 additional communities, affecting nearly 5,000 people, according to data from Israeli rights group B’tselem.

On Friday Israeli gunmen opened fire at a group of unarmed Israeli and Palestinian activists as they attempted to peacefully reclaim Palestinian land seized by settlers in Beit Sahour, just outside Jerusalem. A Catholic bishop and journalists covering the event were also targeted by the attackers.

Mia Biran, from the group Combatants for Peace, said: “They are all the time threatened by the settlers. We were about a hundred activists, our goal was to clean the area, plant some trees, to show presence and to stand with the residents who are very scared. We were on private Palestinian land.”

“I called the police to tell them we are threatened by settlers, the activists who were at the roof saw there was a military Jeep all the time in the area who did nothing.”

After they withdrew from the area, settlers visited the nearby Palestinian home and threatened to burn it down, she added. Settlers regularly launch arson attacks on Palestinian homes. One such attack in 2015 killed a baby and his parents, orphaning their only surviving son.

A post on the National Rail website said all lines were closed between Wickford and Southend Victoria. This meant trains running between London Liverpool Street and Southend Victoria were unable to operate.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said on X that it had deployed inspectors to the site to gather evidence.

BTP declared a major incident on Thursday afternoon after the derailment near Lewes. About 150 people had been on the service from London Victoria to Eastbourne, which was evacuated. Two people were taken to major trauma centres with severe injuries. BTP said on Friday the injuries were not deemed to be life-threatening.

Southern urged customers planning to travel this weekend to check ahead as significant disruption was expected across parts of the network until further notice. Trains are expected to be extremely busy, with customers advised to allow at least one extra hour for their journey.

Frobisher said: “The unprecedented hot and dry weather that we have experienced this summer has presented exceptional challenges to the railway. In response, we have taken several additional proactive steps to manage and mitigate the impact on the railway, including closely monitoring the temperature of tracks, implementing speed restrictions where it is appropriate to do so, and planning track renewals around high temperatures.”

He added: “We will also conduct our own internal investigations, in which we will look at all possible causes and factors. I appreciate the public will be concerned at the news of two derailments of passenger trains over a short period of time, but I want to reassure them that Britain’s railways still rank among the safest in the world and that safety is always our first consideration on the railway.”

John Whitehurst, the chief executive of Greater Thameslink Railway (GTR), which operates Southern, praised four railway workers onboard the Lewes train – the driver, onboard supervisor, a spare driver and an off-duty member of staff – who initial reports suggested had “acted quickly to help make the railway safe and support passengers during the evacuation”.

“Their actions are a powerful example of colleagues putting passengers first in very difficult circumstances,” he said.

After the incident, Whitehurst insisted the railway was safe in hot weather. He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that derailments were “incredibly rare”, adding that what happened “was a very serious incident and I’m deeply saddened by it”. He said “a full investigation” was under way with the RAIB.

Richard Bowker, a former chair of the Strategic Rail Authority, told the same programme that the inquiry would look at the effects of heat on the damaged track, including whether the ground below the track had dried out.

James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat MP for Lewes, told Times Radio that concerns had been raised about tracks being “a bit bumpier in recent months” in the area as a result of the sustained heatwaves.

Gareth Dennis, a railway engineer and author of How the Railways Will Fix the Future, said although there was no firm evidence to connect the two derailments, “the likelihood of two similar derailments in the hottest part of the country happening in quick succession without a common cause is extremely low”.

He added that there was a high likelihood that the derailments were caused by a track buckle, where steel rails that have expanded in the heat snap into a buckled shape under the wheels of a passing train, though there are other possible causes.

Xueyu Geng, a professor in ground engineering at the University of Warwick, said steel rail was known to expand significantly in extreme heat, with a 1C rise in temperature causing approximately 11mm of expansion per kilometre of track.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are aware of a derailment involving a Greater Anglia train near Wickford, Essex. The train is upright, there are no reported injuries and investigators have already been deployed to the site.

“Our railways remain amongst the safest in the world and while incidents like this are extremely rare, when they do occur, they are taken very seriously.”

Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’

People in Stourbridge have described the fires that devastated more than a dozen homes as “horrendous” and “distressing”, with one describing blazes that surpassed the height of residential houses.

Multiple fires spread across the West Midlands on Thursday as temperatures reached record highs of 38.1C in the UK, during the country’s fifth consecutive heatwave.

Fifty-four people, including 19 who were taken to hospital, were treated at eight different fires on Thursday, West Midlands ambulance service said, with the fire service confirming 19 homes in Stourbridge, a market town in Dudley, had been fully destroyed and an additional 18 damaged.

During a visit to Stourbridge on Friday, Andy Burnham said the UK was like a “tinderbox” and announced the commission of firefighting planes to tackle future wildfires. “I’ve never seen scenes like this anywhere in Britain,” he told the BBC.

The Guardian spoke to people who were forced to hurriedly evacuate from their homes in Stourbridge on Thursday, as a wildfire spread near the town’s golf course.

They repeatedly praised the support and efforts of local authorities and neighbours, but are yet to return home, with some staying at a nearby hotel or a makeshift evacuation centre that had been set up at a local boarding school.

Gemma Hobbs, 46, and her partner, Andy, 61, were evacuated from their home on Osmaston Road on Thursday, as the wildfires raged over a mile away. Andy described seeing a house in flames.

Gemma said: “I looked out the windows and all I could see was thick black smoke. My husband came home in a bit of a flap and said: ‘We’ve got to get out. We’ve got to get out immediately.’”

Andy added: “It’s just the fact you don’t expect something to be as exponential as this so quickly. From the span of the area, it’s over 40 acres, that’s what we’ve been told.”

Gareth Jones, 59, was providing shelter to his neighbour John Bairner, who had to be evacuated overnight and said it was a “scene of devastation”, calling the wildfire “terrifying”.

“It was probably one of the scariest days of my life yesterday,” he said. “It was just the speed at which it spread, it was devastating. Absolutely frightening how quickly it spread. Within an hour. It’s a major event.”

Bairner added: “All of the fields have gone, they’re all black. There’s a lot of residents up there, with buckets, hoses, just dampening down because it’s still smouldering away up there.”

The Old Swinford hospital, a boarding school in Stourbridge, was set up as a makeshift evacuation centre for affected people late on Thursday.

As queues of cars and volunteers dropped off donations and supplies on Friday, the headteacher of the school, Paul Kilbride, described the fires as a “devastating experience”, with more than 20 people evacuated from a nearby care home.

“From what I saw, [the evacuees] were very tired and very anxious. I think they also showed great spirits [and] they obviously want to go home now,” he said. “This community suffered a lot yesterday.”

Laurence Green, 66, stayed at the Old Swinford hospital boarding school overnight after he was evacuated from his home on Osmaston Road. Green said he saw “plumes of smoke” on Thursday afternoon before he was directed by police to evacuate to the town hall.

The Guardian view on Nigel Farage: Clacton cannot acquit him

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:06:32 GMT

Reform won a contrived byelection, but scrutiny continues – while the party increasingly attacks the watchdogs and journalists asking awkward questions

Nigel Farage didn’t attend the count of the byelection he forced upon Clacton. Instead, Reform UK’s leader celebrated his win with supporters at a “Farage Fest”, filmed by a friendly TV channel. For a politician who claims to speak for the people, it was telling that at his triumph he preferred an audience of believers.

Mr Farage won because his toughest opponent on the campaign trail was a comedian in a jumpsuit with a bin on his head. That Count Binface nevertheless won 27% of the vote captured the absurdity of a contest the main parties had boycotted as a Faragist stunt. Reform UK’s leader wanted to turn scrutiny of his finances – notably an investigation into whether he failed to report a £5m gift from an overseas crypto billionaire – into a “fight” with the “establishment”. But the result determined who represents the Essex seat, not whether he broke parliamentary or electoral rules.

There is no drop in enthusiasm among Mr Farage’s Clacton supporters. But he engineered an election in the safest territory – and despite facing no significant competition, had 37% vote against him. If even this part of the country can mobilise a substantial anti-Reform protest vote when the main parties stand aside, then imagine what might be possible in marginals where a mainstream challenger would prove more formidable.

Mr Farage also hasn’t escaped the accountability he was trying to outrun. The parliamentary commissioner for standards suspended the investigation when he stopped being an MP; his re-election means the inquiry has resumed. It covers both the millions from the Thailand-based crypto magnate Christopher Harborne, and alleged undeclared support from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

A mandate is not an acquittal. If the commissioner finds a serious breach of the rules and Mr Farage is suspended for 10 or more Commons sitting days, a recall petition in Clacton would follow. If 10% of electors signed it – roughly 1,500 fewer than voted for Count Binface – another byelection would be triggered. This time Mr Farage would face voters after parliamentary censure and a successful recall campaign, not just, as Labour claimed, reeking of the “stench of sleaze”. With the main parties likely to stand, the anti-Farage vote could also coalesce behind one serious challenger – and present a tougher test.

A disturbing pattern is emerging around Reform’s intimidatory tactics. Questions about its funding are repeatedly answered not openly but by attacking those asking. A parliamentary watchdog becomes a “kangaroo court”; Reform deputy leader Richard Tice’s lawyers seek material that could identify sources behind the Guardian’s investigation; and a prominent Farage ally reportedly hired private investigators to examine a Sunday Times journalist investigating the party’s finances.

This is likely to backfire for Reform. Last September the party was polling 32% nationally. After Mr Farage announced in July that he was triggering a byelection, it dropped from 27% to 24% – squeezed by a resurgent Labour, recovering Conservative party and Restore Britain’s more extreme policies. As even supporters such as Tim Montgomerie acknowledge, a political party built on voters’ grievances has now become increasingly preoccupied with its own grievances about the media, investigations and treatment of Mr Farage. The result is that Reform appears inward-looking, defensive and sleazy. That will probably damage the party more than its angry, divisive nationalism, which demonises minorities and shreds Britain’s traditions of tolerance and pluralism.

The Guardian view on booming poetry sales: Homer, meet the Instapoets

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:05:22 GMT

In an unexpected twist, a Hollywood epic has contributed to Britain’s best-ever half-year in poetry sales

In a short story called Career Move, published in the New Yorker in 1992, Martin Amis imagined a world in which screenwriters wrote for little magazines and earned a pittance while poets were global superstars. Amis’s story, a wonderfully ironic inversion of the time-honoured norm, was surprisingly prescient: the film and TV industries have been struggling, with screenwriters facing contracting outlets for their creations, whereas poets are now big business.

The Bookseller reported recently that poetry sales were at a historic high. Part of the increase can be attributed to Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey, which has made Homer hot: editions of The Odyssey and its prequel, The Iliad, have garnered almost £1m in book sales in the UK this year. (As well as valiantly trying to keep the ailing film industry afloat, Nolan has also created a craze for epic poetry.) But Nolan’s film does not solely account for the boom in poetry sales. Even without the Homer run, sales of poetry texts and anthologies were still up by 7.2% from what was historically already a very high base.

The poets leading the charge are not the traditional behemoths – Berryman and the Brownings, Marvell and Milton, Pope and Pound. These remain acquired tastes, read (if at all) in the beleaguered bowers and tottering towers of organised “Eng lit”. The publishing sensations fuelling the poetic sales surge are “Instagram poets” such as Donna Ashworth, Rupi Kaur, Amanda Lovelace and Lucas Jones, whose collection, I Still Believe in Miracles, has netted £400,000 in sales this year.

The appeal of this new generation lies in their directness. They want to be our new best friend. “Maybe you kinda feel how I feel,” says Jones in the introduction to I Still Believe in Miracles. The American poet Lovelace dedicates her 2022 collection, unlock your storybook heart (she eschews capital letters throughout), to “anyone who feels like they’ve yet to find themselves: i promise it’s not too late”. Lovelace advises readers to practise “self-care before, during and after reading”.

Critics dismiss such work as more therapy than poetry, and argue it should be filed under self-help. Since the emergence of Instapoetry online in the middle of the last decade, a fault line has developed among poets as well as critics. Rebecca Watts’ dismissal in a 2018 article in PN Review, a poetry journal, of poets such as Kaur, Kae Tempest and Hollie McNish as “artless and amateur”, laid bare the divisions. The Instapoets have now successfully migrated to print, but the arguments continue. Is this literature for a post-literate age, or a healthy riposte to canonical poets (mostly “male, pale and stale” in the eyes of their detractors)?

A corrective to the canon is no doubt overdue, and poets who appeal to a young readership beset by mental health issues should not be written off. But there are dangers. In June, Faber published Talking in Bed, a slim anthology of Philip Larkin poems in which there is a sense of Larkin being co-opted by the poetry-as-therapy movement. “He finds a way of admitting and delineating our nagging questions and most complicated feelings,” intones the blurb. The acerbic Larkin would not, one suspects, have appreciated this. Poetry should be allowed to be hermetic as well as accessible, and threatening as well as therapeutic.

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:00:33 GMT

Situation ‘very worrying’, says former teammate

Mystery surrounds a highly regarded British Athletics coach who has not been heard from since visiting Morocco around two months ago.

Leon Baptiste, 41, who coaches a number of elite athletes including the Paris Olympic 4x400m relay bronze medallist Charlie Dobson, is believed to have gone to Morocco for the weekend with some close friends for a stag do or golf trip.

However, he has not been heard from since by his athletes or the UK Athletics officials who pay him as a Loughborough-based consultant, with messages to his phone not returned.

UKA have declined to comment, citing confidentiality. The Guardian spoke to a former British teammate of Baptiste, who said: “He was a very calm and sensible chap, in my experience. No one knows what has happened. It is very worrying.”

Dobson has struggled with injuries in Baptiste’s absence and failed to make it out of the 400m semi-finals at the European championships in Birmingham earlier this week.

After finishing fourth in his semi-final in a time of 45.18sec, over a second outside his personal best of 44.14 set last year, Dobson alluded to the situation when he said it had been “an interesting eight weeks”.

He also said he had been struggling with some injury niggles that had contributed to his withdrawal from the recent Commonwealth Games. He did not compete in the heats of the men’s 4x400m on Friday morning and it remains to be seen if he returns to the track for Sunday evening’s final.

In the meantime UKA staff have stepped in to help Dobson and the rest of Baptiste’s group, with former European 400m champion and relays coach Martyn Rooney taking Dobson under his wing.

Baptiste was a talented sprinter who won 200m and 4x100m relay gold at the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi before being forced to retire aged 28 because of a serious knee issue.

Surgery resulted in him missing the London 2012 Olympics before he moved into coaching after deciding not to defend his Commonwealth titles at the 2014 Games in Glasgow.

“As much as I am sprinting and progressing, my body has never fully recovered from my knee surgery,” he said that year. “My coach and I feel that Glasgow Commonwealth Games qualification is a tall order – so the time has come for my focus to move elsewhere.

“The decision for an athlete to retire is never easy, but in essence the decision has been made for me.”

The British Embassy in Rabat has been approached for comment.

Family affair: how pop-star siblings Audrey Hobert and Malcolm Todd stormed the charts in parallel

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:00:33 GMT

Following in the footsteps of Michael and Janet Jackson, and Kylie and Dannii Minogue, the Hobert siblings have simultaneously struck pop gold – with no rivalry

The history of rival sibling pop solo acts is a limited but potent one. Most famous, of course, are Michael and Janet Jackson. Kylie and Dannii Minogue, Billie Eilish and Finneas, Beyoncé and Solange, Natasha and Daniel Bedingfield, Neneh and Eagle-Eye Cherry, Jessica and Ashlee Simpson, and Brandy and Ray J all share the intimate and rare understanding of what it was like to share Lego sets and chart space.

That strange dynamic recently gained a new pairing. The US artists Audrey Hobert, 27, and her younger brother, who performs as Malcolm Todd, 22, have both scored global hits synonymous with the sound of summer 2026.

Two years after Todd released the song Earrings, a lovelorn track sung over the music to Steve Lacy’s 2022 megahit Bad Habit, it started blowing up in April, rising to a peak of No 16 in the UK and No 20 in the US. Just as his song started to slip down the charts, Hobert’s ultra-wordy, ultra-catchy track Sue Me started breaking through, vaulting up the UK Top 40 weekly since early June. It reached a new peak of No 29 this week, and cracked the Billboard Hot 100 two weeks ago.

In 2026, music fans are used to family dynasties ruling over music thanks to the rise of the pop star nepo baby: Gracie Abrams (daughter of director JJ Abrams), Willow Smith (Will and Jada Pinkett Smith), Mabel (Neneh Cherry), Maya Hawke (Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman), Romy Mars (Sofia Coppola and Phoenix frontman Thomas Mars) to name but a few.

The Hoberts are not exactly nepo babies, though they have showbiz links: their father is a TV showrunner who worked on Scrubs and the Nickelodeon kids’ show on which Hobert, a screenwriting graduate, got her start. She then started writing songs with Gracie Abrams, a childhood best friend, resulting in six co-writing credits on Abrams’ second album, 2024’s The Secret of Us.

Hobert’s work with Abrams earned her a publishing deal and later a solo record contract with RCA. She has cited Taylor Swift, Lena Dunham and the comedian Nathan Fielder as inspirations; her loquacious, rhythmic songwriting, full of offbeat narratives about awkward but hopeful loners, mines the sounds of pure pop and pop-punk synonymous with Y2K MTV. She released her debut solo album, Who’s the Clown?, last August. Fellow breakout pop superstar Role Model recently described her slapstick-heavy live show as “one of the best things I’ve ever seen” on the cult How Long Gone podcast. “She’s doing something very new, which is hard to do onstage.”

Todd’s USP, meanwhile, is a sort of blue-eyed, heart-on-sleeve take on indie-R&B inspired by the likes of Steve Lacy and Omar Apollo. He started making music seriously during the pandemic, and postponed going to university in order to pursue pop stardom. It worked: he signed with Columbia and released his debut mixtape for the label, Sweet Boy, in 2024. This week, he appeared in a Gap ad covering Robyn’s Dancing on My Own.

There appears to be no rivalry between the pair, who frequently boost each other’s careers. She directed the video for his 2025 single Concrete; after he covered her song Phoebe on Australian radio station Triple J’s noted covers session Like a Version in April, she returned the favour in May, covering Earrings for the same slot. Last weekend, the pair duetted on Phoebe during Hobert’s performance at San Francisco’s Outside Lands festival, where she drew one of the festival’s bigger crowds.

Todd told the Face that it was no surprise his sister had found musical success, even if the aspiring screenwriter always said that her goals were working in film and TV. “You just have to watch 30 seconds of a video of her when she was eight years old and you’d be like, ​‘Yeah, there’s no way in the world this girl doesn’t become a pop star.’”

Hobert told Triple J that Todd “deserves every good thing that’s happening and it’s just gonna keep on happening … the head on his shoulders is so straight and he’s just never strayed from the guy he is. He’s always been this guy. He is funny. He is smart. He knows he’s talented and his ego does not fill up a room.”

Hobert and Todd’s respective steady rises are symbolic of how breakout pop careers are made today. Rare is the bolt-from-the-blue debut single such as Olivia Rodrigo’s 2021 smash Drivers License (though that built on her years-long Disney Channel career). It took Chappell Roan seven months to blow up after the release of her debut album, which itself came after years of grinding in the pop underground and being dropped by her former label. This year also saw Zara Larsson tower over pop thanks to two slow-burning older hits, last year’s Midnight Sun – and 2015’s Lush Life. TikTok discovery is often the fuel behind these rises.

UK audiences will have to wait to see Todd, who embarks on a long tour of North America in September. But Hobert will appear in the UK later this month, playing solo dates and festival appearances supporting Lorde in London and Bristol.
