Donald Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:00:32 GMT

The FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practice

It is bad enough that the Trump administration blocked a federal criminal investigation when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent killed Renee Good as she was turning her car away from him in Minneapolis the past January. Just before the shooting, Good and her partner had been observing and protesting against ICE officers.

Instead, it turns out the administration has been investigating progressive and even mainstream groups that have been involved in protests against Donald Trump’s sweeping deportations, according to newly released government documents.

That Trump’s deportations have prompted widespread outrage is hardly surprising. The president arguably had an electoral mandate to secure the US-Mexican border but not to raid workplaces and neighborhoods to deport undocumented immigrants.

Most such immigrants in the United States are now settled. They have been in the country for more than five years, and many have US-citizen children, work at regular jobs, pay taxes and are active members of their communities. Few Americans want their neighbors or work colleagues summarily deported.

In January, Minnesota was a center of Trump’s deportation efforts. He deployed about 3,000 federal agents to this blue state to comb the streets in search of immigrants to deport. The public soon took to the streets in opposition, with some protesters using their phones to record detentions while others sounded the alarm that Trump’s agents were in the vicinity.

Yet rather than conduct an inquiry into the deportation agents’ often-unbridled violence, the administration turned its prosecutorial sights on the protesters. In what it called “Operation Puppet Master”, it used its enormous investigative powers to pursue a vendetta against an array of groups that opposed its deportation agenda.

Federal investigators justified the investigation by claiming that these groups might have provided help and money to the allegedly “violent opportunists and agitators” on the street. They also claimed that these groups provided “domestic terrorist financing”. This language parallels Trump’s directive last September expanding the definition of domestic terrorism to include using violence or intimidation to obstruct the rule of law.

Even if violence or other lawlessness occasionally broke out among the protesters, it is a huge leap to suggest that civic groups were criminally complicit. Federal conspiracy law is broad but not limitless. It requires two or more people to agree to commit a federal crime and for the accused to be a part of that agreement.

It would hardly be surprising that various progressive groups banded together to monitor and oppose Trump’s deportations. But those activities are protected by the first amendment to the US constitution. They are completely lawful.

For the Trump administration to transform coordinated protests into a criminal conspiracy, it would have to show that the targeted groups knew the protests would obstruct federal agents “by force, intimidation or threat” and that such criminality was a purpose of their coordination. That is an enormous stretch.

The role of federal prosecutor is powerful. A prosecutor can destroy a target’s life with the reputational sting and financial burden of a criminal prosecution. Before I joined Human Rights Watch, I served for more than four years in the 1980s as a federal prosecutor, mainly in New York City. My experience was that most federal prosecutors were aware of their power and tried to wield it in good faith.

Trump’s criminal hounding of groups that oppose him shows no such deference to the requirements of justice.

The first warning sign was that the Trump administration didn’t even use the justice department or its FBI, which traditionally pursue criminal investigations. Even though Trump has decimated the department, sparking the departure of many career officials who refused to be tainted by the president’s personal vendettas and politicized prosecutions, the administration chose instead to deploy the Department of Homeland Security.

The DHS in turn issued administrative subpoenas, which do not require judicial authorization, and used other intrusive techniques to collect records and wire transfers from certain progressive groups going back three years – long before the anti-deportation protests began. That suggests what prosecutors refer to as a fishing expedition – the abuse of prosecutorial powers, in the absence of concrete evidence of wrongdoing, in the blind hope that something untoward might surface.

Undercover federal investigators also spied on public meetings and even infiltrated group chats on Signal as activists discussed protests and their political opinions. Agents recorded license plate numbers to determine who was attending protest meetings.

For example, at a 31 January meeting in a Minneapolis library, a homeland security undercover officer listened as supporters of a progressive climate group, the Sunrise Movement, discussed sit-ins, de-escalation tactics, and “having a police liaison and safety marshal present during events”. The agent at least had the honesty to report back that the Sunrise Movement organization focused on “peaceful” protests.

However, the Trump administration has charged 15 people with obstructing federal immigration operations in Minnesota using vehicles and other objects. The 94-page indictment does not allege injuries to specific ICE officers or serious violence, but asserts that activists set up blockades around government buildings, threw chunks of ice at federal vehicles and “stalked” agents. Similar charges in parallel cases have already been dismissed or dropped at an unusually high rate.

So far, none of the groups under investigation has been criminally charged, but prosecutors showed a grand jury a PowerPoint slide claiming that 18 groups were part of a conspiracy to impede Trump’s deportation agents in Minnesota.

The broad investigation brings back memories of a prior example of egregious federal misconduct targeting perceived leftist groups. Under the notorious J Edgar Hoover, the FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s conducted Cointelpro to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations, especially those that promoted Black civil rights or opposed the Vietnam war. Exposure of these outrages led to major reforms, which the Trump administration now seems determined to reverse.

Many hope that the coming midterm elections in November will repudiate Trump’s lawlessness. Republicans are at risk of losing one or both houses of Congress. Yet this apparent abuse of criminal investigative powers reminds us that the presidency is powerful even without the legislative power of Congress.

Fortunately, the judicial system has managed to halt much of Trump’s deportation overreaching. Even grand juries, which traditionally show enormous deference to prosecutors, have been rejecting requests to bring charges. Moreover, while politicized federal prosecutors have ignored much of the misconduct by Trump’s deportation agents, some state prosecutors have tried to pick up the ball.

Yet much remains to be done as Trump seems determined to find ways to evade even adverse supreme court judgments. Exposure by journalists, protests by civic groups and outrage by the public are often the only tools we have.

Responding to the Trump administration’s misconduct, Unidos MN, a human rights group in Minnesota, said that the government is “lashing out desperately in hopes of intimidating people and organizations that have shown the power of communities acting together”. This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

Standards watchdog resumes Farage probe as rivals slam needless byelection

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 17:00:23 GMT

Reform UK leader says he stayed away from vote count in Clacton to avoid being ‘humiliated by nobodies’

Nigel Farage’s attempt to draw the sting from inquiries into his financial affairs appeared to have backfired on Friday as the standards watchdog reopened its investigation and MPs from all sides condemned the needless byelection.

The Reform UK leader declared victory in the Clacton vote as he was returned with an increased majority and gained more votes than in 2024, saying he had “stuck two fingers up at the entire political establishment”.

However, parliament’s standards commissioner immediately reopened an investigation into whether he should have declared a series of gifts provided to him shortly before the last general election.

These include a £5m personal gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, and further financial support from his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

Rival parties said the reopening of the inquiry showed Farage’s attempt to avoid scrutiny had failed, with the Labour party chair, Bridget Phillipson, saying he now had “no hiding place” as he tries to “dodge and deflect” criticism.

But at an event to celebrate his win, the Reform UK leader attempted to diminish the significance of the allegations under investigation.

He told GB News: “If I’ve made one sin, it’s that I haven’t filled in a piece of paper. I’ve broken no law, I’ve broken no tax law, I’ve taken no public money … maybe I haven’t filled in a piece of paper. I’m confident I’m right, let’s see where we go.”

While playing down the inquiry, Farage also appeared to acknowledge the watchdog could well find against him over his failure to be transparent. If a separate standards committee of MPs recommend a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, it could then trigger a second byelection.

This would require the approval of more than 10% of the electorate of Clacton – about 7,800 voters – which is less than the number who voted for Farage’s main rival, the satirical candidate Count Binface.

Farage also faced criticism for failing to turn up to the Clacton count in Essex, saying he had been told by police of an organised attempt at disruption.

However, police said they had given no advice to any candidate not to attend and it emerged that an anonymous art collective flashmob in masks were demonstrating 15 minutes away from the venue at Clacton town hall.

At a separate event, Farage gave an explanation for failing to attend the count saying he was “damned” if he was going to stand on a stage to be “demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”. It was not clear if he was talking about the array of more than 30 independent candidates who stood against him or the possibility of a protest.

Tim Montgomerie, a Reform UK commentator and supporter, was among those to criticise his non-appearance.

“He should be on every TV screen this morning,” said Montgomerie, “underlining his win – and with that cheeky, trademark smile on his face … his recently far too dominant aggrieved tone is still with us.

“It’s not good. You don’t skip your own victory count without a much better explanation. Anger from politicians can work but only if it’s on behalf of others – not yourself. He’s distracting from his victory.”

Farage called the byelection early in July saying he wanted voters in Clacton to decide if he was fit to be an MP. However, the stunt did not go to plan after all the main parties declined to stand, leaving him taking on dozens of novelty and fringe candidates, most prominent among them Count Binface.

According to one report, Farage called his own byelection after his team advised that leaving parliament would end the investigation. In fact it only pauses such processes, which resume if the person is re-elected.

Farage has said the investigation was “being used as a political tool”. One Reform MP, Sarah Pochin, called the process a “kangaroo court”.

Lee Anderson, the chair of Reform, said on Friday it was a “fair comment” to describe the parliamentary standards process as a kangaroo court and argued that there were questions over whether it would be impartial.

Farage is expected to be interviewed by the standards commissioner when parliament returns but it is not certain when the investigation will conclude.

Labour said on Friday that the resumption of the investigation showed Farage could not outrun questions about his finances, with at least 10 questions still outstanding, including whether Harborne had given money to any other Reform-linked figures.

Phillipson said: “He forced a byelection he didn’t need to have. He stood again. He spent most of the summer chasing a bin around Clacton.

“And now he’s going to come back to parliament and have to answer some very serious questions, questions he’s been seeking to dodge, distracting and deflecting from the £5m … gift, his connections to a convicted fraudster.

“You know, the scandal just keeps piling up. And now he’s through that byelection, there’s no hiding place.”

A Conservative party spokesperson said the byelection was a “farce started by Nigel Farage to try to dodge scrutiny of his fishy £5m personal donation”.

“All Farage can brag about this morning is beating a bloke with a bin on his head. What he should do is answer the serious outstanding questions about why he hid his £5m from the public,” the spokesperson said.

The Reform UK leader won the contest with more than 22,000 votes – or 63% – on a turnout of 44%.

Friends of Farage suggested he would not be taking much of a break and intended to throw himself back into Reform campaigning and building up a presence in target seats in case of an early general election.

Police Scotland warns ‘robust security’ needed to stop attacks on AI datacentres

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:05:31 GMT

‘A great deal of public opposition is likely’ to a proposed datacentre near Edinburgh, the force says

Police in Scotland have issued a stark warning about the need for “robust security measures” to stop proposed AI datacentres from being attacked by protesters.

There has been mounting opposition to AI infrastructure globally, including in the US where such projects have become a significant political rallying point.

Police Scotland said “a great deal of public opposition is likely” to a datacentre planned in Larbert, about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, in a letter submitted as a part of a planning consultation this month.

The letter encouraged the datacentre’s developer to liaise with the police to prevent “unplanned incursions for the purposes of disruption”.

It appears to be one of the first official acknowledgments of mounting public unease about datacentre development in the UK. Police Scotland declined to comment.

There are hundreds of datacentre projects in various stages of planning in Britain. Only some of these appear to be viable developments, with research groups warning of a glut of “zombie projects” waiting to connect to the grid.

In Scotland there are at least 23 “hyperscale” datacentre developments in the planning process, according to the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS). Combined, they would use more than one and a half times the power that Scotland uses at peak demand.

Groups across Scotland have started organising opposition to planned datacentres. More than 100 people attended a protest in Larbert on Thursday, according to local campaigners. Nearly 7,000 people have filed objections to the proposed development.

Similar protests are planned in the coming weeks, including one in Edinburgh in early September, when the Scottish parliament will be back in session.

This summer, the Scottish National party passed a motion to freeze all new datacentres in Scotland. If that motion becomes Scottish government policy, it could pose a serious threat to the UK’s AI strategy. British officials have been pushing datacentre developers to build in Scotland.

Some of the opposition to datacentres is about the physical footprint of the projects. Michael Maciocia, a Larbert resident who attended Thursday’s protest, said he and others were worried about the 200 diesel generators that Apatura, the site’s developer, planned to install as backup power for the datacentre.

APRS is concerned that these could release significant quantities of nitrous oxide into the air, which could negatively affect the health of people living nearby.

“Where this datacentre is planned to be built, within 50 metres of one of the buildings is a 56-bed care home for the terminally ill … Within 400 metres, there’s the 860-bed Forth Valley Royal hospital,” said Maciocia. “The amount of pollution and the noise created by these things will be horrendous in every direction.”

Hazel McQueen, who also lives nearby, said: “I live extremely close to the proposed site, and since this application was submitted it has become a huge part of my life.” She says she has spent hours on top of her full-time job reading about the datacentre, attending meetings and helping to organise opposition to it.

She says she is concerned for the health of her family, and of her grandson who has leukaemia. “I need to fight this for his future and the future we are leaving for him.”

Cecilia Rikap, a professor at University College London, says there is a larger, symbolic dimension to public anger around datacentre development.

“It’s the physical manifestation of AI, and there is a growing opposition to AI. People are seeing how AI is replacing the good part of their work, people are seeing how AI is undermining younger people’s capacity to think,” she said. “Ultimately, if you want to protest against generative AI or the role of big tech, you would protest at a datacentre. That’s what you can see. All the rest is much more invisible.”

A spokesperson for Apatura said: “We’re committed to developing data centres in line with world-leading safety and environmental standards and in compliance with all planning regulations. We recognise that there has been opposition to the planning application and remain committed to working closely with government and local community throughout the planning process to ensure concerns are listened to and carefully considered.”

Donald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losers

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:03:05 GMT

The pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted them

It’s a shame Nigel Farage ducked the announcement of his victory in the Clacton byelection, which confirmed his return as MP for the seat he had needlessly resigned from just a few weeks earlier. You’d have thought he would have loved it. It was the culmination of a stunt, an exercise in politics as performance. It was a display animated by – and seeking to inflame – grievance, a million miles away from the hard, grinding work of tackling the problems that underlie those grievances. It was an attempt to deflect scrutiny, distract attention and evade responsibility. It was, in other words, everything nationalist populists like him excel at. Indeed, the only thing.

Reform UK said Farage stayed away because Essex police had warned of a “credible threat” to his security, a claim swiftly denied by Essex police. (Add a flexible approach to the truth to that list of nationalist populists’ talents.) Still, it was a slightly odd claim to make. Recall Farage’s favoured explanation – there are others – for the undeclared £5m gift he received from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, which prompted the very parliamentary investigation that so riled the Reform leader he felt compelled to quit his seat and seek a preemptive not guilty verdict from the people of Clacton: namely, that he needed the money to pay for private, enhanced security. It seems £5m was not quite enough to ensure the lucky recipient would be safe standing next to a man dressed as a bin.

Unless, maybe, security was not the whole story. Farage also said he skipped the count because he didn’t want to be “demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”. Quite right. If Nigel Farage is to be demeaned and humiliated, it should be by people of standing. As it happens, he may get his wish. Now that he’s an MP again, the probe into the multiple financial questions that surround him, including over the undeclared support he received from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell, has resumed. A finding against him could necessitate yet another byelection, except this time the major parties will not repeat their boycott and he will have to do battle with opponents even more formidable than an aristocratic trash can.

Naturally, Farage regards the likes of Count Binface and Baron von Thunderclap as beneath him, perhaps because it would be painful to admit the crucial thing they all have in common. To understand what that is, look no further than the man who is both Farage’s hero and the exemplar of nationalist populism.

Ten years ago, less than five months after the Brexit referendum that represents Farage’s greatest triumph, Donald Trump rode a similar wave of US discontent with the status quo and did it in a similar way – by railing against an ill-defined establishment that had ruined everything. A vote for him would make it all better because, as Trump put it: “I alone can fix it.” In 2024, he was elected once again, on a similar promise.

That victory proved Trump’s mastery of a certain strain of politics. His gift for seizing public attention, for channelling a society’s collective anxieties and for persuading people that a simple remedy is at hand, is unrivalled. While Farage plays the same tunes, Trump is the virtuoso.

And yet, look at what happens once the carnival of the campaign is over and the governing begins. Trump’s record is disastrous. He was elected to tackle inflation, which he claimed was out of control under Joe Biden, but inflation is higher now than it was in November 2024, when he defeated his predecessor. Petrol prices, the indicator Trump repeatedly invoked on the stump in 2024, have leapt up. This, more than any other single factor, helps explain why Trump’s approval ratings have cratered, falling to just 34%.

And yet Trump, whose appeal centred on his persona as a successful businessman – a persona that held, despite a career of failure and serial bankruptcy – is doing almost nothing to improve the economic fortunes of those who voted for him. I don’t mean that he’s trying to pull various policy levers and they’re not working. I mean he’s not trying. As Jonathan Swan, co-author of Regime Change, an eye-popping account of the first 15 months of this second Trump term, told me for the Politics Weekly America podcast: “He’s bored by economic policy.”

Of course, those petrol prices did not rise all by themselves. What drove up the price of oil was the decision that seems set to define this presidency: the war on Iran that began on 28 February. It has proved a calamity. It has failed to achieve any of the admittedly shifting goals Trump declared for it: there has been no regime change in Tehran; Iran’s nuclear threat remains unchecked, while its nuclear ambition is now surely greater, if only to deter a repeat of that US-Israeli attack. And it has barely set back Iran’s conventional capability, judging by the regime’s continuing ability to strike its neighbours. As if all that were not bad enough, Trump has succeeded in making the Iranians stronger than they were on 27 February, by handing them an economic weapon of mass disruption, a chokehold on the global economy in the form of their control of the strait of Hormuz.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Trump can do the performance, claiming to have “obliterated” the enemy one moment or to have made a breakthrough peace deal the next – but performance is all it is. While the Iranian missiles keep coming, the US military is fast running out of the munitions it needs either to intercept or hit back. Trump’s top general warned him of this danger from the start, but Trump waved away those objections, convinced that the war would be over quickly. Trump’s gut told him that Iran would go the way of Venezuela, that it would be fast and easy. His gut was wrong.

It keeps happening the same way. Trump will announce an agreement with Iran or between Hamas and Israel, only for it rapidly to become clear that no deal has been done. Trump lacks the patience for the long, painstaking, detailed work such diplomacy requires. He wants the sugar-rush of a social-media post or a headline. Put simply, he is a maestro of politics as it is now conducted, but he is useless at governing.

In this, the nationalist populists who take their lead from Trump are no different. They are good at raging at how things are, but incapable of making them better. They can articulate resentment and exploit grievance, but they cannot cure the ills that fuel that unhappiness. This, ultimately, is what unites Farage with Trump and indeed with those 33 “nobodies” who fought the byelection in Clacton. They are all protest candidates. It’s just that some of them get elected.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Iceberg, romaine, kale: which salad greens are healthiest?

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:00:32 GMT

If you’re trying to meet your daily serving of 2.5 cups of vegetables, you might have some questions

If you want to eat lettuce, that no longer just means iceberg. In our bountiful age, there are many options: romaine, red-leaf lettuce, butter lettuce, beet greens, bok choy, bitter radicchio, every developmental stage of arugula.

Sometimes, it’s simply up to preference. But if you’re trying to meet your daily serving of 2.5 cups of vegetables – or you’re rethinking your salad choices amid the US cyclospora outbreak, you might have some questions about which greens to go with.

Health authorities widely agree that a diet high in nutrient-dense fruits and vegetables is associated with reduced chronic disease risk. But which greens are giving you the most nutritional bang for your buck?

“Nutrient density”, defined as the “nutrients per calorie” of a food, can be a factor when shopping for produce, notes Jamie Mok, a Los Angeles–based registered dietitian nutritionist.

In 2014, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released a study attempting to help people better understand nutrient density via a ranking system that declared watercress a powerhouse champion, with 17 nutrients per calorie – almost twice the nutrient density as kale.

“Watercress is rich in vitamin K, vitamin C, minerals like calcium, manganese, copper and lots of phytochemicals, which are beneficial compounds that we find in plants,” says Mok, who grew up eating watercress in Chinese soups her mother made. “It’s a very light, delicate flavor.”

This doesn’t mean you should opt for watercress and ban other greens from your crisper. While watercress grabbed the CDC’s top spot, many other cruciferous greens, like green or Napa cabbage, kale or arugula, boast similar, substantial health benefits.

“Cruciferous vegetables contain a group of compounds called glucosinolates,” as well as vitamin C, vitamin K and fiber, explains Mok. “These are sulfur-containing compounds that have antioxidant activity.” Researchers believe glucosinolates support cancer-prevention.

Rather than focusing on only the most nutrient-dense greens, experts advise prioritizing variety. Even the fruits and veggies that scored lower on the CDC’s ranking, such as blackberries, leeks and sweet potatoes, offer their own substantial health benefits – they simply don’t have the breadth of nutrients cruciferous veggies pack per calorie.

“I don’t encourage people to focus on finding one ‘best’ leafy green,” says Dr Nina Cherie Franklin, a research scientist and health coach who goes by “That Salad Lady”. “Eating a variety is almost always the better approach. Spinach, kale, watercress, romaine, arugula, chard, collards, mustard greens, turnip greens and dandelion greens all bring something different to the bowl.”

For instance, one cup of shredded cabbage will net you about 2g of fiber and 28mg of vitamin C, but no vitamin A. A cup of spinach contains 1g of fiber, 9mg of vitamin C and 16mcg of vitamin A.

That means easy staples that include various vegetables are a good option, including boxed mesclun mix, which contains different leafy greens, such as mustard greens, arugula and different lettuces, notes Mok.

Many people believe that darker greens are healthier than lighter ones. Experts say that in terms of nutritional content, this is true – the rich hunter green of kale trumps the pallid hues of iceberg lettuce.

“Darker green vegetables are generally richer in nutrients, especially phytonutrients,” a kind of bioactive antioxidant-like compound, says Franklin.

But you don’t have to chuck your head of iceberg. “Lighter greens are far from nutritionally empty,” Franklin adds. “Romaine, butter lettuce, endive and other lettuces still provide vitamins, fiber, hydration and beneficial plant compounds.”

Some of the nutrients in greens are fat soluble – “particularly vitamins A, E and K”, says Mok. Adding healthy fats like avocado, olive oil or eggs to salad greens can help your body absorb their nutrition. “Sauteing them with a healthy fat like olive oil can help improve the absorption” of these important compounds too, says Mok.

Cooking also reduces the volume of greens, making it easier to eat larger quantities; two cups of raw leafy vegetables are the equivalent of a 1-cup vegetable serving.

When eating iron-heavy greens like spinach, Mok recommends pairing them with foods rich in vitamin C, which helps with iron absorption. Citrus, bell peppers and tomatoes are some good options, she says.

Heating to about 160F (71C) can make greens safer to consume, particularly if you’re concerned about risks posed by microorganisms like cyclospora, E coli or salmonella.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

“Washing raw produce can reduce dirt and some contamination, but no home-washing method can guarantee the removal of every organism,” says Franklin. “Cooking is more effective at reducing the risk of foodborne illness.”

If you simply must have a salad, clean your greens thoroughly. “For raw greens, the basics matter,” Franklin says. “Wash your hands and preparation surfaces, discard damaged leaves, rinse loose greens thoroughly under running water and dry them with a clean cloth, paper towel or a salad spinner.”

Up to 9% of foodborne illnesses caused by pathogens in the US are linked to leafy greens. This looks like an estimated 2.3m illnesses annually, costing the nation more than $5bn to address, according to research from the Ohio State University.

When it comes to waterborne pathogens like cyclosporiasis, the physical attributes of leaves make them susceptible to harboring disease, says Kristin Krokowski, a commercial horticulture educator at the University of Wisconsin–Madison.

The leaves of leafy green vegetables are bumpy, says Krokowski: “There’s lots of little places for the cyclospora to attach, and the fact that they’re heads – multiple layers of leaves – allows for space in between the leaves. So water isn’t evaporating quickly, and there’s more places to hide.”

The nooks and crannies of leafy greens also provide hiding places for the pathogens E coli, norovirus and salmonella, though these can also spread through the use of tools like cutters, or during harvest, transport or storage.

It’s one thing to stock up on leafy greens at the store, and another thing to actually eat them in a timely manner; we’ve all felt guilt over limp lettuce and slimy mesclun.

Research has found that some nutrients, like folate and vitamin C, can decrease when stored. But the good news is most vitamins and minerals, as well as fiber, remain stable in produce for days or weeks in the fridge.

“When stored properly, whole leafy greens can remain fresh for one to two weeks, depending on the variety and their condition,” says Franklin.

“There is no single point at which greens suddenly stop being nutritious,” she adds. How quickly nutrient loss happens “depends on factors such as how fresh greens were when purchased, how they were handled, and the temperature, humidity and moisture conditions in the refrigerator”.

“Cutting, bruising or otherwise damaging the leaves can also shorten their useful life,” she says.

Franklin says reusable cotton produce bags can work to preserve the freshness of greens because they allow some airflow without trapping too much moisture. “A regular plastic bag can also work when used properly,” she says. She recommends placing a slightly damp paper towel inside the plastic bag to help “manage humidity without allowing the greens to become soggy”.

You can also place a paper towel inside a plastic clamshell, then flip the box upside down – a method that can keep spinach crisp and odorless for up to two weeks.

“For whole, unprocessed greens that you’re not planning to use right away, I generally recommend storing them unwashed,” says Franklin. This is because washing introduces moisture, which can accelerate spoilage.

Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 16:00:31 GMT

Confirmed deal values club as a whole at £5.5bn

Amit Bhatia will become club’s new vice-chairman

Liverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.

Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.

Elaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.

Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.

FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.

It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.

Gordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.

“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”

With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.

Speaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.

“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”

Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.

Students squeezed out of university courses after bumper A-level grades

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:54:28 GMT

Students narrowly missing grades are being rejected, while some on oversubscribed courses are asked to defer

Students across the UK have found themselves unexpectedly squeezed out of their desired university courses as this year’s bumper crop of A-level grades ​h​as not always translated into ​​the places many were hoping for.

​With close to a third of the A-levels awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving the top A and A* grades this year, universities are taking a tougher stance by rejecting students who narrowly missed their expected grades and who in previous years would still have gained a place.

The stronger competition has tipped record numbers of applicants into clearing, or settling for their second choices, with universities in some cases wanting students to defer for a year.

Cardiff ​University ​h​as asked students on two programmes to defer until 2027, after more than expected achieved their required grades, leaving it with a surplus of qualified applicants for courses such as midwifery.​

The university said it had asked “a small number” of applicants to defer, with limits on its intake previously agreed with the Welsh government.

“We understand this will be deeply disappointing for those affected, and our immediate priority is to support these students and ensure they receive clear guidance as they consider their next steps,” a spokesperson for Cardiff said.

“It is important to be clear that Cardiff University has not over-offered places. As with all universities, offers are made based on detailed modelling of applicant behaviour and historical acceptance patterns. This year, an exceptionally high number of applicants met the conditions of their offers and accepted places, resulting in demand exceeding the number of commissioned places available.

“This has been an extremely difficult decision … and we explored every possible option to avoid activating the university’s oversubscription policy for these two courses.”

At least one applicant said she had complained to the Office for Students, telling Wales Online that Cardiff had offered her a £750 bursary to defer or lose her place. The Office for Students does not regulate universities in Wales.

Ucas figures show that this year, 73% of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland were given firm offers after grades were issued, below the 76% with firm offers in 2024 and 2025. A record 23,000 students have already deferred their places this year.

Figures published on Friday show record numbers of students were eligible for clearing, the post-results process to apply for courses with unfilled places.

The proportion of applicants receiving their first-choice course offer was lower this year at 79%, compared with 82% last year, while the proportion placed at their “insurance” choice increased.

The competition for places has increased as a result of selective universities growing less slowly than last year, despite record numbers of applications. While selective universities received almost 10% more applications this year, the universities have only increased offers by 5% compared with 2025.

The swathe of course closures and staff cuts set off by university restructuring has also affected students. Those offered places on geography courses at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus near Falmouth have now been told to either change courses or be moved to Exeter’s main campus in Devon, after the course closures were suddenly announced on Thursday.

Belgian student strikes gold worth €9m while digging a new sewer

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:52:31 GMT

Kobe, 18, who made discovery on site of former brewery in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, at first thought trove was €1 coins

For a student with a summer job working on a Belgian building site, “money down the drain” has taken on a whole new meaning: excavating the trenches for a sewage system, he stumbled across a hidden trove of gold worth an estimated €9m (£8m).

“We suddenly saw something lying there,” 18-year-old Kobe told the Belgian news network VTM. “At first I thought it was €1 coins. So we started digging them up. Then we saw a gold bar. It turned out to be a bit more than we thought.”

The student, who has not been further identified, was working with colleagues on the site of a former brewery on Van Langenhovestraat in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, about 19 miles (30km) north-west of Brussels, when they made the discovery on Tuesday.

The hoard, which includes gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars, was stashed in a bag in a bricked-in cellar wall beneath the grand villa originally built for the brewery’s owner, Theophilus Van Assche, in the late 19th century.

Kobe said: “It’s just not something you expect when you’re working on a regular Tuesday morning,” adding that the treasure trove appeared to have been deliberately hidden. “It was really bricked in there – not in a safe or anything.”

Brewing on the site began in 1899 and ceased in 1970, and the listed property – the wrought-iron gates of which still bear the initials “VA” – is being completely renovated by the social welfare organisation CAW Oost-Vlaanderen to create new offices and housing.

“The Brouwershuis was a beautiful building, but it is being completely gutted,” Geert Hillaert, of CAW, told the news outlet HLN. “Ultimately, only the walls will remain. Labourers were laying drainage pipes when they stumbled across the gold.”

Kobe and his colleagues called the police and notified CAW as soon as they came across the gold hoard. The treasure has since been transferred to a secure facility in Brussels pending a detailed official investigation to establish its legal ownership.

Hanne Ollevier, of the East Flanders public prosecutor’s office, told HLN that authorities must first verify that the bullion was not stolen property or the proceeds of criminal activity, and was likely to spark a complex civil dispute.

The building contractors, the welfare organisation and any descendants of the once-wealthy Van Assche family could all have a claim to part of the fortune. Belgian law requires finders to wait at least five years for potential owners to claim any treasure.

A former mayor of Dendermonde, Piet Buyse, told HLN that the Van Assche’s fortune had “certainly stayed in the family. It wouldn’t surprise me at all if they had decided to put at least some of it in gold, and then to hide it in a safe place.”

For his part, Kobe said he and his colleagues had understood straight away that they had to hand over such a big find. “If it had been a few coins, maybe not,” he said. “But maybe we’ll get some kind of finder’s reward eventually.”

Smart glasses controversy sidelines the benefits for disabled people

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:22:59 GMT

Guardian readers reflect on the ableism rife in the debate about Ray-Ban Meta eyewear, despite the life-changing difference they can make

Your editorial on Meta’s smart glasses acknowledges their value to blind and visually impaired people, then asks that this “not be allowed to distract” from the harms (The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot, 10 August). As an optometrist who owns a small independent practice, I’d suggest that it is visually impaired people who are being treated as the distraction.

I was reluctant to stock Ray‑Ban Meta, having no fondness for Meta or Luxottica, but colleagues persuaded me of the benefits for people with sight impairment. The reality has surpassed that. The majority of our buyers have a visual impairment or learning difficulty. One man, practically illiterate, now has the world read to him.

For many of these patients, leaving the house is already an act of courage. Unfamiliar streets, unreadable signs, the constant low-level anxiety of navigating a world built for the fully sighted. These glasses have quietly made that easier. A week of coverage branding them “pervert glasses” has now added a new anxiety: not whether they can manage the journey, but whether strangers will assume the worst of them for wearing the thing that makes it possible.

A colleague of mine was recently branded a misogynist online, by another optometrist, simply for suggesting the glasses were useful. Opening a Guardian leader with a nickname worthy of a Murdoch red-top – “pervert glasses” – makes that hostility respectable.

The harms you describe are real and worth regulating. But on a recent holiday I left my own pair in the hotel room, yet watched hundreds of people photographing poolside on their phones, my daughters frequently in the background, with no permission sought and no bans imposed. The glasses at least announce themselves with a recording light. Pubs, parks and beaches are indeed not film sets, but they have been full of cameras for 20 years. Regulate by all means. Just remember who ends up wearing the stigma. Aled BrassingtonRomiley, Greater Manchester

Much of the coverage of Meta’s smart glasses has been dominated by the language of “spy glasses” and “predator glasses”, while disabled people’s experiences have barely featured. To its credit, your recent report recognised how useful the glasses can be for blind and disabled people (‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinion, 6 August). Even so, accessibility still feels like a side issue in the wider debate around smart glasses.

I have severe muscular dystrophy and cannot pick up or operate a smartphone. My Ray-Ban Meta glasses let me make calls, send WhatsApp messages, take photos and record moments by voice. I can start a video call without touching a phone. These are not gimmicks. They give me independence and help keep me connected and safe.

I can’t speak for Mark Zuckerberg or defend Meta’s wider record on privacy. But I’ve met Meta developers and scientists working on accessibility. Their commitment is real. They are listening to disabled people and building features that can change lives.

There are legitimate privacy concerns. Secretly filming anyone is unacceptable. Meta should improve the recording light, prevent people disabling it, act against abusive content and be clearer about data use. Regulation must keep up.

But it is wrong to treat everyone wearing these glasses as suspicious, or to impose blanket bans that may exclude disabled people who rely on them for communication, information or safety. Venues can ban recording without banning the glasses themselves.

Phones, doorbells, dashcams and other cameras can all be misused. The answer is to tackle misuse, not demonise a technology or the people who depend on it. Many disabled people are tired of seeing this demonisation while our voices remain absent from the debate raging around smart glasses. We should not have to choose between privacy and independence. We should insist on both. Colin HughesLondon

As it happens, I am visually impaired and find smart glasses very useful. They enable me to read menus and notices and will even translate foreign notices for me. However, I consider recent moves to ban these products from certain premises to be ludicrous.

There have been cases of people using smartphones for illicit purposes, for example surreptitiously filming up women’s skirts. However, nobody has dubbed smartphones “pervert phones” or sought to ban them. Some of the same premises which are now trying to do this to smart glasses also have CCTV, which films everybody without their consent, as do many cameras in our streets including doorbell cameras and dash cams.

I am sure that the vast majority of smart glasses wearers use the product responsibly and would not dream of filming people without their consent. The theoretical possibility that they might do something bad is not a reason to ban the product entirely. You might as well ban the sale of kitchen knives, in case we use them to stab each other, or even cars in case we use them to run somebody over!Dr Alastair ForbesBridport, Dorset

At a loss as to which Stephen Moss you’re referring to? So are many others

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:22:19 GMT

Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss find the humour in having the same name and working for the same company

At least the Guardian’s Ewan Murray and Sky Sports’ Ewen Murray work for different outlets (A tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identity, 8 August). Stephen Moss (former literary editor, and chess and classical music expert) and I (Birdwatch columnist) both write for the Guardian, causing endless confusion.

A member of Sedgemoor chess club once told me that “We would be very honoured if you could come and give us a game” (they wouldn’t), while a woman, after admitting that she “quite enjoyed” my birding articles, spoiled it by adding “but when you write about classical music, it’s absolutely wonderful!”

To my shame, I did not credit my talented doppelganger. Stephen MossMark, Somerset

With reference to Ewan Murray’s article about meeting Ewen Murray, and the two being mistaken for each other, these days I have resigned myself to being “the other Stephen Moss”.

I manage to write a book about once a decade (at best), usually on some minority pursuit such as chess or cricket. The real, remarkably productive Stephen Moss knocks off bestsellers every other month. The Owl, The Robin, The Swan, The Swallow, The Wren. There are 11,000 bird species. That’s a lot of potential books. But I am NOT bitter.

We are about the same age and, though we have never met, have tracked each other’s careers closely. He wrote for BBC Wildlife; I wrote for BBC Music magazine. The BBC sometimes used to send me his cheques as payment for pieces. Always very welcome. We have both had long associations with the Guardian.

I get very tempting offers of birdwatching holidays across Europe and the US. One day I will accept one, even though I can barely tell a buzzard from a blackbird. I frequently get emails, with a detailed description, reporting a rare bird that a Guardian reader has seen on their local lake. My stock response is to say it’s a short-eared Siberian warbler – the first one seen in the UK since 1711 – and they should report it to the RSPB.

It could all have been so different. Radio 5 Live once confused us and asked me to appear to discuss the killing of garden birds by domestic cats. I politely pointed out their mistake, but now realise what I should have done: go on and welcome this bird massacre. That would have caused a dent in the real, annoyingly successful Stephen Moss’s reputation and sales, leaving me to rule the roost. But I am not bitter!Stephen MossSurbiton, London

Life in the theatre is most revealing

Cathy Scott-Willars responds to an article about the secret lives of theatre workers

I enjoyed your article (The secret lives of theatre workers: ‘People were having full sex in the stalls’, 9 August). I worked many roles front of house and later as operations manager at a busy regional theatre, and it has provided me with some of the most entertaining stories.

My favourite was working at a performance of The Rocky Horror Show in the large main theatre, while in the smaller studio was a play aimed at teenagers. The programming team had provided some post-show entertainment in the form of a DJ and breakdancer for the studio show, which happened to time with the interval of Rocky Horror. The scene I was met with was an usher crying, a furious college tutor shouting at her because her students had witnessed a man in a corset and thong attempt breakdancing, and his balls had fallen out, exposing himself.

Another moment that stayed with me was locking the building up at the end of the night. I was late doing my lockdown and was on autopilot, knocking on dressing room doors and popping my head round to ensure everyone had gone. As I swung open one door, not giving the recipient time to answer, I walked in on Rufus Hound in his pants! Mortified, I apologised and quickly closed the door, while worrying I may get into trouble. Instead he passed on a message at stage door to apologise for leaving late and giving me a fright. What a nice guy.

Sadly, audience aggression towards front-of-house staff was commonplace, and after three years as an operations manager, I decided it was time to move on. Cathy Scott-WillarsPrestatyn, Denbighshire

Reckless ebike users put all of us at risk

Kevin Lloyd is angered by the sheer impunity that radiates from users and calls for regulation

There may be something in the argument identified by Andy Beckett that increased use of ebikes reflects broader changes in urban areas, including the cost of housing (Lime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation?, 8 August). Yet none of that excuses the sheer impunity that radiates from ebike users, worsened by the design of city bikes which encourage the rider to sit back as if on a magic steed from which to survey their kingdom.

Their irresponsibility imposes externalities on other road users and pedestrians: riding through red lights and across junctions with no heed to other traffic, wearing headphones (but seemingly never helmets), being on the phone or apparently scrolling while riding, carelessly weaving just to maintain a conversation, riding far too fast on paths shared with pedestrians, dropping bikes like litter. As for riding home after drinking in the pub – seriously?

As a helmet-wearing cyclist, it is maddening to dodge people who seem barely familiar with a bike, let alone being in traffic. The behaviour needs to change. In the first instance, that must be through regulation and for riders and suppliers to be liable for the consequences of their actions, which sadly are sometimes serious. Kevin LloydHighbury, London

Iberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot wounds

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:07:10 GMT

Marine conservationist says deliberate attack would be ‘act of extreme cruelty’ against endangered population

Spanish officials have launched an investigation after the matriarch of an orca pod known for jostling and ramming boats off the Iberian Peninsula was spotted with wounds suggesting she had been shot by a pellet gun.

On Friday, Spain’s environment ministry said Toñi, the oldest living member of the pod, had been seen swimming in the Strait of Gibraltar with markings on her dorsal fin that were “consistent with shots from a pellet gun”.

A source from the ministry told El País that some of the projectiles remained lodged in her fin, posing a risk of infection. The ministry was in touch with officials in Portugal, the source added, as the markings were detected after the orcas had travelled from the waters off the Portuguese city of Faro.

The orcas of the Iberian Peninsula burst into headlines in 2020 after sailors shared stories of rudders that had been rammed and boats that had been spun 180 degrees or tipped sideways. Since then, a small group of orcas from the pod have been blamed for damaging scores of vessels and sinking at least four boats, leaving scientists scrambling to explain the baffling behaviour.

Scientists have long pushed back against the assertion that the orcas are attacking vessels, instead suggesting that the behaviour could be a form of play or a means of practising their hunting skills.

In the days since Toñi’s injuries came to light, the WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) association have been closely tracking the animal for any sign of weakness. “We know Toñi. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there,” the IOG co-founder Janek Andre said.

“Seeing Toñi, la abuela [the grandmother], like this is devastating,” he added. “If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.”

Researchers have long sought to highlight the many stressors faced by this population of orcas as they navigate life in a major shipping route. Food scarcity, injuries and pollution have left the population on a knife’s edge, reduced to between 30 and 40 individuals.

Digested week: Humid New York or London’s oven-blast heat? Tough one to call

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 15:01:56 GMT

Plus, heartbreakingly brilliant Cats: the Jellicle Ball, summer reads and Taylor Swift’s low-key wedding

I’ve been in New York for two weeks, where the unthinkable has happened. Even for a city accustomed to extremes, it is so hot, so humid, so reminiscent of Mobile in Alabama, or Mumbai that, all over New York, people have been forced to break persona to talk about the weather. “Was it always like this?” (No.) “Can you believe this?” (No.) “Are you having a stroke?” (Possibly.)

Received wisdom has it that heatwaves in Britain and Europe are worse than in the US because we don’t have air conditioning, but as I write this, on my first day back in heatwave London, it’s a tough one to call.

If the south of England feels like Riyadh, with its oven-blast of dry heat, New York comes with total humidity. It is so dense, so impenetrable, so vastly more furnace-like than any previous summer that it makes you angry just walking down the street.

Air conditioning takes the edge off, but it’s like trying to disguise medicine with a mouthful of Coke; it only goes so far. Meanwhile, the sweat pours down your back and the sky burns white.

New Yorkers are about as keen to complain about the weather as they are to point out a celebrity, but in these conditions you can’t not talk about it. While the mayor’s office discusses plans to extend cooling systems to subway platforms, individuals devise strategies to be outside for as little time as possible – like Minnesotans planning a trip across town in a snowstorm.

At least the hospitals are temperature-controlled. In Britain, where nurses keel over with heat exhaustion, it can feel, at times, as if the single adequately air-conditioned space is the Apple Store; only the iPhones stay cool.

Current trends in New York that may or may not make it over here: frozen yoghurt is having a resurgence but it’s the posh kind – Greek, not Pinkberry. The newest snack craze is “dot cake”, an $11 cube of dry sponge topped with icing and hundreds and thousands and served in a cup, which, according to the New York Times, New Yorkers have been lining up at 6am all summer to buy. Not at our local Gourmet Garage, I will say).

Beyond food, two things worth mentioning: “dog Crocs”, seen on several pets in the street to protect their paws from the punishing heat of the pavement and, as the name implies, tiny canine versions of their owner’s shoes, only these come in a four-pack.

And on Broadway, Cats: The Jellicle Ball, a heartbreakingly brilliant interpretation of the original show in which a tired-seeming vehicle, badly damaged by the terrible film version, gets a radical makeover. Jellicle Ball is set in the Black and Latino drag pageants of the 1980s ballroom scene and is led by two legendary performers, André De Shields, who at 80 still brings it, and Junior LaBeija, who many will recognise from the classic 1991 documentary Paris Is Burning. The costumes, by Qween Jean, and choreography by Omari Wiles and Arturo Lyons, all rightfully won Tony’s.

As Andrew Lloyd Webber says, it’s criminal the show closed early last week. It’s the best thing I’ve seen for years. Anyway we went, we screamed, we clacked the massive Jellicle Ball fans and at intermission, the theatre played DJ Murphy’s ballroom remixes of Lloyd Webber’s songs while people lost their minds. Pray it comes to London.

How did you eclipse? We were circling Heathrow in the air with the sun behind us when the sky became marginally less sunny. I will add it to the drawer of memories of other, underwhelming eclipse experiences, including that big one in 1999, when I was stuck on a motorway in France and everyone pulled over, looked up at the sky, then got back into their cars. And the Great American Eclipse of two years ago, when I stood in a big crowd and everyone turned to one another and said: “Is that it?” It’s worse than bird watching.

After it’s all over, there is a lot of anticlimactic posting on social media, although a friend in Spain sends a video and they seem to have enjoyed the real thing. As with so many things, I think the enjoyment is chiefly in the anticipation and the pretext it gives everyone to hang out, however briefly, in a single, unifying experience – and the opportunity to do crafts.

My summer reading is haphazard but heartfelt, and I’m flipping between Playworld, Adam Ross’s excellent, coming-of-age novel set in Great Neck, New York; Once the Deed Is Done by Rachel Seiffert, a brilliant examination of camps for displaced people in Germany after the second world war; and Caroline Fraser’s biography of Laura Ingalls Wilder. The book I’ve loved most so far this summer, however, is a reread of Elizabeth Jane Howard’s memoir, Slipstream, and now I’ve gone down the wormhole and want to read everything she ever wrote.

The writer died in 2014, at the age of 90, and is best known for the Cazalet Chronicles, but Slipstream is a piece of social and literary history it’s hard to match. Given how a great central theme of the book is Howard’s low self-esteem, what’s interesting is how bold she was, insisting on a life that met none of the requirements of her time and class; despite a very well-to-do background which ensures the book is stuffed with cameos by people called Minky and dinner-party guests who, she might add casually, “was home secretary at the time”, Howard bolted out of three marriages, left her child in the care of others, and lived for many years a rackety, bohemian existence characterised by lack of funds and adventurous, penniless travel. Quite apart from her writing talent, it’s a study in courage and resolve.

It’s been six weeks since the wedding of Taylor Swift to Travis Kelce and, amazingly, no one has cracked. All the NDAs are holding! The only public utterance about the event has been from Kelce himself, who said the wedding had been “the best night of my life”, which was “full of a lot of celebration”. Perhaps this is what happens when so many of the guests are near-strangers who simply feel grateful for the invitation.

None of the rest of us, meanwhile, will ever forget it; the spectacle of people who’d met the bride and groom once, if at all, dropping everything to scurry across the country or the Atlantic to celebrate the big, celebrity wedding next to Penn Station. It’s hard, in hindsight, to put your finger on who the most embarrassing attendee was, but I’d say Hugh Grant was right up there, as well as Tom Hanks, and Andrew Scott, most of whom seem to have met Swift backstage at the Eras tour in 2024 – or possibly the Toy Story 5 premiere in 2026 – since when, I guess, they’d forged meaningful friendships. Oh, to be world famous, and have this as your life.

Milk, wine, salad: how your food will be affected by the summer of heat

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 14:40:46 GMT

There are parched fields, overheating sheep and potentially the worst cereal harvest since detailed records began – but it’s a good year for cider apples

As parts of the UK swelter through a fifth successive climate crisis-driven heatwave and nearly three-quarters of England remains in drought, how are six homegrown products faring?

On her farm in Durham on Monday where she was vaccinating sheep, Clare Wise stopped and stood still. For the first time in weeks, it had begun to rain. “We didn’t think of taking cover, we just stayed out and enjoyed it!” she says.

Farmers farther south were less lucky, and the continuing drought, as well as causing distress for animals in danger of overheating, is storing up problems for livestock farmers this winter. Grass growth has been about half of what it should be by this time of year and mowing excess grass in summer is where most get their winter feed.

“This would be the peak season for collecting winter forage, but we have not been able to do that,” says Wise, who is also the acting livestock board chief for the National Farmers’ Union. “Grass growth has completely stalled.”

Some farmers have been forced to dip into their winter feed stores; others will need to supplement their scant supplies with bought-in feed.

Milk production is down, but so far only slightly – by about 1%, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), as cows have less to eat and are discouraged by the heat. Sheep shearers have been in short supply, making it difficult for farmers to make their flocks comfortable.

For future years, farmers can grow trees and higher hedges to provide shade for their beasts, says Tom Cantillon, an analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank. Some with bigger herds might consider air conditioning in their sheds and milking parlours.

But for many livestock farmers, the fear is that this year is just the beginning.

For aficionados of soft fruit, this is turning out to be a glorious summer. Berries are smaller but sweeter as the sunniest July on record in the UK has concentrated flavours. Strawberries and raspberries have done particularly well; stone fruit such as peaches, greengages and plums have ripened quickly, and cherries and blueberries have been cheap and plentiful.

Cider drinkers can also rejoice at the smaller and sweeter apples. Supermarkets tend to choose apples based on size, notes Cantillon, so if fewer of them make the grade, shoppers may be disappointed but drinkers will see the benefits. “It could be a bumper year for cider-making,” he says.

The picture is “genuinely mixed” for other produce, says Martin Emmett, the horticulture and potatoes board chair at the NFU.

Most fruit in the UK is grown covered on substrate, so a lack of rainfall in the fields has been less of an issue. But horticulturalists are worried about their water supplies. About half of the UK’s potato crop, for instance, is irrigated, often using groundwater from boreholes or abstracted from rivers. Many farmers would find it easier to store more of their own water on the farm, but constructing on-farm reservoirs requires complex planning permission.

Britain could be in for its worst cereal harvest in four decades, with wheat, spring barley and oats all substantially down on their 10-year average, according to estimates from the AHDB analysed by the ECIU. This year’s cereal and oilseed harvest is forecast to be 18.5m tonnes, which would make 2026 the worst since detailed records began in 1984.

After a wet start to the year that affected late planting for spring wheat, a dry April hit winter wheat at a crucial growing stage. The record heatwave in May also deprived grains of the moisture they need to plump out.

Further heatwaves in June and July added heat stress, while the drought continued to stunt the grains. Since mid-June, there has been no rainfall or none of significance across much of England. July was the driest month ever recorded in southern England.

Yields on wheat are normally about 7.9 tonnes per hectare in the UK; that is forecast to be down by more than a tonne per hectare, at about 6.7 tonnes this year.

Estimates taken in early August, with about half the harvest gathered, showed that the loss of about 2.5m tonnes compared to early estimates would amount to about £390m in lost revenue for farmers.

Tom Lancaster, an analyst for land, food and farming at ECIU, says: “From the wettest winter on record in 2024, to the hottest summer in 2025, and now unprecedented heat and drought this year, we are in danger of UK farming entering a climate doom loop, as repeated impacts undermine the capacity of farmers to drill next year’s crop.”

Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, who farms in Cambridgeshire, says this year has been “brutal”, especially coming on top of two previous consecutive poor harvests. “Harvest this year has been a real kick in the teeth,” he says. “I’ve never known it this dry and hot on our farm. Even farmers I know who were sceptical of climate change are now saying they’re really worried.”

Europe is not faring much better, with heatwaves and fires contributing to a forecast of €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue.

While traditional British crops are suffering, many vineyards are thriving. WineGB, the trade association representing the UK’s wine producers, says it is optimistic about the size and quality of the 2026 harvest. Producers are reporting healthy vineyards, clean fruit and encouraging ripening after stable summer conditions.

Nicola Bates, the chief executive of the trade body WineGB, said: “Whilst it’s too early to definitively say the overall impact on this year’s UK harvest – and what happens over the next few weeks will be crucial – the vineyards look strong and we’re optimistic.

“That said, seasonal conditions remain variable and producers continue to adapt, so building long-term resilience plans is essential for protecting our vineyards and to future-proof English and Welsh wine.”

Although some growers in Kent, the heartland of the British wine industry, suffered from late frosts most have managed to maintain fruit health.

Tim Spakouskas, a grower with 7 hectares (17.5 acres) of vineyard in North Yorkshire, says his farm has had very little rain for at least two months but his long-established vines are doing well as they have deep roots able to tap into moisture well below the sun-baked surface.

He is acutely aware that his wider family, who farm a variety of other crops, are “struggling a bit” in the hot dry weather which is not Yorkshire’s usual fare. Spakouskas says some of his newer vines planted last year are also showing signs of stress and he fears he may lose some if the weather does not change.

We may like to eat salad in the heat but lettuce is not a big fan of very hot weather. Its ideal growing temperature is about 20C, according to farmers, and it starts to get stressed at 24C. Over 35C, it won’t be suitable for sale, so the recent bouts of hot weather have been tricky for growers.

Ben Andrews, a salad farmer based in Herefordshire, posted on Instagram on Thursday: “There is still no rain and the veg is really struggling.” He said lettuce heads were likely to be smaller and it would probably take two to make up a portion, hitting takings.

Other leafy vegetables such as spinach and pak choi have also entered “thermal dormancy”, where they stop growing in the intense heat, according to Oddbox, which sells boxes of imperfect or surplus fruit and vegetables.

Even those growing in the controlled environments of greenhouses and polytunnels are struggling with the heat which topped 30C in parts of the UK again on Thursday.

Jan Bentley, the managing director of WS Bentley, which supplies salad cress, microgreens and pea shoots to restaurants and supermarkets grown in hydroponic systems, said yields had been reduced by “heat stress and some poor germination and crops destroyed when extremely hot”.

Oddbox also said the quality of cucumbers had been affected as “plants are stressed in the extreme heat, which causes them to misshape”.

It is not just people, animals and crops that have sweltered this summer: the water around Britain’s coast is also hotter.

Cornwall’s coastal waters are experiencing marine heatwave conditions for the third consecutive year, registering temperatures 3-4C warmer than at this time of year a decade ago, bringing challenges and opportunities for Britain’s fishers as Mediterranean species of fish and shellfish move into UK waters, while cod and haddock are migrating farther north.

Britain’s southernmost county is experiencing its largest octopus bloom in 75 years, according to the Marine Biological Association, thought to be linked to the warming seas.

As the octopus population has exploded, a record 130,000 tonnes has landed at Newlyn’s fish market so far this year. In previous years, less than 100 tonnes of octopus would have been brought ashore at the market, says Chris Ranford, the chief executive of the Cornish Fish Producers’ Organisation.

The fishing industry is “split down the middle whether it’s an opportunity or a problem”, says Ranford. “The volume has got to the level where it is a really solid export market, and the price has held up fairly well.”

Octopus is popular in countries including Spain, but there is little domestic appetite. UK fishers are also finding octopus have broken into their shellfish pots and eaten the crab and lobster inside, reducing catches of these species that are more popular with British diners.

Ranford, who is also the current chair of the National Organisation of Fishermen’s Federations, says there are concerns that a very cold winter or drop in water quality could suddenly cut octopus numbers, leaving fishers with little to catch as crab, lobster and scallop populations take time to recover.

Belt and braces PM: what wearing suit braces says about Burnham

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 14:09:22 GMT

Mod fashion, nod to 80s excess or symbol of tradition? Andy Burnham’s wardrobe choice transcends class divisions

The sartorial evolution of Andy Burnham reached another milestone this week when the prime minister appeared at a photocall in Derbyshire wearing a pair of braces under his suit.

Navy, slimline and button-on rather than clipped, they were barely visible while he posed for a photo in Ilkeston. It was only when he unbuttoned his suit jacket to embrace members of the public that they were on view.

Burnham’s £595 navy suit was made by Oliver Brown, a traditional tailor with shops in London and Chester, and is the same style worn in his official portrait. Called the Eaton suit, it is made from a 100% merino wool cloth woven by Alfred Brown in Yorkshire, and is made to measure. A spokesperson for the tailor said that while the suit was definitely theirs, the braces were not.

If the trousers didn’t fit, wearing a belt would have been out of the question as they don’t have belt loops. And yet, says Chloe Chapin, a fashion historian and author of the forthcoming book Suitable: The Sartorial Revolution and the Fashioning of Modern Men, “the trousers do have side fasteners, so he doesn’t really need braces at all, at least functionally”.

A political insider who has worked on Burnham’s campaigns for the last two years told the Guardian: “Andy is not the teleprompter type of politician. This stuff is simply what he wears.” The former Greater Manchester mayor and his team think about his clothing and context, though, and it certainly isn’t an afterthought. “His clothes are trying to strike a balance between professional and capable politician – but also let people know that he’s different to other politicians,” the source says. As the first TikTok PM, no one understands this better than Burnham. “The optics are not divorced from the reality.”

Braces originated in France in the 1700s as strips of fabric that were buttoned to a waistband. They quickly spread across Europe, like many French trends, though it wasn’t until 1820 that Albert Thurston started making the leather versions we know today. Back then, they were considered undergarments and to show them was inappropriate.

Sign up to Fashion Statement

Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved

after newsletter promotion

Braces had a resurgence in the UK during the 1960s and 70s, worn by mods and skinheads as a form of subversion. The pinnacle of this probably occurred in the 80s, when they became as popular on Wall Street financiers as they did on punks. Wearing this “underwear as outerwear intentionally was a bit like Madonna wearing her Jean Paul Gaultier cone bra, a real statement”, says Chapin. If the 60s version represented working-class pride and anti-establishment rebellion, the 80s “was about a heightening of excess. They transcended class and in an age of abundance showed just how subversive fashion could be.”

While Burnham has always been transparent about his journey from Westminster yes-man to “king of the north”, particularly through his wardrobe, could the braces signal a move to formality? In many ways they are the ultimate symbol of tradition, especially in politics, where Winston Churchill and Michael Portillo were fans.

It’s more about context, says Chapin. Just as a Labour politician will wear red if they want to convey strength, grey or purple if they want to be bipartisan, or blue if they’re talking to Tory voters, if something can be posh and working class at the same time, this is precisely the sort of ambiguity a politician might want to exploit if they’re trying to connect with the public.

If nothing else, Burnham wearing braces points towards fashion’s core tension – is clothing about function or aesthetics? Much like his approach to politics, the answer is probably both.
