Nine life lessons from the happiest man in the world: from embracing tiny changes to not overthinking meditation

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 14:00:29 GMT

Stressed out, endlessly scrolling and never satisfied? Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, the Buddhist monk with off-the-charts levels of contentment, may have the answers …

By some metrics, Buddhist monk Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche is the happiest man on Earth. In brain scans, researchers noted that Mingyur’s neural activity showed off-the-charts levels of activation in the left prefrontal cortex, an area associated with positive emotions such as happiness, enthusiasm and joy. In other tests conducted when he was 41 years old, his brain reportedly “resembled that of a 33-year-old”. He also laughs a lot.

Can happiness be taught? I met Mingyur (Rinpoche is an honorary title meaning, roughly, “precious one”) to discover his strategies for a richer life.

“As the Dalai Lama says, we have everything at the touch of a finger, and so when we start to feel lonely, incomplete, bored – we protect ourselves with whatever: eating ice-cream, our smartphone, coffee,” says Mingyur. “We try to get away from them, but those feelings are wisdom, in a way. The really important thing is to sit with them, embrace them as a path to explore.”

For instance, if you find yourself bored while watching a Netflix romcom and simultaneously scrolling on your phone, that’s a signal that ever more stimulation will never be satisfying (science backs this up: one recent study suggests flicking between videos on social media makes us more bored, not less). Take it as a sign to switch everything off, look inward and stop trying to fill the vacuum with superficial stuff.

In 2011, Mingyur left his monastery in the middle of the night with nothing but the clothes on his back, intending to live as a homeless yogi. About three weeks in, he developed severe food poisoning and spent days paralysed by exhaustion and pain – but he now sees this as the moment he started to truly understand the Tibetan Buddhist idea of relinquishing control.

Does he think it’s possible to experience that sort of thing without going through something quite so unpleasant? “Absolutely, of course. Especially nowadays – modern life is full of adventure. When you turn 18, start a new job, start a new relationship – each of those are opportunities for change.” But you don’t have to wait for these bigger moments: meeting a new group of people or taking up a new challenge can help increase your comfort levels with new things. Try implementing one small change every time you feel like you’ve spent a day just going through the motions: a new route home from work, or cooking with one ingredient you’ve never used before. Something I find helpful is to keep a little list of things I want to try whenever I come across them, then when things get stultifying, I’ve got a ready-made buffet to choose from.

“I felt bored the first time I learned meditation,” says Mingyur. “I said, ‘Today is breathing. Tomorrow, again, breathing. The rest of this week, breathing. This is stupid.’ But for meditation, you need to know two things. One, you can make everything support for meditation – you can meditate anytime, anywhere, with anything. Second, you have to have some creative element with your meditation: everything becomes a friend to the meditation.”

To put this another way, if there’s traffic noise outside, or the person next to you is watching TikTok videos, the idea is to let that become a source of focus and calm. This is easier said than done. Mingyur suggests building up to it by listening to music, then waterfalls or birdsong, then loud conversations or construction. Eventually, he says, you should be able to meditate while a baby is crying (I won’t be trying this).

“We think about three things in Tibetan Buddhism: view, meditation and application,” says Mingyur. “View is the mindset: we believe that everybody has an inner sky, the qualities of awareness, love, compassion and wisdom. We practise meditation, and then we practise application – building new habits. So it’s easy to say: ‘Oh, people aren’t nice.’ But of course there are a lot of great qualities in a lot of people, and if you see that, it will manifest. But it’s a habit: you have to keep doing it, and doing it, and then you change.”

Mingyur suggests doing this in a small way every day. Maybe one day try appreciating your family, and the next, find positive things to say about your most annoying colleague.

Yes, gratitude lists can feel a bit peak 2021, but one approach is to go from the incredibly general to the extremely specific. “I appreciate that I have senses, that there’s a roof above me, that I have at least one or two friends or family,” says Mingyur. “When you begin to appreciate these things, you start to appreciate the quality of your life and everything around you.”

This doesn’t necessarily mean you need to start a gratitude journal. After a few days, it can feel a bit too easy for your mind to scribble another ‘I’m grateful for my children’. Instead, the idea is to use little moments of downtime to notice how nice it is to be in the specific moment, whether you’re sitting in a comfortable chair or watching your child swing a stick around in the woods.

“I had panic attacks when I was young,” says Mingyur. “When I began to learn meditation from my father, I asked him how to fight them. He said: ‘Don’t fight.’ The first reason is that if you fight, panic becomes stronger. It’s like saying: ‘Don’t think about orange’ – suddenly it’s all you can think about.

And the second thing my father said is, there’s no need to push panic away, because it’s like a storm cloud in the sky. A storm cloud can’t change the nature of the sky – it comes and then it goes. You just have to connect with the inner sky.” To put this another way, whatever inner turmoil you’re going through, remind yourself that it isn’t actually changing anything fundamental in your brain: it will pass and things will feel better.

At times of extreme distress, this might feel impossible. In which case, Mingyur suggests we focus on physical sensations – the temperature of the room, the sounds around you – to help deal with the panic in that moment, rather than trying to tell ourselves everything is fine.

“Genuine happiness is when we let go of that feeling of dissatisfaction, incompleteness, that something is missing,” says Mingyur. “But if you only look for happiness, then you will get the opposite. People often think, ‘I’ll be happy if I make more money, or if I move to this new country or get this new job or win the lottery’ – but that just changes your happiness a little bit and then you go back to baseline, right? But if you practise breathing, love and compassion, you can move that baseline over time.”

To start, simply sit and breathe naturally, focusing on the rise and fall of your abdomen or the sensation of the air passing through your body. As you’re doing this, you might try mentally repeating a simple mantra (“May I be happy and free from suffering” is a common one) to cultivate love towards yourself, and then extending that compassion to loved ones, pets and, eventually, all the other people in your life.

“What we call awareness is like sunlight, and our emotional patterns are like frost on the grass in the morning,” says Mingyur. “When the sunlight manifests, the frost melts automatically – there’s no fight. I talk to some business leaders who are really stressed. They have to do so many things at the same time, so they build the habit of being stressed or angry all the time. They come to me and say: ‘My relationship is not good,’ or ‘There’s a problem between me and the boss.’ I say, ‘Just catch the anger. Be with the anger. Just for a second.’ Once you catch it, you have a choice, it can transform.”

To put this another way, when you’re momentarily furious at someone – at work or at home – you don’t need to meditate for 10 minutes; just avoid your autopilot response of snapping at them by noticing the fact that you’re angry, and then watching as the emotion melts away. From experience, I can say that this takes practice – but it’s definitely worth working on.

“If you can really help others, you feel a different level of happiness from having an ice-cream or a coffee,” says Mingyur. We all know this, obviously – but how often are we actually doing it? Check in on a neighbour in need today

What does Clacton get for its loyalty to stroppy Nige? Next to nothing

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 13:17:12 GMT

Why bother to improve people’s lives – or even show up – when getting votes is this easy? In many ways, though, the stunt hasn’t paid off

What can Clacton possibly have done to deserve this? Is this some cosmic karma for a past existence in which the town executed hundreds of innocent women and children? Surely, even then, enough is enough. For the past few years Clacton seems to have been the centre of some abusive psychological experiment. The sort the Americans used to run in the 1950s and 60s, that have long since been banned. One run by Nigel Farage and designed merely to fuel his narcissistic dreams, with the voters mere cannon fodder.

Clacton’s relationship with Nige is and always has been entirely one-sided. The town’s job is merely to vote for him, whenever he commands. Even for byelections that are entirely unnecessary and will possibly have to be re-run before the end of the year. On a turnout of just 44%, little more than 60% of the voters duly obliged on Thursday, even though none of the main parties were standing and Nige’s main opponent was a man with a bin on his head. Maybe parts of Clacton are waking up, and are fed up with Farage taking the piss out of them.

Here’s how it works. For a few weeks during an election campaign, Nige breaks the habit of a lifetime and makes two or three visits to the Essex coast. He gets someone to buy him a beer or an ice-cream – most local businesses don’t take crypto – and poses with a pet supporter his team have rounded up for the day. He then gets the hell out of Clacton as fast as he can. And that’s all it takes for Nige to win. He isn’t a man who puts in the unnecessary hard yards.

And what does Clacton get in return? Next to nothing. An MP who scarcely bothers to turn up to Westminster. And who, when he does, invariably fails to give his constituency a second thought. The Jaywick ward of Clacton was the most deprived area in the country when Farage was first elected in 2024 and nothing has changed since. Nor does Nige appear that bothered. All he needs to do is to dispense a bit of unmediated grievance and the votes come tumbling in. Why bother to make people’s lives better when it’s that easy? It’s the ultimate dysfunctional relationship.

It was past dawn when the returning officer was ready to announce the result. Ploughing through a ballot paper that’s almost a metre long to accommodate the more than 30 candidates takes time. And where was Nigel at his moment of triumph? Absolutely nowhere to be seen. Surely now was the time for him to put on his public face. The Mr Congeniality. The common man. The politician who can connect with the little people. Except he just couldn’t bring himself to do it. There are limits even to Nige’s artifice. He just couldn’t conceal the fact he was having a giant strop.

Nige couldn’t escape the reality that he had been out-thought and out-played at every stage since his disastrous decision to call a byelection. He had hoped to kill off the investigation into the £5m gift he received from the Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne that, even with the benefit of an extra six week’s thinking time, he has been unable to explain convincingly.

If anything, Reform’s finances have been looking even murkier over the past six weeks, with money apparently flying between George Cottrell (the man-boy who calls Nige Daddy), Fiona (Posh George’s unfortunate mother), Richard Tice and the Reform bank account. In Reform World everyone gets to be a millionaire for 15 minutes. Except the suckers who vote for the party.

Then there was Farage’s absurd attempt to portray the election as the people v the establishment. Only it became ever clearer that Nige was – always has been, always will be – the establishment. No more so than in a two-way fight between himself and a comedian with a dustbin on his head, claiming to be a space warrior from Planet Sigma Nine.

This was a psychological wound too far for a Nige close to breakdown. He just couldn’t bear to be seen standing next to a bunch of jokers, losers and Laurence Fox. So he pulled a sicky.

Dicky Tice tried to give it a positive spin. The police had insisted there was a “credible threat” and had advised Nige to stay away from the count. However, it is understood Essex police did not advise anyone to stay away, and had believed they had everything in hand. The only disturbance they had been expecting was a few heckles and a Led By Donkeys-style stunt. But that was too much for Nige. His facade too fragile, his self-esteem in tatters. Just a giant ball of childlike need. He couldn’t even bring himself to give the “major speech” he had promised for Clacton at 10.30am. He needed a quiet room in which to lie down. Sulks don’t come much bigger than this.

You might have thought Nige’s team could have persuaded him to make an ersatz display of charm, dignity and gratitude. You know the sort. “I’d like to thank the voters of Clacton for placing their trust in me. I won’t let them down.” Through gritted teeth and crossed fingers. Because he had every intention of letting them down. But Nige couldn’t do that.

All he could do was post on X: “The result in Clacton speaks for itself.” This was a little too close to the mark. Because 9,500 voters had chosen Count Binface rather than a career politician. The Reform bubble was bursting in front of Nige’s eyes. This was not the landslide he had been hoping for. Just a stunt that had backfired. Indeed, the speech of the night was made by the Count, observing that he was the clear winner of all those who had bothered to turn up.

Meanwhile, Reform retreated into their own world. Turning Clacton into a little bit of Glastonbury with their very own Farage Fest. If you can count a few members of the Reform elite dancing awkwardly and trying to look as if they were having a good night. Though perhaps, like some Glastonburys, this was a night where the aim was to forget rather than to enjoy yourself. It felt like the end of days.

Come Friday morning, reality was beginning to hit. This wasn’t the end of a victorious election campaign, but the beginning of a new one. With Lee Anderson insisting Reform would thoroughly cooperate with the reopened investigation. There’s a first time for everything.

As online dating goes into ‘salvage mode’, can AI solve all its problems?

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 13:00:28 GMT

Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ grows

Bumble was supposed to be different. When it launched in 2014, it offered women a simple proposition: if you matched with a man, you had to make the first move. The rule was meant to make online dating safer and less intimidating, while giving women control over who got to speak first.

This week, Bumble abandoned it.

The change follows the introduction of Opening Moves, which had already softened the original rule, and comes as Bumble prepares to abandon another defining feature: the swipe.

The company says it is responding to changing user behaviour and wants to encourage more meaningful connections.

But there is another way of reading the changes.

Bumble was created to fix what many saw as Tinder’s chaotic and aggressive hookup culture by shifting the power dynamic entirely to women. Now it is dismantling those features. And it is not alone. Across the dating-app industry, the swipe-and-match model that transformed how people met is being quietly reworked while companies race to put artificial intelligence at the centre of whatever comes next.

“Bumble is in salvage mode,” says Luke Brunning, a philosopher who studies the ethics of technology and relationships. “They’ve already reorganised, restructured and cut jobs in response to declining revenue. This risky, standout pivot suggests they’re wondering how, despite all that, to keep going.”

The number of Bumble’s paying users fell sharply over the past year and its share price has been under sustained pressure. The company cut about 30% of its workforce this year.

“It’s going to be fascinating to see whether they can weather it,” Brunning says. “But they’re not alone: a lot of the major players are also in salvage mode, trying to figure out how to position themselves in a market that is increasingly fed up with them.”

Brunning’s research shows dating apps are now often used grudgingly, because people feel that they are necessary, rather than with the excitement that accompanied their rise.

The online dating industry, estimated to be worth almost £10bn globally, is keenly aware of this. Its solution? To go full AI.

Grindr – seen as a testbed for the wider industry – is transitioning into an “AI-first” platform. Tinder is testing Chemistry, an AI-powered system intended to reduce “swipe fatigue”. Bumble has been developing an AI matchmaking assistant called Bee.

Other startups are dispensing with swiping altogether. London-based Fate describes itself as an “agentic AI dating app”: instead of browsing profiles, users are interviewed by an AI about what they want from relationships to find similarities with potential partners.

So why aren’t we talking about being on the brink of a brave new world of dating apps, where AI will successfully sift the candidates to find our one true love? Why, instead, is the debate about whether the apps will even survive?

Adam Peacock, a researcher of technology and intimacy, thinks the issue is that the industry is misreading what people are objecting to.

“There’s a kind of emerging cultural backlash against allowing AI into our intimate lives as well as the additional concern that someone you’re talking to on these apps, is actually filtering the whole conversation through an AI concierge,” he says.

Peacock says gen Z in particular are concerned as to whether dating apps are even being designed to make good connections between users but are, instead, opaquely tweaked to monetise the time users spend on the site. That, in a cynical twist, the apps are deliberately profiting from keeping people lonely.

“The dating industry has turned intimacy into an enormous source of data,” Peacock says. “Dating apps can know where people live, what they look like, who they are attracted to, what they say to potential partners and, increasingly, how they behave.”

Elsa Kugelberg, a philosopher who researches gender and relationships, says online dating has become too embedded in modern life to fail. But the first generation of dating apps – the era of the profile, the swipe, the match and the message – may be reaching its end.

Peacock thinks the apps may evolve into something broader: “More of a social media, lifestyle product than a dedicated dating app.”

But the question is whether any iteration of dating app will make the experience better, or whether the extra layers of AI will simply function as a temporary facade on an exhausted model.

Brunning believes AI on dating apps doesn’t have to be like this. “There can be ways of trying to do digital better, that doesn’t involve giving people AI tools to talk to each other with,” he says.

Better moderation, clearer policies, better ways of presenting yourself and more control over how the environment works could all improve online dating without handing more of it to machines, he says.

The critical point is this, he says: “You can’t just take a product that’s out of favour, put AI on top of it and say: ‘OK, now we have a product that works.’”

Putin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mount

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 13:00:27 GMT

Russia is losing 30,000 casualties a month, and the country’s regions are under pressure to feed the ‘meat-grinder’. Experts say it may not be enough

In kitchens and Telegram chats across Russia, the same question is being asked with growing frequency: will Vladimir Putin order another mobilisation?

Nearly five years into the war, Russia is scrambling to find enough soldiers to replenish its ranks, as voluntary recruitment slows and its forces suffer heavy losses on the battlefield in Ukraine.

With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache.

“The problem for the Kremlin is that it is getting much harder to find people willing to fight, even for crazy money,” said Aleksei Tabalov, a human rights activist and director of an organisation that helps Russian conscripts.

Putin last resorted to mobilisation in September 2022, when a series of dramatic battlefield setbacks forced the Kremlin to call up 300,000 reservists to stabilise the front.

Since then, Moscow has avoided another deeply unpopular call-up by relying largely on high paid voluntary contracts to fill the ranks with roughly 1.3 million contract soldiers Russia has recruited since.

Men, particularly from Russia’s poorer regions, have been offered life-changing signing bonuses and salaries on open-ended contracts amounting to several years of local wages, alongside substantial payouts to their families if they are killed.

But Russia’s heavy losses mean it must continue finding new soldiers at a high rate.

Western estimates put Russian casualties at more than 30,000 killed and wounded a month, a toll that reflects the army’s attritional “meat grinder” tactics, in which troops are repeatedly sent forward in small assault groups despite heavy losses.

Moscow, meanwhile, now recruits roughly 1,000 soldiers a day, according to calculations by Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which means most new recruits are used to replenish depleted units rather than expand Russia’s offensive capacity.

That has once again raised the prospect of mobilisation.

Top Russian officials have dismissed reports of an impending call-up, with former president Dmitry Medvedev describing them as “nonsense” and a “lying provocation” by Ukraine.

Two people familiar with discussions in Moscow also said there was no indication that Putin had decided to order another mass mobilisation. A senior western official likewise said there were no signs that a decision had been taken.

But fears that another call-up may be on the way have nevertheless increasingly entered everyday conversations.

In Telegram chats used by local sports teams, work colleagues and groups of friends, Russians swap rumours about a possible mobilisation and share advice on securing exemptions or avoiding the draft. Some speculate that a new call-up could come after September’s elections to the Duma.

“It’s guesswork right now whether mobilisation will actually happen,” said Ivan Chuviliaev, a spokesperson for Get Lost, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert.

But he said the renewed speculation was already being exploited to boost recruitment.

“The panic around mobilisation is being used by officials to pressure men into signing contracts,” Chuviliaev said. “The message is: mobilisation is coming anyway, so you might as well sign a contract now and get a payout before you’re forced to fight.”

For now, people familiar with the Kremlin’s thinking say the authorities appear determined to strong-arm more men into signing contracts rather than risk another mobilisation.

Over the summer, lawyers and activists have documented increasingly coercive recruitment tactics in several regions, with men detained on the street by police, taken from workplaces or summoned to stations – before being brought to military recruitment offices and pressed to sign contracts.

“It has turned into a hunt for people,” said Tabalov. “Under various pretexts, through deception, blackmail, violence and threats, they are forcing them to sign contracts.”

Tabalov said recruiters were increasingly targeting what he described as “socially marginalised” men, including those with debts, criminal cases or other vulnerabilities that could be used to put pressure on them to enlist.

In the southern Penza region, where some of the most aggressive draft methods have been reported, videos posted online have shown men being driven away in vans as relatives protested outside recruitment offices. Activists say some have been threatened with prosecution or beaten until they agreed to sign.

The search has widened elsewhere too. Universities, technical colleges and vocational schools have been encouraged to recruit students into newly formed drone units, offering another source of manpower for the military. Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army, including people convicted of “serious and especially serious crimes”.

Much of the responsibility for finding soldiers has been pushed down to Russia’s regions.

Governors and local administrations are expected to meet recruitment targets set by Moscow, giving the Kremlin some distance from the drive while leaving regional officials responsible for finding enough men in their own territories.

Around that system, a lucrative recruitment industry has emerged. Regional governments offer thousands of dollars not only to soldiers who sign contracts but also to those who find them, with “bring a friend” schemes paying residents for every person they persuade to enlist.

Private recruiters and public-sector employees scour social media for candidates, while advertisements for military contracts have become ubiquitous online. Russian regions have paid recruiters at least 7.7bn roubles ($96m) since such schemes were introduced, according to the independent Russian outlet IStories.

One recruiter in central Russia, speaking to the Guardian on condition of anonymity, said his organisation was expected to find between 20 and 30 men each month, with bonuses for exceeding the target and penalties for falling short.

“It was easier last year,” the recruiter said. “Now it is getting harder.”

The recruiter said mobilisation was also being discussed in his office, but that there had been no orders or indications that a new draft was imminent.

Another mass call-up, however, would carry significant political risks for the Kremlin.

The 2022 call-up triggered one of the biggest episodes of domestic disruption since the invasion began, prompting a mass exodus of Russians and a sharp drop in Putin’s approval ratings.

It would also come at a potentially sensitive moment. Recent polling suggests confidence in the course of the war is weakening, with the share of Russians who believe the campaign in Ukraine is going well falling to its lowest level since April 2022.

For now, analysts say Moscow is more likely to step up recruitment efforts through higher bonuses, pressure on regional officials and increasingly coercive tactics.

Whether that will be enough could ultimately determine if Putin resorts to another mobilisation, said Tabalov, the activist.

The options before the Kremlin, Tabalov said, could range from another mass call-up to a more selective mobilisation, sending existing conscripts to the front or quietly calling up reservists for frontline service.

“I don’t think they’ll be able to recruit enough people under the current system,” Tabalov said. “Then they’ll be faced with the question of what form mobilisation should take.”

‘Disgraceful’: what one election photo tells us about British politics in 2026

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 12:23:04 GMT

Results from coastal town of Clacton have been interpreted positively by Nigel Farage and Count Binface, but one spoiled ballot tells its own story

UK politics live – latest updates

It ended, perhaps fittingly, on a rather baffling note. After 34 days of campaigning to regain the parliamentary seat of Clacton on England’s east coast, Nigel Farage, the leader of the Reform UK party, declined to turn up to the town’s leisure centre to hear himself declared the winner and MP. It was quite the thing. The last high-profile winning candidate to fail to enjoy his moment of victory was Bobby Sands in 1981. The IRA man had his reasons: he was on hunger strike in a prison in Northern Ireland, and went on to die 26 days later.

Instead Farage attended a gathering of his supporters at an airfield on the outskirts of Clacton billed by his party as “Farage Fest”. He told fans he would be damned if he was going to stand on a stage “having won a resounding victory” and “be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”.

But he also said Essex police had advised him of an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”. A Reform UK spokesperson went further: “Essex police advised Nigel not to attend the count tonight due to a credible threat against him.”

Not true, suggested the police. No such advice had been given. One of the shoutiest members of Farage’s anti-immigration party, Lee Anderson, had a slightly refreshed explanation by 8.10am when interviewed by the BBC. His leader had not wanted to disrespect those who had flocked to Farage Fest. He was, actually, if you will just listen just for a moment, a man of principle. “It was a great occasion that it is only right that he spends that time with his members, with his activists, with his supporters,” Anderson fumed.

Count Binface and the other Clacton candidates await the byelection results. Photograph: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock

Count Binface and the other Clacton candidates await the byelection results. Photograph: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock

Keep scrolling

All this left one intergalactic explorer, with his arms raised and a bin on his no doubt sweaty head, to take the starring role at Clacton leisure centre. The candidate who went by the name of Count Binface made a declaration on social media: “I came first in the Clacton byelection! Of the candidates who bothered to turn up for the results.”

Count Binface, for those who have not been following this latest fever dream of a moment in British politics, is the parody figure who declared himself the unity candidate when Farage triggered the byelection by resigning the seat back in July.

Farage had explained his resignation at the time as a challenge to the establishment that would show them that the people did not want him scrutinised and investigated by the parliamentary authorities over an undeclared £5m gift from a crypto billionaire or any of the other financial scandals orbiting Reform UK.

The other major political parties called his bluff. It was a stunt, they said, and none of them stood, leaving Count Binface, a familiar and striking figure at elections, whose real name is Jon Harvey, to harvest the anti-Farage vote. And he could reasonably be said to have done rather well, given that he won just 95 votes at the recent byelection in Makerfield, in Greater Manchester, where Andy Burnham, now the prime minister, won his parliamentary seat.

Binface, who describes himself as an “independent space warrior” from the planet Sigma IX, won 26.93% of the ballot with 9,455 votes, leaving him second to Farage who secured 22,239 votes (63.34%). There was a healthy 44% turnout.

Perhaps – and it is only a theory going round the leisure centre in Clacton – Farage was actually not at the count because he did not fancy the inevitable photograph of him next to his ludicrous competition?

“That means I’ve got – against Nigel Farage – 10,000% more votes than I got against Andy Burnham,” Binface later said of his electoral tally. “What does that tell you? Well it tells you that Nigel, who said that he didn’t want to be humiliated, maybe has been. As for me, I’m over the moon – I’m over your moon, I’m over my moons – and what comes next, well we shall see. But you know what, we know this for a fact: over one in four people in this constituency would rather have Count Binface as their MP than the leader of Reform UK.”

That was the Binface take on an election estimated to have cost the public purse £250,000. Others were available. For the fired-up Anderson, who scolded the BBC presenter Justin Webb for being “very rude” for interrupting him on Friday morning, there was one clear reading of that night’s events.

“[Nigel Farage is] celebrating a stunning victory in Clacton and the people have decided: they’ve stuck two fingers up to people like the BBC, the establishment, the blob, the whole of Westminster,” Anderson said. “There has been a constant witch-hunt by people in the media.

“There’s been a witch-hunt against Nigel Farage and he said: ‘You know what? Enough’s enough. Meet me at the ballot box.’ And when it comes to a crunch, when he does throw the gauntlet down to the other political parties, what happens? They run away like the cowards they are. He challenges them at the ballot box and he wins.”

Naturally enough, that wasn’t how the other main parties saw it. “All Farage can brag about this morning is beating a bloke with a bin on his head,” said a Conservative party spokesperson. “What he should do is answer the serious outstanding questions about why he hid his £5m from the public.”

Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the governing Labour party, said: “There’s no hiding place now and Nigel Farage needs to answer to the public as to exactly what’s going on.”

As election workers sorted through the voting ballots at the leisure centre in the early hours of Friday morning, one moment caught by photographers also tells a story.

Across the 90cm long ballot paper containing all the names of the parody and independent candidates for the seat of Clacton (it was the longest ballot paper in UK electoral history), a disgruntled voter had made their mark: “What a disgraceful waste of money.”

Three hours after Farage’s victory was declared, the suspended parliamentary standards investigation into the Reform UK leader over accusations he failed to declare gifts and donations had resumed.

‘Murakami saw his book come alive!’: the Japanese company bringing the author’s science fiction masterpiece to the stage

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 12:00:27 GMT

A play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic tale

Tatsuya Fujiwara is no stranger to London’s Barbican theatre. It was here nearly 30 years ago that one of Japan’s biggest film stars, now 44, made his stage debut. He was just 15, plucked out of an audition of more than 5,000 hopeful youngsters by the revered theatre director Yukio Ninagawa for his play Shintoku-Maru. It kickstarted Fujiwara’s career, and three years later he landed a role in the cult dystopian film Battle Royale, going on to star in hit TV dramas and blockbuster films, all the while continuing to perform in Ninagawa’s acclaimed productions.

Now, Fujiwara returns to where it all began, to perform in a stage adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s science fiction novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World. The story alternates between two seemingly unrelated narratives: a cyberpunk thriller set in Tokyo, and a surreal fantasy that unfolds within a mysterious walled town. Directed by the French choreographer Philippe Decouflé, the play premiered in Tokyo in January, toured Japan until March, then Singapore in April. After the Barbican run this autumn, the tour will wrap up in Paris.

“When performing in Japan, you become accustomed to your own audience,” says Fujiwara. “You develop a feel for what reaches them and how they receive you. The moment you cross a border, that certainty disappears.”

We meet in April, backstage at the Esplanade theatre in Singapore just a few hours before the production’s first performance to an English-speaking audience. (The play is performed in Japanese, with English surtitles.) The response was rapturous, the audience more animated than with any performance during the Japan run, according to the director and cast. The Singapore house laughed freely, while in Japan the comic moments did not land with such warmth.

Whether that’s due to cultural differences in self-expression or humour is up for debate, but backstage during intermission the cast are giddy. “It definitely gives us confidence for London,” says the director.

This play arrives at a time when Japanese culture is experiencing a global boom, particularly in London. The last five years alone have seen a cluster of UK exhibitions about Japan. The British Museum has curated shows on manga, Hokusai and the samurai; the V&A did the history of kimonos; Oxford’s Ashmolean explored art and photography from Tokyo; and Somerset House celebrated 50 years of Hello Kitty. However, productions that have broken through to a mainstream audience overseas have largely been based on anime and manga. This summer saw a musical adaptation of Death Note at the Barbican, as well as Pretty Guardian Sailor Moon at the West End’s Here at Outernet and Koko in Camden Town, and Spirited Away, which enjoyed a six-month run at the London Coliseum in 2024.

“The barriers are considerably lower,” says Miyako Kanamori, senior executive and veteran producer at HoriPro. As one of Japan’s largest entertainment companies, HoriPro has been exporting Japanese theatre to the UK for many decades. “Thirty years ago, when we first brought [Yukio] Ninagawa’s productions to Britain, that cultural landscape simply did not exist. Today, there is a far broader curiosity about Japanese storytelling and aesthetics, and I feel audiences approach our work with a greater sense of familiarity.” Perhaps now is the time for homegrown theatre to shine. Plus, as a global bestseller, Murakami’s name carries instant esteem and recognition.

However, the world of Murakami does not naturally lend itself to the stage. His novels can be cryptic and allegorical, making them hard to adapt for its native audience, let alone an international one.

Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World spans 400 pages and features curious creatures such as unicorns and the “Murks”, monsters that lurk in the sewers. Fujiwara plays Watashi, the protagonist of the cyberpunk narrative the Hard-Boiled Wonderland, a human data processor known as a “Calcutec” who is essentially a cyborg. He encrypts data using a technique known as “shuffling”, described as a supernatural kind of mind alteration. His routine job slowly reveals a darker conspiracy buried deep within his own consciousness.

The parallel narrative is even more peculiar. End of the World unravels within a mythical walled town. Upon entering, the second protagonist, Boku – played on alternating nights by Kiita Komagine and Ryunosuke Shimamura – is stripped of his shadow and all his memories, and tasked with reading dreams from the skulls of dead unicorns. The two plots eventually converge, and while they are both totally removed from the reality we know, the stories are strangely relatable.

Murakami wrote the novel more than 40 years ago, but in an age of AI and algorithmic control, his questions about what remains when memory and selfhood are stripped are more pertinent now than ever.

“At first I thought it was impossible to do anything with [the material],” says Decouflé, who is best known for directing music videos for New Order and Fine Young Cannibals, as well as France’s 1992 Winter Olympics opening ceremony. “I’m not Japanese, so I can never fully grasp what lies beneath the text, but then I thought: ‘They’ve asked me to do it, so I’m going to do it my way, with my dreams, my ideas, my vision.’”

For the production company, bringing in a European director with a background in movement was a deliberate decision. Having worked on several adaptations of Murakami’s novels – Ninagawa’s Kafka on the Shore in 2015 and Simon McBurney’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle in 2023 – producer Kanamori learned that expressing the spiritual and psychological dimensions of the author’s world through dialogue alone was “profoundly difficult”.

after newsletter promotion

She came to realise that “music and physical expression might offer a more truthful theatrical language for his work”, particularly for a play that was intended to be performed to a non-Japanese-speaking audience. Working closely with Japanese scriptwriter Ako Takahashi to decode the text, Decouflé has made a highly visual adaptation. He casts ballerinas as unicorns, dressing them in golden leotards and pointe shoes with stilted forelimbs. Street dancers armoured in urchin-like spikes writhe and scuttle through the sewers, while Tokyo-based dancer Rikubouz moves in long, liquid phrases to connect the two worlds between scenes.

Murakami came to rehearsals himself. “He was always very contained, very still,” says Decouflé. “And then suddenly he saw the stage. He saw it alive. And I could see that he was happy – happy that I had given life to his dreams, to his book.” After the premiere, the author made a short speech. “He said something like: ‘I wrote this novel 40 years ago, and I had forgotten everything. Tonight, you all reminded me of what I created.’”

Decouflé had made two productions in Japan before – once 30 years ago, another 15 years ago – and has observed the rise of Japanese dance in that time. “Thirty years ago, we could not find dancers of the quality we needed. Even 15 years ago it was so-so. And now Japan has some extraordinary dancers.” He was also impressed by the professionalism of the performers. “I never heard anyone complain,” he says. “I gave them hard work, I really pushed them. And at the end, they were overjoyed. It was a great luxury to work that way.”

Cultural exchange has always been a crucial part of Japan’s story and how its art travels. Back in the Edo period, artisans commonly used discarded Ukiyo-e prints to package ceramics. These were later discovered by the impressionists, inspiring the Japonisme movement and artists such as Monet, Van Gogh and Klimt. The dialogue that followed, between eastern aesthetics and western modernism, moulded the development of modern art on both sides.

Perhaps something of that pattern persists here. The play’s star hopes international interest in Japanese theatre will also ignite a new energy back home. “It would be amazing if theatre in Japan could one day command the kind of broad cultural engagement it has in the UK, where it’s truly part of public life,” says Fujiwara, who knows better than most what it takes to carry culture across borders. At the Barbican in 2015, performing Ninagawa’s Hamlet on Shakespeare’s home turf, the pressure was paralysing.

“It’s a bit like a British company staging kabuki in Japan,” he says. “But this time it’s different because it’s Murakami. There’s more room to breathe, and more hope that we can offer something that reaches people broadly.”

End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland is at Barbican theatre, London, 8 to 11 October.

‘We get 200 tourists a day’: when your house becomes a TV star

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 12:00:26 GMT

What’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell all

Half the world recognises the apartment that Carrie Bradshaw lives in. Or the New Jersey mansion where Tony Soprano ate, slept and obsessed over the ducks in his swimming pool. In the 1990s, if you asked a good chunk of the global population where Will Smith lived, they would instantly picture a huge, white abode in Bel Air.

For the real people who call those places home, this can be an issue.

“We had loads of problems with people just walking in during Covid,” says Kate Fox, who lives in a house that featured in British soap Emmerdale, for the years it was filmed entirely in her West Yorkshire village of Esholt. “Somebody actually came and just stuck their head through our front door. Maybe once a month you’ll get somebody opening the door or doing something inappropriate like peeking through your windows. People have no issues about completely invading your space – but you get used to it.”

Public intrusion is a common experience for the residents of TV-famous homes. In 2015, Vince Gilligan, the creator of Breaking Bad, had to urge fans to stop paying homage to his show – because they were recreating a scene where an entire pizza is thrown on to the roof of the house whose exterior was featured as Walter White’s bungalow. And last year, the owner of the apartment made famous by Sex and the City’s lead character erected a gate outside it because “at any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos, engaging in loud chatter, posting on social media, making TikTok videos or just celebrating the moment”. Eventually, the owners of the Breaking Bad house followed suit, erecting a 6ft iron fence – not that it stopped fans. “They still try to throw pizzas even though she’s got a gate, she’s got signage,” said Frank Sandoval, who runs Breaking Bad tours to the house in an RV. “They even try to climb the gate.”

But not everyone treats the arrival of hordes of fans as a bad thing. “At first, I was confused why they would want to come in,” says Glenda Kenyon, whose place in Barry, south Wales, features in BBC sitcom Gavin and Stacey as the home of Stacey’s mum, Gwen. “I just said, no, sorry, I can’t do it. Then the second year I thought, no, I’ve got to change it, so I started opening up.”

Glenda turned her home into a walk-in tribute to the show. It has a collection of memorabilia including fridge magnets, key rings, tea towels and “nearly every T-shirt you can buy”. She’s set up a photo opportunity in the kitchen with the frying pan Gwen uses to cook her infamous omelettes, as well as a face mask of the character visitors can put on. She even ended up partnering on tours with a coach firm, whose “Dave’s Coaches” bus regularly appeared in the show, and another run by Knock-off Nessa – who impersonates Ruth Jones’s character. Last year, she welcomed 168 busloads of people to her home, and it has given her a renewed purpose.

“I was lonely before, so lonely,” says Glenda, who lives alone and has experienced depression. “It has changed my life, because before I was so quiet, and now I can open up. I’m a hell of a lot better than I used to be. When you’re meeting people, you’re not thinking about the depression. I had no friends before, and now I got everybody.”

Having a home that’s famous for being on TV doesn’t just change the life of its owners. If the show is big enough, it can change an entire area – as a pocket of London’s Richmond found out after Ted Lasso was set there. The high-end jewellers and panama hat boutique that line the chi-chi alleyway of the soccer goof’s home are now joined by the Ted Lasso Store, featuring a recreated locker room decked out with a “Believe” poster, and a replica shirt for every player – available to purchase alongside a selection of mugs, scarves and snow globes. Over the road, an Italian restaurant attracts customers with a £5 “Eat like Ted” offer that entitles you to a box of Ted’s favourite shortbread biscuits.

“I didn’t realise it would be such a big deal,” says Reece Kent – who lives above, and is the general manager of, The Prince’s Head pub – Lasso’s regular. “Before I started working here, I was like, OK, we might get a few tourists. But I get 150 to 200 a day. At first it was just people from America, but now it’s Germany, Australia, Japan. I had a couple from Jamaica the other day.”

Richmond is far from the only place this has happened to. Over 37 years, a suburb of Melbourne was thronged by more than a quarter of a million soap opera fans on bus tours, desperate to see the real-life cul-de-sac that moonlighted as Neighbours’ Ramsay Street – resulting in a security guard being permanently stationed there. Esholt had its share of soap fans, too, with regular coach tours turning up. But Richmond is still packed with fans – and the pub has transformed one table into a designated fan area, next to a big AFC Richmond logo, replica shirt and signed pictures of the cast. They’re now the end point of a Lasso tour, which leaves them regularly flooded by big groups of tourists wanting to see the non-existent dartboard that featured in the show, and fiercely competing to sit at the table where Lasso held chats with his footballing assistant coach Beard. There has been one unexpected consequence of it all for Kent, though: needing to convince fans that he didn’t inspire a character in the show, the similarly named Roy Kent.

“A couple of weeks after I started, this tourist came in who’d seen my name on the website and had made all these connections that Roy Kent was based on me,” laughs Kent. “Luckily, after a while, they believed that it was actually based on Roy Keane. I would have loved to be Roy Keane, but I’m not.”

Being confused with a star of the show isn’t the only strange side-effect of having a TV show filmed in your home. “The end of our house had a vet’s waiting room and surgery in when I was growing up,” says Fox, who spent a chunk of her childhood having to pick her way around cables and lights, and being instructed to be as quiet as possible during takes. Until, that is, Emmerdale moved production to a set, and decided to create a mock-up of Fox’s home as one of the highlights of the now-defunct Granada Studios tourist attraction. “So there was an exact copy of my front lounge in a studio. Me and my mum went a few years ago. It was just a bizarre, bizarre place to be.”

Its effect on residents’ finances also doesn’t hurt. “When we were kids we sold tours of the house when my parents were out. We’d charge like 50p and let people have a look around,” says Fox. “I think the tourists liked getting a tour from a child. I never got any complaints!”

The owners of TV-famous homes who want to sell up also have very little to complain about. When the owners of Walter White’s Breaking Bad home eventually tired of fan attention, they sold it for $1.3m – reportedly to a streamer who intends to “treat it like a monument” – not bad compared to the $350-400,000 neighbouring homes are valued at. Esholt has attracted superfans “who have moved here specifically for the Emmerdale connection”, according to Fox. And two of the houses featured in Gavin and Stacey have been bought by superfans recently – one of which was sold very much as seen, because, they said, “To be able to own the original furniture was the cherry on top of the cake for us.”

Having a house associated with TV stars can also work the other way round too. Fox’s family may no longer have their home if it weren’t for the relationship they struck up with an Emmerdale star.

“At one point, Mum and Dad were at risk of losing the house to the council. Leah Bracknell [who played Zoe Tate] contacted the press and said: ‘You need to write about this,’” says Fox. “She’d appear in photos with them as well, and they did end up being allowed to buy the house off the council. We’ve still got all the press clippings now. She was really, really nice.”

A number of the Ted Lasso stars also became fond of their filming locations. According to Kent, “they’d pop in on days they weren’t filming – for lunch or just a drink”, although Lasso himself wasn’t the main culprit. “Jason Sudeikis [who plays Lasso] only popped in once. I had Coach Beard in a couple of times. Dani Rojas was the main one – he’d have lunch and bring friends. They were lovely.”

Despite getting to meet celebs, living somewhere TV famous isn’t for everyone. “People who moved here during filming or since, they really do struggle with the tourists – they think it’s so rude and shocking that people just walk into your house,” says Fox. But, ultimately, for some people, it brings a real sense of happiness – particularly if you’re a fan of the show.

“I was over the moon when I first saw my house on telly. Every time I watch, I’m going: ‘That’s mine! That’s mine!’” says Glenda.

“People tell me that I’ve put Barry on the map and I do feel like that’s true. I’ve had people from India, Africa, New Zealand, Swindon – you name it, I’ve had them. I’m very proud. I’ve done something in my life I can be happy about.”

Karoline Leavitt leaves behind a legacy of lies. What’s next for the Trump aide?

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 11:00:27 GMT

The press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administration

Karoline Leavitt, 28, is leaving her demanding job as Donald Trump’s press secretary to spend more time with her two young children and her 60-year-old husband. According to a post by Trump On Truth Social, Leavitt will be departing her role at the end of the month and will serve as one of Trump’s “top outside advisors”.

In other words: the official version of events is that Leavitt is resigning on her own terms for family reasons and not because Trump’s approval ratings are at record lows and she’s a rat fleeing a sinking ship.

But is the official version of events the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Don’t bother asking Leavitt – I’m not sure she knows much about the T-word. She may have been the youngest White House press secretary in history, but there’s no denying her communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in the Trump administration. I won’t muck about with euphemisms such as misrepresented or stated without evidence or made false claims. Leavitt’s legacy in government was attacking Trump’s enemies and spouting lie after lie after lie.

Being a lowly writer means I am held to far higher standards about what I can say than the departing press secretary or her boss, the president of the United States. Unlike Leavitt or Trump, I actually have to provide facts and evidence to back up my assertions. So here we go: here are a few fun facts about Leavitt’s tenure in public office.

First, there’s her role in promoting lies about the economy. One of the most significant economic policies of Trump’s second term has been his global tariffs, which were initially extended even to volcanic islands inhabited only by penguins. During a press briefing in March 2025, Leavitt told reporters that tariffs were a “tax cut for the American people”. Economists have said this is nonsense. “Economists don’t agree on much, but we agree tariffs are taxes on consumers,” Tara Sinclair, a George Washington University economist told the fact-checking website Politifact. The non-partisan Tax Foundation has also run the numbers and said that in 2025, the Trump tariffs “amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000” per US household.

But what’s $1,000, eh? It’s nothing to Trump, who made a staggering $2.2bn during the first year of his second term in various questionable ways. One imagines it’s also not much to Leavitt, who earns just under $200,000 in her role and whose husband, Nicholas Riccio, manages what has been described as a multimillion-dollar real estate business.

And if you feel aggrieved about tariffs increasing the already sky-high cost of living, according to Leavitt, you should just work harder (or marry a real estate tycoon). “Some of these kids, and I call them kids because they are in their 20s and have never had real jobs, and they’re complaining things are expensive,” Fox News’ Jesse Watters told Leavitt last month during a conversation about young Democratic party voters. “Yes, things are expensive when you don’t have a real job.” Leavitt agreed, adding that her generation had been raised with “silver spoons in their mouths, just getting everything handed to them”. That was un-American, she suggested, because this country “was built on meritocracy and hard work, pulling up your sleeves, pulling yourself up from your bootstraps”.

It’s not just tariffs where Leavitt’s math seems to be off. In January 2025, the press secretary justified Trump’s order to freeze federal funding to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) by claiming it was wasting money.

“[T]here was about to be 50m taxpayer dollars that went out the door to fund condoms in Gaza,” Leavitt said. “That is a preposterous waste of taxpayer money. So that’s what this pause is focused on: being good stewards of tax dollars.”

To be very clear: that condom claim was a lie. Documents shows that no condoms were sent anywhere in the Middle East, let alone to a place undergoing what many experts have termed a genocide. The US did, however, provide billions of taxpayer dollars to help Israel destroy Gaza, which has arguably reduced births a lot faster than condoms would have. The dismantling of USAID, justified by Leavitt, has also increased pregnancy complications and maternal death in poor countries. A study published in the Lancet journal last year estimated that US funding cuts could result in more than 14 million deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under age five, by 2030. I guess, if you’re Leavitt, being “good stewards of tax dollars” means contributing to mass death and immiseration. Money well spent!

As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure. Last October, for example, SV Dáte, Huffington Post’s senior White House correspondent, asked Leavitt via text message who had suggested Budapest for a meeting between Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss Ukraine. Her response? “Your mom did.” When Dáte then asked if Leavitt thought that was funny, she replied: “It’s funny to me that you actually consider yourself a journal [sic]. You are a far left hack who nobody takes seriously, including your colleagues in the media, they just don’t tell you that to your face. Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bullshit questions.”

That was a brief look at Leavitt’s past. What’s in store for her future? Despite her comments about her family, don’t expect her to go full tradwife. None of the ambitious women advancing the Trump administration’s anti-woman agenda want to devote their own lives to the domestic drudgery they extoll for others. They’ve got less privileged women to do the childcare and the cooking and the cleaning for them. No, rather than being a tradwife, one imagines Leavitt might end up with a nice little gig on Fox News or Bari Weiss’s CBS. Or perhaps, like Sean Spicer, her predecessor under Trump 1.0, she might go the reality TV route and regale us all on Dancing With the Stars. No doubt there will also be a “tell-all” book in her future in which, depending on which way the political winds are blowing, she’ll tell us all the things she thinks will rehabilitate her reputation.

And, of course, for now there’s her new role as an “outside advisor”. I can’t tell you exactly what that entails but I can tell you that, going forward, communications with Trump and his outside advisers can apparently be considered privileged. On Monday, after Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general, the justice department’s office of legal counsel issued a 21-page opinion about the president’s “executive privilege” which protects communication between Trump and advisers who don’t work for his administration. This makes a future Democrat-led investigation into the Trump administration a lot harder as his advisers – who will now include Leavitt – will not be able to be comprehensively questioned by Congress. Exactly the sort of move you’d expect from a president that Leavitt has called the “most transparent” in history.

Best of luck, then, to Leavitt in her future endeavors. I’m sure she’ll roll up her designer sleeves, pull herself up by her bootstraps and find a way to make huge amounts of money. And best of luck to all of us. If there’s one thing that you can be sure about when it comes to the revolving door that is the White House, it’s that no matter how bad the person leaving is, the replacement is always worse.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows it

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 10:29:27 GMT

The Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bear

Nigel Farage is a rattled, embattled politician. Perhaps he feels buoyed up by securing slightly more votes in a byelection boycotted by all the main parties than he did in the general election two years ago. That was despite 10,000 fewer people turning out to vote. But there was never any question that he was going to win a byelection he called purely to deflect scrutiny of his undeclared £5m personal gift from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and donations from a convicted fraudster.

Farage chose Clacton as his parliamentary launchpad for a reason. It was here that his previous outfit, Ukip, secured its breakthrough in the byelection of 2014. It is one of the most pro-leave seats in Britain, while Electoral Calculus estimates that almost no other constituency is this rightwing.

When I visited, I found no shortage of voters who were defiant about Farage’s scandals. They saw no problem with a politician being showered with dosh by a foreign-based billionaire, arguing that Farage deserved it because he was a “nice man” and even suggesting he might invest it locally. They bought the narrative that the establishment was out to get their man, as if a millionaire ex-City broker who is a sometime friend of the US president is some plucky outsider.

They are representative of about a fifth of the country who laud Farage as the mainstream politician most hostile to immigration, and who are contemptuous of a Conservative party that failed even on its own terms in office. What should concern Farage, however, is that most Britons are more opposed to him than ever, and are determined to block him from power. That majority delivered victory to the Greens in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, and to Andy Burnham in June’s Makerfield byelection.

That the parody candidate Count Binface won more than a quarter of the vote in this ultra-rightwing heartland is a warning in itself. Yes, this “independent space warrior” secured plenty of media attention, but he had precious little ground game – that is, an army of volunteers to get out the vote. Many voters I spoke to hadn’t even heard of him. It seems plausible that some of those who made Count Binface the most successful joke candidate in history had previously voted not just Labour, Lib Dem or Green, but Conservative too.

Farage refused to attend the official declaration of this election he chose to call. That suggests not just petulance and contempt for his own voters, but the insecurities of a jittery man. He claims Essex police had told him about an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”, but the local force said there had been no “incidents or issues” related to the byelection and that attendance was up to candidates. And did Farage not claim that his £5m personal gift was needed to pay for his security?

The explanation is probably more mundane. Being mocked on stage by a man in a bin does not exactly provide the optics of a heroic struggle against the establishment.

What next for the Farage show? If he thought the byelection was an effective ruse to deflect from his money issues, reality caught up with him quickly. The parliamentary watchdog has now reopened its investigation into Farage’s gift and donations, and another byelection may be forced if there is an adverse ruling.

But it is not just finances that have plunged Reform UK into crisis. Farage’s proud association with Donald Trump – toxic even to most Reform voters – has become an ever greater drag. Absorbing so many former Conservatives was surely another big error. The last government was bitterly rejected for a reason, not least by Farage’s own supporters, and filling Reform’s ranks with its former leading lights hardly helped the party’s anti-establishment pretences.

And then there is the pivot to ever more toxic rightwing politics, perhaps partly driven by pressure from the even further right Restore Britain, founded by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Farage now talks of “anti-white discrimination” – rhetoric once confined to the ugliest reaches of the far right. His talk of “pure cold rage” after the conviction of Henry Nowak’s murder – just hours before riots over it – rightly disturbed many.

Then there’s Zia Yusuf, his home affairs spokesperson, whose increasingly aggressive social media posts speak to Reform’s authoritarian underbelly. Yusuf repeatedly describes his opponents as “traitors” – his latest target was the Tory former defence secretary Ben Wallace – and threatens that an unspecific “reckoning is coming”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

All of this alarms most Britons, who have concluded that Reform must be kept from power and will vote tactically if needs be. Yet this is of scant comfort to the absurdly underscrutinised Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, because Reform’s hardened core shows no interest in returning to her camp. Rightwing Britain, then, is divided.

It would be a mistake to write Farage off, however. We are in the midst of the Andy Burnham bounce. Voters are relieved to be rid of Keir Starmer, and for now Labour is tempting back some progressive voters who defected to the Greens. But Burnham has yet to be forced into many big decisions. Britain’s economic plight, its crisis-stricken public services and Burnham’s slowness to hike taxes on the booming rich could all come to a head in October’s budget. Disillusionment could swell, and Reform could benefit – unless, of course, Burnham calls a snap election first.

But you have to ask whether Farage’s heart is really in this. Reports that he received his £5m gift after saying he would need “a million a year” to serve as an MP are telling. Here is a man who appears to enjoy the high life and feel parliamentary politics damages his earning potential. He seems increasingly riled by the sort of scrutiny he has long managed to avoid. Perhaps, after a pointless triumph over a bin, he may simply decide he has had enough.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

El Niño may peak at the worst time for the Amazon – and it should worry us all

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 10:00:25 GMT

Delay to rainy season in forest already damaged by human-driven heating could trigger powerful ‘Godzilla’ El Niño

As a supercharged climate scorches Europe with wildfire and deluges Asia with floods, the Amazon is bracing for a drought that strikes fear into the hearts of forest defenders and food producers alike. But it should worry even more of us.

Scientists are predicting that the peak of El Niño will occur at the worst possible time for the world’s biggest tropical rainforest: the end of the dry season between October and December, when rivers are at their lowest and undergrowth is most likely to be tinder dry. This will be a period of extreme vulnerability for the forest, which plays a globally important role in stabilising the climate and irrigating crops.

The planet’s life-support system is already reeling from a double whammy. Human-driven climate disruption, caused by burning fossil fuels and trees, is relentlessly heating the world and amplifying extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and storms. On top of this long-term trend is the latest El Niño, a naturally occurring phenomenon of high Pacific Ocean temperatures that leads to warming – and drought and fire – for much of the rest of the world.

Scientists say this El Niño is on course to be the strongest in 150 years by a “mind-blowing margin.” Even in its incipient phase, it is wreaking havoc havoc across the planet.

Western Europe has endured the hottest June and July in history, with exceptionally low rainfall, sparking extreme wildfires in France, Greece and other Mediterranean countries and water shortages in the Seine, Rhine and Danube basins. Three-quarters of England is in drought and baked by what is forecast to be the hottest UK summer on record.

In Asia, South Korea and Japan are sweltering in a record heatwave, while China has been battered by Typhoon Dolphin, which has turned Shanghai’s streets into rivers, torn roofs from houses and forced the evacuation of more than 1 million people. Floods have killed more than 100 people in India’s Assam state, with more rain forecast.

Swathes of the world are burning. In Canada, “out of control” wildfires have forced tens of thousands to flee British Colombia and darkened the skies of distant New York. Huge fires are also raging on Java Island in Indonesia and Utah in the US, which has also been scorched by a record July heatwave.

In Africa, the UN is predicting a severe hit to food production. In the Middle East, local temperature records are being broken almost every day, with the United Arab Emirates registering 51.2C in Al Dhafra.

Meanwhile, sea surface temperatures are trending far outside previous parameters, threatening coral reefs and other marine life. Because the oceans are the world’s main heat absorber, their temperatures are a prelude to what follows on land.

But among the greatest concerns about what comes next is the Amazon, which is essential for maintaining biodiversity and ensuring rainfall for food-producing regions across South America.

A few decades ago, the idea of drought in the rainforest would have seemed outlandish. The Amazon is the world’s biggest river and its principal tributaries – the Xingu, Negro, Tapajós, Madeira, Purus, Juruá and Japurá –are among the planet’s main sources of freshwater. The forest around them has always been famed for humidity, with giant trees that sucked up moisture and pumped it into the atmosphere, generating “flying rivers” that cooled and watered an entire continent. The trillions of trees and plants in the Amazon also draw down huge quantities of carbon dioxide with benefits to the entire planet. Any weakening of this function adds to the risks of instability, food insecurity and extreme weather.

Now, the Brazilian meteorological agency has released a forecast that the unusually strong El Niño will delay the onset of the Amazonian rainy season, raise temperatures, deplete rivers and intensify fire risks.

As in many other parts of the planet, this creates an emergency within an emergency: the onset of a natural but extremely powerful “Godzilla” El Niño that could last well into the new year, on top of human-driven warming.

Scientists and Indigenous residents say the Amazon is struggling to recover from the devastation caused during the last El Niño in 2023-24, which left some of the world’s greatest rivers at record-low levels, sparked unprecedented fire outbreaks and caused mass deaths of dolphins and fish.

With a third of the Amazon now degraded by farming, mining and human-caused climate disruption, the trees and undergrowth are more flammable and vulnerable to “megafires,” raising concerns that many parts may tip beyond the point of no return.

The government is trying to address this with satellite monitoring, enforcement operations and greater investment in firefighting capacity. This produced positive results last year, when the burned areas of the Amazon fell to their lowest level since records began in 1985.

But one year is not long enough for the forest to recover, and it now faces a far greater threat.

Three previous El Ninõs (1997-98, 2015-16 and 2023-24) proved disastrous for the Amazon. Prof Jos Barlow, an Amazon specialist at the Lancaster Environment Centre, said the prospect of a still stronger phenomenon was deeply worrying: “It is hard to imagine the outcome of even more severe droughts and heat.”

The Amazon fire season has already started but the peak is still a couple of months away.

Indigenous communities are setting up their own firefighting units to cope with outbreaks in deeper parts of the forest. Dr Erika Berenguer, a forest expert at Oxford University and author of a book on how to deal with rainforest fires, said: “It’s crazy. The humid forest should not be burning.”

A major part of the problem, Berenguer said, was multiple El Niños hitting in a relatively short space of time: “It’s similar to if you are already sick and then you get an infection. That infection is going to have much greater impacts on your body because your immune system is already compromised fighting the sickness.”

The brutal conditions are likely to drag on – and possibly intensify – in 2027 because there is a lag of about three months between the peak of El Niño warming in the Pacific Ocean and temperature rises elsewhere in the world.

Carlos Nobre, a professor at the University of São Paulo and one of Brazil’s leading climate scientists, said: “The Amazon has to be very prepared from now through the beginning of 2027, at least up to March, because this El Niño is very likely to induce a severe drought.”

Farmers are bracing for a turbulent year. “Fellow ranchers, GET READY FOR EL NIÑO,” reads a post on a popular WhatsApp group for beef producers in the Amazonian state of Pará. “El Niño will impact Brazilian cattle farming by causing heat stress in animals, reducing pasture quality, and leading to ‘water scarcity’. This drives up supplementation costs and can reduce weight gain and milk production.”

Other agricultural businesses post apocalyptic images of parched soil or flooded cities (the south of Brazil is forecast to get much more rain). “The 2026 Super El Niño has evolved from a mere weather phenomenon into a symbol for a new era of global instability,” warns one post.

The industry magazine Agroforte reports that Brazil’s soya bean harvests have fallen during previous strong El Niño years, but omits any mention of the human causes for the more hostile climate: deforestation – usually by farmers – and the burning of fossil fuels.

Indigenous groups, in contrast, tend to preserve the forest and help to maintain a stable climate – but they, too, face the triple threats of a global heating, forest clearance and El Niño.

The government has warned that traditional lands will face increased fire risks, and has stockpiled food in case of shortages. During the previous El Niño, some forest communities in the Xingu and Tapajós basins were left isolated, thirsty and worried about hunger when rivers – the main transportation route – ran dry and vegetable gardens shrivelled up. Anything worse next year and Brazil could face the apocalyptic scenario of drought refugees in a rainforest.

That this is even a possibility should alarm the world. A severely weakened Amazon will further disrupt the climate and agricultural production at a time when farmers across many parts of the world are already saying that changes are too quick for them to adapt. Global food prices are at a three-year high as falling harvests combine with the fuel inflation caused by the US-Israeli attack on Iran. The UN is predicting that 49 million more people are likely to face acute hunger because of El Niño.

Much more needs to be done to protect biomes such as the Amazon, on which the world depends. Investing more in firefighters is a necessary short-term step, but it only deals with the consequences rather than the local and global causes. Unless deforestation is halted and fossils fuels are phased out, the atmosphere will continue to warm and amplify extreme weather. Even this year’s Godzilla El Niño will seem like a pussycat compared with what is coming.
