‘I’ve never done anything like this in my life’: Marina Abramović on making art with balloons

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 10:00:25 GMT

The artist’s latest swerve sees her creating an alien inflatable landscape for New York’s Balloon Museum

Oversized inflatable blades of grass graze my face as I wind a path through the glowing white gallery space. Little papery squares of snow blow, some sticking to my hair. The path through the room curves so that only what is right in front of me is visible: initially, it seemed like I would reach the far side of the room in mere seconds but still my journey, magically, continues. I am at Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z, the latest installation by the performance artist Marina Abramović. It opened earlier this month at New York’s newly opened Balloon Museum, which bills itself as “the first permanent home for inflatable art”.

“I’ve never done anything like this in my life,” a smiling Abramović said, speaking on Zoom from her Manhattan apartment. “But if you give me an assignment then I’ll try to see what I can do with it.” As she began researching balloon art her first thought was that it was “so kitschy – basically for kids and games”. However, the more she contemplated the balloon, the more she saw its resonance with her own practice. “You put air in it, and at some point the air comes out. Or you pinch it and it disappears. The temporality of this is very close to what I’m doing: performance art.”

Following the success of a 2023 pop-up in New York, the Rome-born Balloon Museum chose the city for its flagship. It rented and revamped the hollowed innards of Jean-Georges’s ill-fated Tin Building, replacing the chichi food hall with an inaugural exhibition titled Daydream, which presents 14 installations from artists including Turner Prize-winner Martin Creed, Balloon Museum mainstay Karina Smigla-Bobinski and the commercial AV installation studio Onionlab.

The installations I liked best were those that destabilized me: Swiss composer and artist Thom Kubli’s Black Hole Horizon showed oversized gramophone-style horns that bellowed resonant sounds and spat out soap bubbles. To experience the work of Boris Acket, a Dutch artist, I lay on a padded floor, hypnotized by a fabric wing that revealed and then obscured my reflection in the mirrored ceiling.

Oh, the mirrors. As is the case at many of these immersive sites, the Balloon Museum is full of them, and it sometimes felt as if the museum was tailoring the installations to meet visitors’ desires to take selfies. (My tour guide insisted that all the mirrors were the artists’ own choices.)

At her institute in Greece, Abramović asks attenders to walk through the forest backward using a hand mirror to see, challenging people to disorient themselves and submit to slowness. But her installation at the Balloon Museum is among those that forgoes reflective surfaces. Before entering Planet Z, I donned wireless noise-canceling headphones through which the artist recited the names of exoplanets in a slow monotone. This personal soundscape added to the sense that I wasn’t only moving through an alien space, but that I was somehow outside of earthly time too. As Abramović said: “I’m giving you the work, but you have to give me time. This is the exchange. If you invest yourself into the work, then you have an experience.”

When we speak she is dressed in red, a color that she’s said she wears to energize her. After many years of performing, the now-79-year-old thinks “it’s time for the public to have a direct experience” of the kind of presentness she’s advocated for throughout her career.

“I really love the completely random propositions people give to me,” Abramović chuckles. In the past couple years, she’s applied her approach to products such as olive oil and a series of tinctures, plus a facial lotion. Since 2002, she’s created arty espresso cups with the coffee purveyor Illy. She’s appeared in a video by Jay-Z inspired by her blockbuster MoMA retrospective The Artist Is Present. The Balloon Museum is just another challenge.

Abramović compares her taking on these projects to Renaissance artists who were commissioned by the clergy and aristocracy. Most of the time, the patrons wanted the depictions of the same conventional pieces: the Madonna and Child or the crucifixion of Christ. “How many of these crucifixions were made for just a few incredible masterpieces?” she asks. “I like it when a team gives you very strict rules, then you have to make a masterpiece out of them. It’s very difficult to do. Sometimes you completely fail, and failure is a very good thing. It’s about courage.”

Roberto Fantauzzi, the Balloon Museum director, hopes that the institution will split the difference between kid-friendly “playgrounds” such as New York’s Museum of Ice Cream and traditional art institutions. “We are completely in the middle, and this is our strength,” he said, as we spoke beside the museum, overlooking the wide-eyed inflatable outdoor sculptures that have become its mascot (you can buy plushy keychain versions in the gift shop).

“I haven’t seen the final result yet,” Abramović told me when I asked her about her response to Planet Z. I knew she wouldn’t say if she felt she’d “failed” or succeeded; when we speak, she recounted a performance she knew in her stomach was a failure “right away”, but refused to say the name or year. It was “famous” and beloved, but the thought of it made her sick. “I don’t care what the public says or the critics say,” she said.

The Balloon Museum is fun, sure. I smiled; at times I felt disarmed by the sense of wonder evoked by some pieces and the contemplative quiet offered by others. I don’t doubt that if I were a child, it might have opened me to possibilities of contemporary art. But I left and the levity dissipated; I was unchanged. The experience had been consumed.

But what did I expect? As Abramović said in a droll tone when I asked her my final questions about the show: “What else do we need to talk about? I mean, it’s just the Balloon Museum.”

Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z is at the Balloon Museum, New York

How can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars?

The Guardian Fri, 14 Aug 2026 07:00:21 GMT

Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of us

In this fragmented but supposedly mild country, watching and talking about the weather forecast is meant to be a reassuring, unifying activity. Collectively, we have created and maintained a national climate narrative of small disappointments and pleasures. The first weather forecaster to appear on British TV, George Cowling, made his debut on the BBC in January 1954, predicting that “tomorrow would be rather windy”, but “a good day to hang out the washing”. For most of the 72 years since, such brief, carefully calibrated broadcasts have provided people from Aberdeen to Penzance with practical information, small talk and minor grumbles about essentially the same situation: living in a country where the weather is constantly changing, in a paradoxically unchanging way.

Yet like the traditional British climate, that common weather culture may now be evaporating. “Met Office considers issuing red ‘extreme heat warning’ across Britain while nation enjoys ‘incredible summer’,” said the headline above the forecast on the GB News website on Monday, caught between terror and delight at the latest heatwave. As the climate crisis has affected this country in more and more unmistakable but uneven ways, TV weather forecasters have increasingly struggled to find the right language to describe this transformation’s daily consequences. Their struggle influences and exemplifies that of many Britons to understand, and work out what we think about, the apparent end of the weather patterns we expected to shape our whole lives.

Across all the British TV broadcasters, sometimes within the same bulletin, or even the same sentence, weather forecasters now present sunshine as welcome and oppressive; high temperatures as miraculous and unbearable; rain as an inconvenience and desperately needed; cloud cover as depressing and a relief. Tanned forecasters in sundresses, emphasising the positives for domestic holidaymakers of another record-breaking summer, alternate with grim-faced forecasters suggesting we are experiencing a weather apocalypse.

Meanwhile, the wildly differing effects of the climate crisis on different areas, and from one season to another, are further fracturing Britain’s weather conversation into a babble of separate, sometimes conflicting discourses. This year, parts of the country have experienced such contrasting summers – wetter than usual in western Scotland, desert-like in southern England – that we can no longer say they share broadly the same northern European climate, as had been assumed for centuries. In an era of separatism and nationalism, another major binding element of the UK may be falling away.

Beneath the relatively placid surface of our previous weather culture, there were always some tensions and contradictions. In a 2025 academic paper, British Heatwave Discourse (1985–2023): from Ice Cream to Armageddon?, Thijs van Dooremalen and Philip Smith analysed articles about heatwaves in the national press. They found that until 2000 positive and negative coverage coexisted in roughly equal quantities, “often in the same newspaper”. From 2000 to 2014, the balance shifted slowly towards the negative, as the climate crisis became a mainstream worry. Yet only from 2015 did an “Apocalyptic genre” of heatwave articles begin to become dominant; and a “Romantic genre” of celebratory coverage remains. In a country where many people still spend much of the year feeling cold, the idea of hot weather as a liberation is likely to linger, for some, for decades to come.

For other Britons, heatwaves have become political flashpoints, their causes to be furiously contested, their existence even denied. During the record heat of 2022, “weather forecasters faced unprecedented levels of trolling”, the BBC reported, including “hundreds of abusive tweets or emails questioning their reports and telling them to ‘get a grip’… ‘it’s just summer’”. Some of these climate crisis deniers described advice on how to stay cool as “pandering to the ‘woke brigade’”, and accused the BBC and Met Office of “scaremongering” to help the then Conservative government impose unneeded green policies.

This summer, some of these conspiratorial arguments have re-emerged. But with the Tories having in effect turned against net zero, joined by Reform UK, Restore Britain and most of the rightwing media, disagreeing with weather forecasters who express alarm about our changing climate has become more mainstream. Discussing the weather is no longer just small talk, but also a battlefield in the culture wars.

No wonder forecasters often sound unsure or extremely cautious about what tone to adopt on air. In 2023, the BBC’s Tomasz Schafernaker gave a very careful interview to the Big Issue. “While our language remains largely the same,” he said, “we have adapted it to include references to climate change. We must be mindful that prolonged periods of sun and heat are not always good news … However, there are often areas in the UK where the weather is much more comfortable, [so] highlighting that it’s not ‘all bad’ is important. It’s a balance that we assess on a daily basis.”

Yet three years on, his broadcasts have become less neutral. “The savage summer continues across Europe,” he said on the BBC weather website last Thursday afternoon. “It’s been excruciatingly hot …” On BBC One last Sunday evening, while giving this week’s UK forecast, he kept making gestures of helplessness and disbelief. It was like a weather bulletin from a dystopian drama.

Such interventions no longer seem melodramatic. “The climate of the 20th century has now gone,” says Mike Kendon, a Met Office scientist and co-author of State of the UK Climate in 2025, published last month. So far, this year’s weather has been more extreme. Even more than the heat, summer drought and winter floods, its key feature has been the weather getting stuck in one state for months – a characteristic of harsh continental climates, rather than the changeable one around which our society has been built. So it’s possible that next summer will feature relentless rain, not drought, and that other seasons will continue to stall as well, damaging the economy, everyday life and public health.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Britons are world famous for their weather stoicism. But this stoicism has been created by centuries of relatively minor weather discomforts and disasters. How the forecasters, and the rest of us, will react as the climate crisis intensifies – in our private behaviours and assumptions as well as our public lives – is a question we are only in the early stages of answering.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Senate Hopeful in Alaska Says ‘No Thanks’ to Kamala Harris’s Support

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The campaign of Mary Peltola said it was focused on issues important to Alaska and did not approve a message of support from Ms. Harris.

By Tim Balk

For former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, to win the Senate race in Alaska this year, she would have to drastically outperform former Vice President Kamala Harris’s showing in the state in the 2024 presidential election.

So after Ms. Harris, who lost Alaska by 14 percentage points, signed a recent fund-raising email from her PAC supporting Ms. Peltola, Republicans saw an opening for an attack — and pounced. Ms. Peltola’s campaign, in turn, quickly said it had not approved the appeal and did not seek the former vice president’s endorsement.

In the fund-raising appeal, sent Wednesday, Ms. Harris urged supporters to “stand behind Mary,” describing the battle in Alaska as a “must-win race” for Democrats in their quest to reclaim the Senate. The well-funded Ms. Peltola is running as an independent-minded centrist against Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska. Limited polling suggests the race is competitive.

The email from Ms. Harris’s political action committee links to a donation page for a Democratic PAC and urges supporters to split their donations between Ms. Peltola’s campaign and Ms. Harris’s committee. It says: “If there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats — it’s Mary.”

A day after the email went out, the campaign arm of Senate Republicans, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, moved to tie Ms. Peltola to Ms. Harris. A spokesman for the group, Nick Puglia, declared in a statement that Ms. Peltola had worked “hand in hand with Kamala Harris to put Alaska last, so it’s no surprise that Harris is backing Peltola.” (Ms. Peltola’s brief tenure in Congress, a little more than two years, overlapped with the Biden administration.)

A spokesman for Mr. Sullivan’s campaign, Nate Adams, piled on, saying in a statement, “No matter how hard Mary Peltola tries to hide from the endorsement, Alaskans can see exactly whose team she and Kamala Harris are on.”

Ms. Peltola’s campaign pushed back.

“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,” the campaign said in a statement that cited the support Ms. Peltola has captured from several Alaska labor groups.

The Peltola campaign said that it did not approve the email from Ms. Harris’s organization, and that it had no knowledge about it before it was sent out.

A representative for Ms. Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was not the first fund-raising appeal Ms. Harris’s political action committee, the Fight for the People PAC, had sent trying to use Ms. Peltola’s candidacy to raise funds for its own coffers.

On Jan. 12, the day Ms. Peltola announced her run, the PAC sent a similar message to supporters. “This is the race that may determine control of the Senate,” the January email began. But the timing of the latest solicitation stood out with the state’s Aug. 18 nonpartisan primary just days away.

Ms. Peltola is widely expected to advance Tuesday to the November general election. Under Alaska’s election system, the top four candidates in the primary move on. But Primary Day will offer the candidates a spotlight to deliver their messages and set the stage for the general-election race, along with an audience that is likely to be paying closer attention.

Defending Republican attacks linking Ms. Peltola with Ms. Harris is probably not the message the candidate had in mind for this important moment.

The appeal by Ms. Harris’s group also arrived as she considers running for president again. In the spring, she told the Rev. Al Sharpton that she “might” run, and she has spent recent months making public appearances across the country.

Ms. Peltola did not endorse Ms. Harris in 2024. The former congresswoman’s campaign slogan this year is “fish, family and freedom.”

State Representative Rebecca Himschoot of Alaska, an independent, said the email from Ms. Harris’s group could be somewhat unhelpful for Ms. Peltola, but that it was just a small part of a deluge of messaging from outside Alaska flooding the Senate race.

“I pity the voters in Alaska this cycle: it’s tremendously manipulative, all the stuff we’re getting,” Ms. Himschoot said, even as she described the outreach by Ms. Harris’s organization as “really dumb.”

“She’s riding Mary Peltola’s coattails,” Ms. Himschoot added. “And she’s not even running for anything that anyone knows of yet, and didn’t do well here to begin with.”

Alaska has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly two decades, though the state has an independent streak and has showed signs of shifting toward Democrats in some recent election cycles.

Most Alaska voters are politically unaffiliated. Senator Lisa Murkowski, a centrist Republican, won re-election in the state in 2022 by beating a Trump-backed rival.

Republicans also worry that the arrival in the race of another Dan Sullivan, a former elementary-school teacher with no political experience, will confuse supporters of the senator with the same name, potentially siphoning away some of his votes and lifting Ms. Peltola to victory.

Republicans have claimed that Ms. Peltola’s campaign planted the second Mr. Sullivan in the race to trick voters, but the Peltola campaign has denied coordinating with him. That Mr. Sullivan waged a successful court battle to remain on the ballot after elections officials tried to remove him.

With “Coyote vs. Acme,” Ian Frazier, a soft-spoken reporter and humorist, has finally gone Hollywood.

Ian Frazier, who has written for The New Yorker since the 1970s, in Montclair, N. J. Credit... Bryan Anselm for The New York Times

Supported by

By Steven Kurutz

In 2022, Ian Frazier, a longtime writer for The New Yorker, received an email from a friend named Hannah Albee in Albuquerque, N. M.

They had met years earlier at Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen in Manhattan, where Frazier was a volunteer and Albee was an employee.

“Congrats,” she wrote. “They’re filming ‘Coyote’ on my street.”

Albee was referring to “Coyote vs. Acme,” a potential summer blockbuster featuring the Looney Tunes characters Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner.

The movie is based on a humor piece Frazier wrote more than three decades ago. In it, he imagines Wile E. Coyote suing the Acme Corporation for the many harms he has suffered while stalking his prey with the help of its malfunctioning devices.

It appeared in The New Yorker’s 65th anniversary issue, dated Feb. 19, 1990. Then it was optioned for film. And then it fell into an endless-seeming Hollywood limbo.

When Frazier heard from his friend, a movie version was the last thing on his mind.

“I had actually forgotten about it,” he said over lunch at a Vietnamese restaurant in Montclair, N. J., where he lives with his wife, the novelist Jacqueline Carey.

“Coyote vs. Acme,” a blend of live action and animation, will finally be released on Aug. 28 — 36 years after he tapped out his idea on an Olympia manual typewriter.

Frazier, 75, doesn’t fit the usual idea of the urbane New Yorker writer. Known to friends as Sandy, he has a manner suggestive of his upbringing in Hudson, Ohio. But beneath the mild exterior is the idiosyncratic mind that produced the humor collection “Dating Your Mom” and perhaps his best known book, “Great Plains,” a sprawling meditation on the Midwest.

From small-town Ohio, he made his way to Harvard College. He wrote for The Harvard Lampoon and became friends with Jim Downey, who would go on to be one of the most prolific writers at “Saturday Night Live.” After graduating in 1973, Frazier put in some time writing captions for a pornographic magazine, Oui. Then he found a professional home that suited him better, The New Yorker.

He distinguished himself with pithy dispatches for the Talk of the Town section, stylish feature stories and reliably funny humor pieces. In 1990, his thoughts turned to Wile E. Coyote.

He was 39, living with his wife and infant daughter in Park Slope, Brooklyn. In those days, he was a regular reader of American Lawyer, copies of which he borrowed from a downstairs neighbor. He was especially drawn to the legal arguments of Gerry Spence, a silver-tongued cowboy lawyer who defended Imelda Marcos on racketeering charges. Frazier decided to write something in the voice of Wile E. Coyote’s lawyer.

“The idea was to take the language of an opening statement to describe something quite preposterous,” he said.

Like the millions of Americans who had grown up watching Saturday morning cartoons, he was deeply familiar with the beleaguered Wile E. Coyote. The creature tries — and repeatedly fails, in disastrous ways — to catch his fleet-footed nemesis, Road Runner, using a variety of Acme gizmos.

“It occurred to me that if you take a pair of roller skates and put small jet engines on each skate, obviously something is going to go wrong,” Frazier said. “The Acme Corporation suddenly became a character in my mind.”

Wile E. Coyote and Road Runner were created for Warner Bros., the company behind the Looney Tunes franchise, by the animator Chuck M. Jones and the writer Michael Maltese. In his memoir, “Chuck Amuck,” Jones wrote that he drew inspiration from Mark Twain’s 1872 book, “Roughing It.” Twain described the coyote as “a long, slim, sick and sorry-looking skeleton” and “a living, breathing allegory of Want.”

Frazier knew the Twain passage and suspected it had an influence on the character. He saw in Wile E. Coyote’s all-consuming desire a kind of pathos. “He’s trying to be murderous, but there’s something about him — he’s just can’t be murderous enough,” he said. “And there is that peaceful moment of knowing. Sometimes he gets very peaceful at the end, when he runs off the cliff. The moment of realization is always very touching.”

The story, which he titled “Coyote v. Acme,” came quickly, at just 1,600 words. Frazier photocopied his pages and trudged off to the mailbox, wondering if what he had written would impress his editor at The New Yorker, Veronica Geng, an acclaimed humor writer herself. “Her ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on an idea would totally determine if it was worth doing,” he said.

Soon after the piece appeared in the magazine, it became the subject of a literary contretemps: Another humor writer, Joey Green, gave interviews to Newsweek and The New York Observer in which he accused Frazier of plagiarism.

In 1982, Green had published a three-part series, “Cliffhanger Justice,” with the very same premise in The National Lampoon. “I loved the Road Runner cartoons, and the big question was why Coyote hadn’t sued for faulty merchandising,” Green said in an interview from his home in Florida.

Frazier said he was unaware of Green’s piece before he wrote “Coyote v. Acme.” Over lunch in Montclair, he still seemed pained by the accusation. “How do I prove a negative?” he said. “I wasn’t reading National Lampoon. It was a complete bummer, to be honest.”

It was a bummer for Green, too — especially when “Coyote v. Acme” gained more attention as the title story of Frazier’s 1996 humor collection, a book that won the inaugural Thurber Prize for American Humor.

“I feel like the Coyote,” Green, 68, said. “The catapult sprang, and the boulder fell on me.” Now that the movie is about to come out, he would like to be paid by Hollywood, just as Frazier was. “If it’s based on his, it’s based on mine,” Green said.

Both stories use deadpan legalese to describe cartoon violence, but Frazier’s light touch made “Coyote v. Acme” a model of humor writing at its smartest and silliest. To wit: “Mr. Coyote lost control of the Rocket Skates soon after strapping them on, and collided with a roadside billboard so violently as to leave a hole in the shape of his full silhouette.”

The novelist Jonathan Franzen considers it a classic of the form. He read the piece aloud on a 2015 episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour, calling it “a real high-wire act” and praising Frazier’s deft use of language in the pursuit of “humor for its own sake.”

In the 1990s, Eric Steel was in the habit of clipping articles that caught his attention and tacking them to the bulletin board in his office. That’s how “Coyote vs. Acme” began its second life.

At the time, Steel worked for the producer Scott Rudin, who would later come under fire for his hostile, demeaning behavior toward staffers. Known as a visionary, Rudin was the force behind mid-1990s hits like “The Firm,” “Addams Family Values” and “Clueless.” Steel imagined that a movie based on Frazier’s story could be something like “Who Framed Roger Rabbit,” a 1988 blockbuster that featured Looney Tunes characters and set a new standard for live action blended with animation.

“Frazier’s piece worked because it was a clever twist on something we all knew well,” Steel said. “My thought was, What if you did a really big turn? What if you used other Warner Bros. characters, with courtroom drama as the framework?”

In 1998, eight years after the article appeared, Scott Rudin Productions bought the rights to it. Frazier received a modest check, with the promise of a significant payout if a film was made. But there was a complicating factor, Steel noted. The production could not move forward without the approval of Warner Bros.

The option expired after a year. Rudin extended it. Then came a second extension — and a third. Frazier picked up small checks along the way. (He declined to specify dollar amounts.) The only time he really got his hopes up was when a Rudin assistant called to say the producer himself was about to give him a ring. The call never came.

“I was a Scott Rudin cancellation,” Frazier said.

In 2004, Rudin let the option lapse. Steel, who was by then working as an independent producer, took out a new option, only to decide against renewing it when it expired in 2006.

For the next decade, the project lay dormant. Not that Frazier was losing sleep over it. He was busy with New Yorker assignments and a nonfiction book, “Travels in Siberia.” Further, he had no secret desire to become a Hollywood player, though he did act in “Blue in the Face,” an indie movie co-directed by Wayne Wang and Paul Auster. When Frazier saw it at an art house in Missoula, Mont., he was the only person in the theater.

“I don’t go to movies,” he said. “For a long time, I watched one movie a year — ‘Spaceballs.’”

James Gunn, the director of the “Guardians of the Galaxy” films, was another fan of Frazier’s story. In 2015, he pitched the idea to Warner Bros. itself and got a yes.

“When Warner Bros. came along, I thought, ‘It’s got a better shot,’” Frazier said.

Six more years went by. Multiple drafts. A new production team. A merger of WarnerMedia and Discovery. Finally, in 2022, filming began.

Even then, Frazier’s 1990 story was guiding the approach of the producer Chris DeFaria, the director Dave Green and the screenwriter Samy Burch. “Ian’s piece was always this thing to aspire to, tonally,” Burch said. Green called Frazier’s story “funny and deep all at once,” adding, “It’s the thing that lit my flame and made me laugh out loud, hard.”

After the $70 million movie was shot, a release date was set for July 2023. And then it went over a cliff: Warner Bros. Discovery decided to shelve it, not because “Coyote vs. Acme” was bad (test audiences loved it), but because burying it allowed the company to take a $30 million tax write-down.

Frazier said he was disappointed less for himself than for the cast and crew. “I read that the people who did the explosions were sorry that people weren’t going to get to see them,” he said. “I sympathized with that. I mean, you do a good explosion … ”

The movie spent 2024 in purgatory. Then, showing Coyote-like resilience, it found a new distributor.

Now that “Coyote vs. Acme” is about to come out, Frazier seems nervous about seeing it. “I feel superstitious,” he said. “I so badly want it to be good.”

Four years ago, when he was tipped off by his friend in Albuquerque, he got in touch with his literary agent, who contacted Warner Bros. Discovery. No one at the studio had bothered to inform him that “Coyote vs. Acme” had started filming, and he had not received the big check that typically goes to the writer of a movie’s source material on the first day of production.

When it finally arrived, Frazier decided to splurge.

He bought a Toyota Camry hybrid.

“I have never loved an object that much,” he said.

One of the clever things Ian Frazier does in his essay is to humanize a cartoon character. In the story — and the new film it inspired — Coyote is persistent and relentlessly hardworking. Despite his failures, he never gives up. He is, in a funny way, a model for us all.

Steven Kurutz covers cultural trends, social media and the world of design for The Times.

Luigi Mangione Pleads Guilty

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

Also, an Alaska Democrat says no thanks to Kamala Harris’s support. Here’s the latest at the end of Friday.

By Matthew Cullen

Luigi Mangione showed little emotion as he pleaded guilty today to a pair of federal stalking charges tied to the 2024 killing of Brian Thompson, a health care executive. He sat in a Manhattan courtroom, in ankle shackles, and admitted: “I shot Mr. Thompson.” He added, “I knew what I was doing was illegal.”

Mangione acknowledged that he had killed Thompson with a gun he made using a 3-D printer. His comments lasted just a few minutes, but it was the first the public had heard from him since the shooting. The family of the victim, who was the chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, was seated in the front row.

Prosecutors said they would seek a life sentence. Mangione, 28, still faces a separate murder charge in state court, where he is scheduled to go on trial next month. His lawyers said they were seeking to dismiss that indictment on double jeopardy grounds, which bars someone from being tried twice for the same offense. Experts said exceptions might apply in this case.

The case has riveted the country. Many Americans were shocked by what appeared to be a brazen assassination. But others were sympathetic to Mangione’s deep anger at the health care industry.

For more: My colleagues talked to people who knew Mangione and traced the pivotal months before the killing.

Jason Arday, the Cambridge University scholar whose remarkable rise to stardom was followed by a rapid fall from grace in recent weeks, has died, his family said

Last week, Arday resigned from Cambridge amid accusations that he had plagiarized parts of his academic papers, embellished elements of his recently published memoir and fabricated aspects of his life story.

In their effort to take control of the Senate, Democrats are counting on candidates in red states, like Mary Peltola of Alaska. Polls indicate she is a real contender, but in order to win, Peltola will have to vastly outperform Kamala Harris, who lost the state by 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

Maybe that’s why Peltola was quick to distance herself from Harris after the former vice president signed a fund-raising email supporting her. Peltola’s campaign indicated that it had not approved Harris’s note and did not want her endorsement.

In other politics news: Members of Congress have collectively traded well over $100 million in individual stocks this term. These are the biggest traders.

Months ago, Vladimir Putin gathered Russian leaders for a secret briefing. Their goal for 2026, he said, is “the collapse of NATO and the E. U. from within.” Moldova, a tiny nation bordering Ukraine, is central to this effort.

A new Times investigation found that the Kremlin had conducted an audacious election interference campaign in Moldova — including training camps run by Russian spies and a sophisticated vote-buying scheme. And they almost pulled it off. Pro-Western forces barely squeaked by in recent elections. “We won the battle,” a Moldovan official said. “But we did not win the war.”

Related: Listen to today’s episode of “The Daily,” on a Russian spy network in Japan.

White House: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to allow construction to proceed on the president’s ballroom project.

Washington: A woman was charged with two felonies after officials said they had observed her spray painting the World War II Memorial.

Economy: Retail sales recorded their biggest drop in more than a year.

Afghanistan: The Taliban kicked the U. S. out five years ago. Now, in an interview with The Times, the foreign minister is inviting the Americans back.

Judiciary: The Supreme Court often gets emergency appeals from inmates facing the death penalty. This week, the justices received one on behalf of a dog named Bruce.

Alcohol: Brad Pitt said he was drinking again — this time in moderation — after seven years sober.

Art: Works by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse, swiped from a museum in under three minutes this spring, have been recovered. They are worth at least $10 million.

On a recent trip to Denver, Nancy Kreulen, a retired teacher, was surprised to find that no restaurants offered chislic. The dish — skewered mutton bites, fried and served with garlic salt, saltines and a cold beer — is a staple in the area around her hometown in South Dakota. But, as Kreulen’s friends pointed out, it has hardly crossed state lines.

Officially named South Dakota’s “state nosh” in 2018, chislic has become more popular and more varied. Many of the state’s restaurants now use beef instead of mutton or a griddle instead of a deep fryer. Some even serve it without the skewer.

Have a savory weekend.

Thanks for reading. I’ll be back on Monday. — Matthew

Jason Arday, Cambridge Scholar Who Resigned Under Scrutiny, Is Found Dead

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mr. Arday resigned last week after the university announced an investigation into allegations of plagiarism and fabrication.

By Mara Hvistendahl

Jason Arday, the former Cambridge University scholar whose remarkable rise to stardom was followed by a rapid fall from grace in recent weeks, has died, his family said on Friday.

“Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse” in the years since he accepted a role at Cambridge, his family wrote in a statement. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”

The Metropolitan Police of London said that an ambulance was called on Friday afternoon to a South London residence connected to Mr. Arday after a report that a man there had been found unresponsive. The man was pronounced dead at the scene, the police said, without confirming his identity, in keeping with British police practice.

The death was being “treated as unexpected” but was not believed to be suspicious, the police said.

“We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news,” Professor Deborah Prentice, the Cambridge vice-chancellor, said in a statement. “Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”

Mr. Arday, who was 41, grew up in a working-class quarter of South London, the child of Ghanaian immigrants. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties. He wrote in his memoir that he could not speak until age 11 and could not read until age 18, charting a remarkable trajectory from nonverbal preteen to Ph. D.

Mr. Arday, who had written and lectured on racism in higher education, became Cambridge’s youngest Black professor in 2023 when the university hired him for a prestigious post, an established chair of education at the school’s Jesus College.

Last month, a public firestorm over Mr. Arday’s career erupted after a blog post accused him of plagiarism in his dissertation and embellishing his personal story. It was written by a scholar known for work suggesting that Black people were genetically predisposed to be less intelligent than white people.

Scrutiny intensified ahead of the publication of Mr. Arday’s memoir on Tuesday by Simon & Schuster, as journalists found more inconsistencies in his story. He resigned from Cambridge last week.

Allegations about Mr. Arday’s work circulated within Cambridge for years, but the institution disregarded repeated warnings about possible duplication in Mr. Arday’s work, according to the academic integrity site Retraction Watch.

The elite university initially defended Mr. Arday but in a letter sent to faculty on Tuesday promised an independent investigation of his hiring and called the case “an aberration” and “troubling.”

Some faculty had supported Mr. Arday. Others signed an open letter questioning the university’s handling of the allegations and criticizing it for “crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential.”

Nick Clark, who has known Mr. Arday since childhood, described him in an interview last week as a caring person who would go out of his way to make others feel comfortable in everyday social settings. Mr. Arday was modest when discussing his career with his friends, said Mr. Clark, but those who knew him personally took pride in his accomplishments. “He’s always been that kind, caring, friendly character,” he added. “That’s Jason.”

“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son,” Mr. Arday’s family said in its statement.

The intense attention took a toll on Mr. Arday, he wrote in a blog post upon resigning from Cambridge. “The years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack,” he wrote, adding, “The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love.”

Neil Vigdor and Leo Sands contributed reporting.

Mara Hvistendahl is an investigative reporter on the International desk. You can reach her at mara. hvistendahl@nytimes. com

As Army Fails to Protect Palestinians, Israeli Leaders Sympathize With Settlers

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Defense Minister Katz called for the military to turn over to the police the responsibility for protecting Palestinians after two West Bank families were besieged by violent settlers.

By David M. Halbfinger and Adam Rasgon

Reporting from Jerusalem and Tel Aviv

The Israeli army’s faltering attempts this week to rescue two Palestinian families who have been besieged in their West Bank homes by violent Jewish settlers prompted a striking statement on Friday morning from Israel’s defense minister, Israel Katz.

He said he wanted to get the Israeli military out of the business of protecting Palestinians in the occupied West Bank from rampaging settlers and would try to shift the responsibility to the Israeli police.

As a practical matter, only the Israel Defense Forces have the thousands of personnel needed to patrol and respond quickly to attacks in the scores of communities plagued by settler violence this year. Moreover, experts say that giving responsibility to the Israeli police would essentially put the fox in charge of the henhouse, because the police are overseen by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, an extremist settler himself.

For Mr. Katz, an ambitious member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party who hopes to succeed him as its leader, his recommendation was a political move to duck responsibility, analysts said.

Rather, for example, than letting the army use administrative detention to lock up settlers who break the law, a crucial tool previously used by the government, Mr. Katz is saying he prefers that soldiers avoid getting between settlers and Palestinians in their moments of “friction,” as some Israelis euphemistically call such attacks.

“It is not the I. D. F.’s role, and it is unable, to address the enforcement of civil matters” in the West Bank in light of the “welcome increase” in the number of Israeli settlers there, Mr. Katz said.

As the occupying power, the Israeli military alone bears responsibility under international law for protecting Palestinian civilians in the West Bank and has held authority for law and order since Israel captured the territory in the 1967 war.

The police have a division in the West Bank, given the hundreds of thousands of Israeli civilians living there in settlements widely considered illegal under international law. But handing the police responsibility for protecting Palestinian civilians could be seen as another step toward creeping annexation of the territory, a goal shared by many in Mr. Netanyahu’s government.

On Friday, settlers who have trapped two Palestinian families in their homes in the village of Qusra all week set up a tent there, before soldiers took it down, according to the local mayor, Abdul Azim al-Wadi, and an Israeli military statement. Settlers, however, remained in the vicinity as of early evening, while soldiers stood nearby, Mr. al-Wadi said.

“If the Israeli authorities want stability, they need to arrest the settlers,” he said. “That’s the only solution.”

In its statement, the military said that throughout the day, “soldiers operating in the area remained engaged in efforts to evacuate the Israeli civilians from the area of the closed military zone.”

For years, Israeli leaders including Mr. Netanyahu have downplayed settler violence as the work of a “handful of kids,” or of a few dozen or a few hundred wayward youth, often saying that many came from broken homes, suggesting they should be pitied rather than prosecuted. The effort to minimize the violence has continued even as the number of Palestinians killed by settlers has climbed since January, paired with beatings and the torching of hundreds of houses, car and mosques.

But now, with an army that has defeated vastly more powerful enemies failing to achieve the task of making it possible for two Palestinian families to live safely in their own homes, members of Mr. Netanyahu’s government are making clear on which side of the issue they stand.

Not surprisingly, Mr. Ben-Gvir, the minister overseeing the police, insisted that the settlers’ siege in Qusra was the military’s responsibility.

In a radio interview Thursday, he said he wasn’t familiar with the details of the Qusra situation but hastened to take the side of settlers encroaching on Palestinian communities. “There are some among them who truly need to be arrested and addressed; I’m not saying all of them are righteous,” he allowed. “But most of these guys, who settle the land of Israel, who build outposts — I admire them.”

Mr. Ben-Gvir, who leads the supremacist Otzma Yehudit, or Jewish Power, party, also argued that the real violence was not being committed by settlers. “I know what’s happening here in Judea and Samaria,” he said, using the biblical names for the West Bank. “I live here. For now, the danger is that the Arabs throw stones, the Arabs throw Molotov cocktails, the Arabs shoot.”

Mr. Netanyahu himself has not addressed the standoff in Qusra. But a lawmaker from his party, Amit Halevi, chose Thursday to meet and be photographed with a group of extremist settlers, including one who has been sanctioned by several countries for violence. Mr. Halevi did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The events in Qusra are forcing the issue of settler violence — or, as a growing number of prominent Israelis now call it, “Jewish terrorism” — to center stage in the midst of an enormously consequential political campaign ahead of Israeli elections in October.

Members of the political opposition lambasted the government for failing to curb the violence. Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who once led the umbrella organization for West Bank settlements, called it “acts of terrorism.” He faulted the Netanyahu government for responding so slowly that, according to the U. S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, the Trump administration had urged it to intervene in Qusra.

“We need to denounce this and root out violence from within, not wait for the Americans to tell us to do so,” Mr. Bennett said in a radio interview.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief of staff who now is the front-runner in opinion polls for prime minister, called the Qusra situation a “severe expression of the failures and weakness” of the government.

“In the face of anarchy and violent violations of the law by an extremist minority, the government is abandoning I. D. F. commanders to fight the battle alone,” he wrote on social media.

Israeli military officials have long complained that the police take a lax approach to violent settlers and that judges rarely impose tough sentences. But critics of the military say it, too, often hesitates in the face of settler violence and fails to use all the tools at its disposal.

On Wednesday, a group of army reservists released an open letter calling on the military “to act with determination against Jewish terrorism” and “to uproot it.” The letter, addressed to Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the army’s chief of staff, had 465 signatures by Friday, organizers said.

“Nationalistic terror in Judea and Samaria is not stopping,” the letter reads. “We are required again and again to stand between ‘friction incidents’ in territory under our responsibility, without a real mandate to prevent them.”

The letter adds: “The lack of backing and guidance from the I. D. F.’s senior leadership, the turning of a blind eye to Jewish terrorism and to the known places from which it emanates, and at times even the political echelon’s support for it, endanger us and leave us abandoned.”

Moshe Karadi, who commanded the Israeli police from 2004 to 2007, recalled the police taking aggressive action against settlers in the past but said that it was unclear that certain police commanders could be counted upon now, because of Mr. Ben-Gvir’s influence over them.

Mr. Karadi called the handling of the settlers’ siege this week in Qusra a “disgrace,” saying that “terrorists need to be handled with force.”

Still, he said the military made a strategic error by not calling the police to remove the settlers immediately after they started besieging the Palestinians. Soldiers are trained to fight Palestinians, not Israelis, he said, while the police are trained to confront both.

“In my opinion, it appears the officers in the military are afraid of the political level,” he said. “They don’t know how their actions will be interpreted so they prefer to do nothing.”

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Here Are the Biggest Stock Traders in Congress

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Some lawmakers and their families have traded millions of dollars worth of stocks since the start of this term.

By Olivia Diaz

Reporting from Washington

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are facing increasing voter pressure to ban congressional stock trading, a practice that has long given members an ability to profit from their access to market-moving information in closed-door meetings.

Roughly a quarter of legislators on Capitol Hill have traded individual stocks this term, with some buying and selling millions of dollars in shares. Since the start of this term in January 2025, members and their families have collectively traded $160 million to $664 million in individual stocks, according to a New York Times analysis of data collected from members’ required financial filings by 2iQ Research, an analytics firm.

Members are required to disclose their trades. But instead of declaring precise values, they report their trades in broad ranges, making it difficult to determine with precision how much stock they bought and sold.

A law passed in 2012, the STOCK Act, emphasizes that insider trading is illegal among lawmakers, as it is for the general public, and requires them to periodically disclose trades of shares held by them and members of their families. Existing laws do not prohibit lawmakers from trading individual stocks and do little in terms of enforcement. Critics of the system say that creates potential conflicts of interest and leaves open the possibility of members profiting from knowledge about legislation and nonpublic committee briefings.

Over the years, members of both parties have introduced bills cracking down on congressional stock trading, with some proposals more stringent than others. Last month, the House passed legislation limiting the ability of members, their spouses and their dependents to trade individual stocks, though it would allow lawmakers to keep the shares they already own and carve out exemptions for trusts and some other assets.

Nearly all Democrats opposed the bill after Republicans added an unrelated measure requiring voters to present photo identification in federal elections. Its prospects in the Senate are uncertain.

Here are the five lawmakers who have disclosed the largest individual stock trades made by them and their families, according to the Times analysis, based on the maximum dollar amount of their transactions reported since the start of this term on Jan. 3, 2025, through early August.

Mr. Khanna’s family traded shares valued at about $24 million to $147 million, according to the Times analysis.

The representative, first elected in 2016, disclosed that his family has traded about 7,200 times this term, the data reported as of Aug. 12 shows.

Mr. Khanna has said that he supported one version of a congressional ban, and that neither he nor his family directly make trades. His office declined to comment for this article but pointed to previous instances in which he has explained that his family’s finances are handled by outside advisers.

“My household’s only investments are held in a diversified trust my in-laws set up before marriage for my wife and children, managed independently by a third-party trustee,” he wrote in a May newsletter.

Under some proposals for stricter trading limits, members and their families would have to divest their blind trusts. The House bill that passed in July, which Mr. Khanna voted against, carved out an exemption for them. Most proposals have some exemptions for family trusts.

The former speaker has reported trades of shares valued at nearly $18 million to about $84 million across 17 transactions since the beginning of this congressional session. Paul Pelosi, Ms. Pelosi’s husband and a venture capitalist, owns each of the stocks traded. Two 2025 sales in particular were valued at a combined $10 million to $50 million in Apple stock.

A spokesman for Ms. Pelosi said in a statement that she “does not own any stocks and has no knowledge or subsequent involvement in any transactions.”

The “Pelosi Tracker” app has for years logged Mr. Pelosi’s investments and allowed its users to mimic his trades. Republicans in Congress have long singled out Ms. Pelosi for criticism for her family’s investments.

After initial hesitation, Ms. Pelosi said in recent years that she would support a congressional ban on stock trading. In July, she voted against the partisan House bill.

Mr. McCaul’s family bought and sold between $28 million and $75 million in individual stocks since January 2025, over the course of more than 1,100 transactions. All individual stock trades disclosed by Mr. McCaul came from his spouse, Linda Mays McCaul, according to the data. Mr. McCaul’s lawyer, Elliot Berke, said in a statement that a third-party manager makes the purchases without Ms. Mays McCaul’s direction.

One of Ms. Mays McCaul’s largest trades occurred last June when she sold between $500,000 and $1 million worth of shares in Nvidia, the California-based chip-making giant.

In July, Mr. McCaul voted in support of the House bill prohibiting the purchase of new individual stocks. Mr. McCaul, elected to the House in 2004, is retiring at the end of his term and is not up for re-election to his Austin-area district.

Mr. Shreve, a freshman member, traded between $16 million and nearly $42 million worth of shares through about 550 trades in 2025. The office of Mr. Shreve, who had run a company that built storage facilities across the Midwest, said last year that he would stop trading individual stocks. The data shows that neither he nor his family has traded individual stocks since then.

The shift came after a report by the publication NOTUS revealed that Mr. Shreve had made over 100 stock trades worth millions in the days after President Trump imposed sweeping tariffs on imports from many U. S. trading partners. Mr. Shreve’s chief of staff, Jeff Bishop, said on Thursday that trading activity occurred within a trust managed by a third party, which the representative set up to make charitable donations.

Mr. Shreve voted in support of the House’s Republican-led bill banning stock trading.

Mr. Armstrong traded about $8 million to $41 million worth of shares across nearly 700 individual trades.

He was appointed to the Senate in March after Markwayne Mullin resigned to become the new homeland security secretary. A former energy executive, Mr. Armstrong made the bulk of his trades during the week he was sworn in, the data shows.

At the time of his appointment, Mr. Armstrong led the board of directors at Williams Companies, a giant natural gas pipeline operator based in Tulsa, Okla. In June, Mr. Armstrong and his spouse sold between $5 million and $25 million in Williams stock, according to a financial filing.

The senator’s office said in a statement on Friday that the trades stemmed from a fund that Mr. Armstrong had no direction over. His spokeswoman noted that Mr. Armstrong had an annual salary of $750,000 before becoming a senator, and is now making a fraction of that.

“The focus should be on the folks that have built wealth while making a salary of $174,000 per year,” his spokeswoman wrote, referring to the allotted compensation for most members of Congress.

Mr. Armstrong will leave the Senate at the end of his term in January.

Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

Olivia Diaz is a congressional reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Stock Trading by Lawmakers Becomes a Campaign Attack Line

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Republican and Democratic challengers are both using the issue to attack members of Congress as unethical, seizing on a common practice that enrages voters.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

Since the day she began her campaign for Congress, Paige Cognetti, the Democratic mayor of Scranton, has centered her pitch to voters on the prodigious stock trading of the House Republican she is seeking to unseat, Representative Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania.

“This year he’s already made 600 trades,” Ms. Cognetti said in the announcement video for her campaign in September. “Sold Chinese stocks the week of a tariff. Buys missile stocks before a war. Buys jet stocks before a big contract. Oversees crypto? Buys crypto stocks before a vote.”

It may be the district where the issue rings the loudest. Democrats are running ads highlighting how Mr. Bresnahan profited from a data center development by trading stocks related to the industry, and recent polls show Ms. Cognetti with a narrow lead. But she is not alone in zeroing in on stock trading by members of Congress as a potent line of attack in this year’s midterm elections.

Like many members of Congress who trade substantial amounts of stock, Mr. Bresnahan, the wealthy former chief executive of an electrical contracting company, has said he relies on a financial adviser to make his trades and never knows about the transactions before they happen or when they occur.

Mr. Bresnahan’s campaign said that Ms. Cognetti’s descriptions of his trades were “lies” and that he has “taken legitimate steps to ban congressional stock trading.”

Still, at a time when many voters are experiencing economic hardship and have grown increasingly suspicious that the political system is rigged, the mere possibility that a member of Congress could be profiting from the job has become politically toxic.

Roughly a quarter of legislators on Capitol Hill have traded individual stocks this term, with some buying and selling millions of dollars in shares. Since the start of this term in January 2025, members and their families have collectively traded $160 million to $664 million in individual stocks, according to a New York Times analysis of data collected from members’ required financial filings by 2iQ Research, an analytics firm.

An overwhelming majority of voters in both parties view stock trading by lawmakers with great suspicion and say they support barring them from doing so. The public backlash has fueled efforts by members of both parties, so far unsuccessful, to enact new legislation banning the practice.

In the meantime, both sides are leveraging the issue in the fight for control of Congress.

Democrats and Republicans alike are seeking to weaponize incumbents’ trades, particularly those where they can show the appearance of a conflict of interest, and putting them at the forefront of ads and campaign attacks in the country’s most competitive districts. It is a way to portray their opponents as corrupt and out of touch with the financial realities of working-class Americans.

In Northern New Jersey’s competitive Seventh Congressional District, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has been targeting Representative Thomas H. Kean Jr. for continuing to trade stocks while missing more than 100 votes during an extended absence for what he later said was treatment for depression. Mr. Kean’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

In Virginia, Democrats are attacking Representative Rob Wittman for trading more than $2.5 million in stocks between 2015 and 2023 while serving in Congress — including buying defense stocks like Lockheed Martin and Honeywell while serving on the Armed Services Committee.

“There’s a vicious cycle in Washington: Politicians trade stocks in the industries they’re supposed to regulate, then protect those industries instead of you,” said the caption with a campaign video that his opponent, Shannon Taylor, a prosecutor, posted online. “Let’s ban congressional stock trading — for good.”

(An outside group supporting Mr. Wittman apparently views this line of attack as effective: This week, it began running an ad highlighting his vote for a watered-down stock trading bill that passed the House passed in July, noting that he voted to put an end to the “greed and corruption” of “fat cat lawmakers.”) Mr. Wittman’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Republicans have also identified the issue as resonant with their voters.

In New York’s competitive Third Congressional District on Long Island, Michael J. LiPetri Jr., a Republican former state assemblyman, routinely attacks the Democrat he is running to unseat, Representative Tom Suozzi, for “the millions he’s pocketed from stock trading in Congress.”

Mr. Suozzi made nearly 600 stock trades involving 161 companies totaling as much as $24 million when he served in Congress between 2017 and 2023, according to public filings. In 2021, he faced an ethics investigation for failing to report about 300 stock trades in the required 45-day window. The House Ethics Committee later cleared him after concluding that it was not a willful violation, but a mistake.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Suozzi said all of his purchases were made at the discretion of his broker, without his direct input. She added that he has stopped purchasing stock altogether since returning to Congress in 2024, although he has sold some.

And in Nevada, Marty O’Donnell, a Trump-endorsed Republican running against Representative Susie Lee, a Democrat, often highlights Ms. Lee’s stock trades, claiming that she “has used her office to enrich herself with information the rest of us don’t have.” He has pledged that “unlike Susie, I will not trade stocks while representing Nevada in Congress.”

Ms. Lee, who was married to the chief executive of Full House Resorts, which operates casino facilities, has traded up to $2.8 million worth of stock since her divorce in 2024.

A spokeswoman for Ms. Lee said that all trades done before her divorce were executed by a money manager or her ex-husband. Since the divorce, Ms. Lee “received stocks as part of her divorce settlement and committed to divesting from them, which involves the selling of individual stocks in order to invest in other allowable instruments, like E. T. F. s and mutual funds,” the spokeswoman said, referring to exchange-traded funds.

In one instance where a former lawmaker is running for her old seat, an incumbent is trying to use the attack that is typically employed by a challenger.

Representative Jen Kiggans, Republican of Virginia, frequently accuses her opponent, former Representative Elaine Luria, of “insider stock trading” during her four years in Congress. Ms. Kiggans’s campaign did not point to any instances of insider trading, which is illegal, when asked about the allegations.

Instead, the campaign highlighted Ms. Luria’s previous opposition to a congressional stock trading ban (she now supports one). And it noted that Ms. Luria owns between $5 million and $25 million in NVIDIA stock, which she held when she voted for a $280 billion industrial policy bill enacted in 2022 that provided tens of billions of dollars for semiconductor manufacturing and research.

A spokesman for Ms. Luria dismissed Ms. Kiggans’s attacks as “lies,” and said that the bill in question did not increase her stock value. “Elaine supports banning congressional stock trading and preventing politicians from using their public offices for private gain,” he said.

The campaign trail focus comes as House Republicans have recently pushed through a bill that would impose some restrictions on lawmakers who trade stock, but stops short of a more stringent ban backed by a bipartisan coalition.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, has promised to bring the bipartisan alternative to the floor if Democrats win control of the House next year.

Donald K. Sherman, the chief executive of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a Democratic-aligned watchdog group, said it was not surprising to see the attacks on the practice coming from both political parties, because the issue is more salient than some others in government.

“You don’t need to be an ethics expert to understand it,” Mr. Sherman said. “An individual member of Congress can have an impact on a stock price, whether it’s tough questions at a hearing or an oversight hearing or confirmation of a particular cabinet secretary.”

Former Representative Tom Malinowski, Democrat of New Jersey, whose political career ended in part because he did not properly disclose dozens of stock trades, said a stock trading ban would do little to address far more serious issues that have eroded the public’s trust in political leaders.

“Stock trading by members of Congress should be banned, but it’s still a very poor substitute for attacking the real sources of corruption in Washington: unlimited dark money and Trump’s blatant selling of the presidency,” Mr. Malinowski said in an interview. “Those are significantly bigger problems. But candidates have seized on it as an all-purpose explanation for corruption.”

Olivia Diaz and Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

So Are We Eating Lettuce Again?

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Cyclospora Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

As the largest cyclospora outbreak in U. S. history wanes, experts weigh in on whether iceberg and other fresh produce are still a risk.

By Alice Callahan

It has been a summer of food-borne illness in the United States. Since May 1, tens of thousands of people have been sickened by cyclospora after eating contaminated iceberg lettuce. And in August, a salmonella outbreak associated with jalapeños affected at least 345 people in 27 states.

In a CBS News poll conducted in late July, 40 percent of the nearly 2,200 U. S. adults surveyed said they were eating less produce because of the cyclospora outbreak, and almost half said they had little to no confidence in the Food and Drug Administration to address it.

Kyle Diamantas, the acting commissioner of the F. D. A., said in a CNBC segment on Monday that the food supply was safe and that “Americans should feel confident in eating fresh produce, including leafy greens.”

We asked experts to weigh in, and to clarify the risks of eating the various foods implicated in recent outbreaks.

Much of the cyclospora risk this summer has come from iceberg lettuce that was linked to an outbreak in 17 states and was grown in Mexico and supplied by Taylor Farms. Health officials have confirmed more than 9,400 cases in this outbreak, and about 400 hospitalizations and two deaths.

While cases are continuing to climb as officials confirm and report older cases, there are some signs that the worst of the outbreak is behind us, said Daniel Weinberger, a professor of epidemiology at the Yale School of Public Health. Fewer cyclospora tests are coming back positive nationwide, he said, and fewer people are visiting doctors for diarrhea.

“Nothing in life is risk-free,” Dr. Weinberger said, but we may be back to a normal level of risk when it comes to eating lettuce and other leafy greens. “I feel comfortable eating my salad,” he said.

Donald Schaffner, chair of the department of food science at Rutgers University, said that because the affected lettuce was out of the food supply by now, it’s probably safe to resume eating lettuce, including from bagged salads, restaurants and cafeterias.

“I think the risk from iceberg lettuce has largely passed,” he said, “and it’s been passed for weeks now.”

Before health officials identified iceberg lettuce as the main culprit in the cyclospora outbreak, many experts recommended caution around summer produce linked to past outbreaks of the parasite, including raspberries, cilantro, parsley, basil, snow peas and snap peas.

In July, health officials in North Carolina said that many of the people sickened with cyclospora in that state had reported eating cilantro and parsley before they became ill. But on Aug. 11, the North Carolina health department said in a statement that the number of new cases there had declined, “suggesting that the most common sources of exposure have already passed through the food chain.”

There is no evidence that berries, herbs or other summer produce are making people ill, Dr. Schaffner said, so it’s safe to continue eating those foods.

The F. D. A. is currently investigating three additional and ongoing cyclospora outbreaks — the largest of which has 172 cases. The agency has not identified the source or location of those outbreaks, so it’s possible that health officials will recommend avoiding new foods in the future.

That said, the risk of contracting cyclospora from one of those smaller outbreaks or other produce is relatively low, said Ellen Shumaker, a food safety extension specialist at North Carolina State University. It’s normal for cyclospora cases to rise in the summer, when warmer temperatures allow the parasite to grow, she said.

If you are in a vulnerable group — including young children, older adults and those who are pregnant or immunocompromised — you may want to take special care, such as cooking produce rather than eating it raw, she said.

On Aug. 5, federal health officials announced a salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeños grown in Sinaloa, Mexico, and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors. Of 191 people interviewed as part of the outbreak, the F. D. A. reported, 93 percent said they ate at Mexican-style restaurants, including Chipotle and Qdoba, before getting sick. The agency said that as of late July, those chains were no longer serving the affected jalapeños and that it was safe to eat at those establishments.

Dozens of prepackaged foods containing potentially affected jalapeños — including salsa, guacamole, pico de gallo and diced jalapeño products, as well as some prepared burritos and sandwiches — have been recalled at Whole Foods, Hannaford, Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Trader Joe’s and Walmart locations in various states. Many of those products were sold to stores by Taylor Farms.

If you purchased any of those items, health officials advise that you toss them or return them for a refund. All recalled products have “best if used by” dates through Aug. 16.

Health officials have not said that whole jalapeños sold to grocery stores have been implicated in the outbreak, Dr. Schaffner said.

The “vast majority” of produce sold in the United States is safe to eat, Dr. Shumaker said, and the benefits of consuming fruits and vegetables far outweigh the risks.

Still, even if the worst of the cyclospora and salmonella outbreaks is behind us, there is always a risk of consuming contaminated food — whether it’s from a grocery store or a restaurant, said Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University. “I can’t say that next week we won’t see another outbreak,” she said.

Dr. Kowalcyk said she was concerned that the size of the cyclospora outbreak may indicate that our food system is becoming more vulnerable to safety issues. Funding cuts and staffing losses at federal and state health agencies, for instance, have meant that they may be slower to respond to outbreaks and trace their causes, she said.

There aren’t clear answers on how to manage the risk of food-borne illnesses going forward, Dr. Kowalcyk said. Everyone has different tolerance levels, she said.

One of the best things you can do is to stay vigilant about food recalls, Dr. Schaffner said. A good way to do that is to sign up for alerts on the F. D. A.’s website.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.
