How Do You Report on a Presidential Ruse?

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Insider

President Trump’s Air Force One subterfuge duped potential adversaries — and the press. Here’s what happened.

By Megan DiTrolio

With Peter BakerDoug Mills and Richard W. Stevenson

Megan DiTrolio is a senior editor on the Trust team, focusing on efforts to help readers understand The Times and its journalism.

Last month, President Trump climbed the stairs of Air Force One in Turkey, then turned and waved to journalists before boarding. When the plane landed in Britain hours later, he marched off.

But, as news organizations and the public learned this week, it was a deception. Mr. Trump had been secretly whisked off the plane, into a catering container and put on a military jet. According to two senior U. S. officials, a threat against the president and Air Force One from Iran prompted the subterfuge.

Moving a president for security reasons is not unusual. But hiding the matter after the fact, including from reporters who cover Mr. Trump and those who were unwitting passengers on the “decoy” plane, raised questions about the public’s right to know the president’s whereabouts and how the administration handled this episode.

We discussed those questions this week with Doug Mills, a Times photographer who was on Air Force One that day, as well as Richard W. Stevenson, The Times’s Washington bureau chief, and Peter Baker, the chief White House correspondent. We also dug into how The Times reported on the ruse and pressed the White House on it. These excerpts have been edited and condensed.

What was your initial reaction this week when you learned that President Trump had been secretly transported off — then back on — the old Air Force One plane that day?

RICHARD W. STEVENSON: We had our own reporting going on this, so when The Washington Post published its scoop, a small group of our journalists was able to move quickly to match the story and add to it. But even though it was not a total surprise, it was still stunning to think about. There were some deadly serious issues, including the nature of the threat that led the White House and the Secret Service to engage in this deception, and of course the question of why and how a plane full of mostly unwitting staff members and journalists were used as decoys.

DOUG MILLS: My initial reaction was shock, and then it was disbelief. How did they do this? Why did they do this? How did I not know that this was something that was going on? Clearly they did a great job of disguising it. But there were red flags that, frankly, maybe I missed and I think a lot of other people missed.

What were some of those red flags?

DOUG: First off, leaving Turkey, we were told to put our window shades down. The last time that happened to me was when I traveled with President Obama to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan.

Once we loaded back up on the Qatari-donated Air Force One in Britain, reporters asked President Trump, Why do you think they made us put the shades down? He was kind of surprised by that question. And then he said, Well, they didn’t ask me to do that. In hindsight, it was because he wasn’t on our plane.

I wish he had just told us on the plane ride to the United States when he came back to brief reporters. I’m disappointed that he didn’t say, Hey guys, there were some serious threats back there. I need to tell you about an operation that took place before it gets out.

PETER BAKER: It was pretty stunning to learn — not just that it happened but that it stayed secret for a full month afterward, even as everyone was reporting pretty aggressively on the swap-out for the Qatari-donated plane. It can be hard to report out secrets, especially in the national security realm, and the White House has tried to make it harder, even trying to subpoena our colleagues for their sources on the earlier plane stories. But this reminds us that there’s sometimes more to the story and we have to keep digging.

What next steps did you take in reporting out the news and trying to get to the bottom of what had happened? What questions were on your mind?

DICK: We focused the reporting on a few key questions: What was the threat to President Trump and how credible was it? How, in detail, did they pull off this deception on an airport tarmac? What did it say about this White House and this president that a plane full of staff members and journalists were in effect used as decoys? And why was it that the White House chose to keep the whole episode secret long after the president was safe?

PETER: I found it astounding that they still sent Air Force One into the skies with the secretary of state, the treasury secretary and top White House staffers. Not to mention the pool of journalists who normally travel with the president. They were effectively made into decoys, or even potential targets. Questions that came quickly to mind included:

1) Who was left on the decoy plane (what some of my colleagues irreverently dubbed the “martyr plane” — oy!)?

2) Were they aware that the president wasn’t on board and that they were on a plane that had been targeted?

3) Did the government do anything extra to protect the decoy plane?

4) Why didn’t they simply ground Air Force One, at least until the president secretly left the danger zone, and then either announce that he was now gone, so that the original plane would no longer be seen as a target, or have the people on board travel home by other means?

We got some answers to No. 1 (Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Steven Cheung, Stephen Miller), No. 2 (Rubio was said to know) but not to No. 3 or 4.

The public (and the media, including us) were actively misled by this ruse. How much of a right do journalists and the public have to know about a president’s whereabouts, even when there is a security issue? How have we handled similar situations in the past?

DOUG: I think the public has every right to know where the president is.

Now, the trust of what he’s saying and what the staff is telling us in the press pool is always going to be questioned. It is one of those things that will take time to heal. Even when we went to Ohio the other day, one of my questions to one of the staff members was, Is he flying with us today, or is he flying on another plane? We have to ask those questions because there has been a lack of transparency.

DICK: It’s important to separate out some distinct elements. There are legitimate security issues around the travels of any president. We take those seriously, and as Peter and Doug know, we are generally willing to work with any White House in dealing with them. Then there is the safety of the people traveling with the president. We obviously feel strongly about this. A third is ensuring that there are agreed-upon protocols in place to assure that the journalists who make up the press pool traveling with the president know where he is and to a reasonable degree have access to what he is doing.

So how do you address all those factors?

DICK: There has to be a balance between security and transparency. You can argue about precisely what that balance should be at any given moment, but clearly in this case, transparency was thrown entirely out the window, replaced by outright deception. That’s a terrible precedent. And the fact that it left journalists and staff members unknowingly exposed to a potential threat made it much, much worse.

PETER: As Dick says, we are very sensitive to not jeopardizing a president’s safety and have worked with administrations of both parties under tough circumstances to take reasonable measures to not disclose information in real time that would put a president at risk.

There was always a trust between the White House and reporters when it came to the president’s whereabouts in extreme circumstances. But we consider it supremely important to have journalists with a president anytime he is outside the fortified confines of the White House or Camp David.

Why?

PETER: Two reasons in particular: The J. F. K. scenario. Reporters were with John F. Kennedy in Dallas in 1963 and could report on his assassination immediately to a nation that needed reliable, independent information. And the 9/11 scenario. Journalists — including Doug — were with George W. Bush on the day of the terrorist attacks when a president’s crisis decision-making and communications were profoundly important.

Did we talk to the White House or other administration officials about the deception and possible dangers that those on the decoy plane faced?

DICK: The White House Correspondents’ Association has already raised these issues with administration officials, and we will be monitoring those discussions closely and weighing in where necessary.

I’ve been involved in covering presidents going back to the Clinton administration, and there has always been a foundation of trust between the press corps and the White House when it comes to matters of security. We have gone along in the past with requirements that we not disclose trips presidents are taking to war zones, for example. But in those cases, journalists traveled with the president and were free to report on the trips as soon as he and they were out of danger. In this case, no reporters were with the president or knew that he was on another plane, and the deception only became public because The Washington Post broke the news.

DOUG: I have talked to probably three or four staffers and asked them, What did you think? They’re all like, Well, we didn’t even know it was happening. There were staff on the plane who didn’t know. There were other staff on the plane who we have been told knew, and they were very coy about it.

PETER: The White House didn’t respond when I sent an email asking about the deception and the possible danger for those still on the decoy plane.

It was interesting talking with veterans of past White Houses. Some said it was outrageous that officials and reporters were made into “human shields,” as one put it. Others said that, Hey, if you travel with the president, you know there are certain risks, which is true enough. Doug has traveled with presidents since Ronald Reagan; Dick covered the White House for years; we had colleagues, including Doug, who were in Butler, Pa., when Trump was shot at. We are all aware that if something happens, journalists can get caught in the crossfire.

What about you?

PETER: I was in the pool with George W. Bush in Tbilisi, Georgia, in 2005 when someone threw a grenade at him. We were all incredibly lucky it didn’t go off. What was different here was that Doug and his colleagues who were in the pool with Trump that day didn’t know that they were being flown with a specific target on them.

DOUG: We’re covering a president who’s had a number of assassination attempts, including the one in Butler, where I was. This is what we signed up for. We are in a new world as far as threats to the president.

I’ve been doing this long enough to know that this is not the easiest job; it’s not going to a war zone, but we are not completely protected. Riding on Air Force One, I would always tell my family: I’m on the safest plane in the world. And now I’m not. It’s obvious that I’m no longer on the safest plane in the world because the president has so many threats against him.

The Secret Service’s mission is to protect the president, not us. I’ve always known that. But I do feel like they should have come clean when we got back, or on the way back.

Our bond with readers is based on getting the facts right and publishing new and accurate information as we learn it. It’s also based on correcting things that we get wrong. How did you think about our original reporting in July that said Trump left Turkey on Air Force One? Was it wrong? Outdated? And once we had new information, what decisions did we make about next steps in addressing our July articles?

DICK: One of the first things we did was update our story from last month that reported that Trump had flown out of Turkey on the old Air Force One. We placed language on the top of the story, published on July 8, noting that new information had surfaced and that “Mr. Trump did not fly out of Ankara on the old Air Force One as he said he would do.” We also took another look at the reporting we had done last month about the concerns with the adequacy of the security on the new plane acquired from Qatar and added to the Air Force One fleet after a rush to modify it for Trump’s use.

We feel that the reporting on the risks associated with the new plane holds up in light of what we learned about the deception, even though the plan for getting the president out of Turkey was way more complicated than we knew at the time.

Peter, as you wrote this week, the government has obfuscated over time to safeguard presidents from possible jeopardy. In those cases, what considerations do we make when excavating the truth and deciding to publish a story?

PETER: As Dick said, we’ve always been willing to work with the White House when it came to specific security concerns. We would never knowingly mislead our readers, but we might not report what we know until it’s safe for a president.

Say more about that — in what circumstances?

PETER: For instance, when Joe Biden traveled to Ukraine in the middle of a war zone, it wasn’t safe to fly so he had to take a nine and a half-hour train to Kyiv. He brought only two journalists with him (a writer from The Wall Street Journal and a photographer from The Associated Press) to report back to the rest of us. That is a long time for a president to be incommunicado. We knew about it at the time, but kept it to ourselves until he was secure. But even in those instances, we expect that we’ll be able to publish once the immediate risk is over. The White House didn’t try to keep it from us in perpetuity.

DOUG: As Peter said, it happened when Biden went to Ukraine; it was a very covert operation. And on 9/11 when I was with Bush. They took the pool from 13 people down to five, and I was one of them. There’s a lot of trust that the White House instills in us.

We embargo photos; we only transmit them when the White House tells us we can transmit them, out of concern for the safety of the president. The pool does everything it can to abide by the rules that the White House states to keep the president safe. When we are in these covert or dangerous situations, photographers are thinking about nothing other than the president’s safety and that of the traveling party.

I have left on these secret trips before and have not told my editor. I’ve landed in Afghanistan with a president, and my editors didn’t even know I had left. I want to make sure I don’t break that trust. We have an allocated seat for a New York Times photographer on Air Force One. Meaghan Looram, our director of photography, is fully aware of that, so she knows that wherever the president goes, there’s a New York Times photographer with them.

As many administrations that I’ve done this with, whether it’s Bush, Clinton, Bush, Obama, Biden, Trump, whoever, there’s this trust, and you can’t break that trust. That was why I was disappointed that they just didn’t come out and say what had happened, after the fact.

What did we learn from this reporting and experience that may inform our work as this story continues to unfold?

DICK: The deception here was quite elaborate. Trump actually climbed the steps and got on the old Air Force One in Turkey, turned and waved, and went through the door. After the plane landed in England, Trump got off it. We had no reason to doubt that he had flown on it. And yet, he hadn’t. The whole escapade was a reminder to be humble about what we know and don’t know, to ask a lot of questions and not to make a lot of assumptions. It’s probably good for any journalist to be reminded of those lessons now and then, and not just when it comes to presidential travel.

PETER: This has been a good reminder that as we travel with the president we should report only what we know and not take even basic things on faith. In the pool reports that journalists traveling with the president typically file, we sometimes write phrases like “your pooler did not actually see the president get onto the plane” or “get into the limousine” or what have you. We generally assume that he did, but are careful not to let assumptions become reported facts. Now, as a result of this episode, we have to be even more aware that we may be being deceived.

Dick, will we be putting our journalists on Air Force One in the future? What, if any, new steps or precautions will we take?

DICK: Yes, I’m sure that we will continue to travel with the president, and in general to cover him with the same intensity we always have. No single incident, not even one of this nature, is going to deter us from that mission. All of us who have done that job know that there are risks. But as Doug said, we’re in a new world when it comes to threats against the president and those around him. And at least when it comes to this administration, we will need to work with other news organizations to insist on greater communication and transparency from the White House, recognizing that a bond of trust was broken here and needs to be repaired.

Doug, do you worry?

DOUG: I can’t use that line anymore, that I’m on the safest plane in the world. But do I think we should still be doing this? Absolutely. That is our role as journalists. We need to be there.

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.

Doug Mills has been a photographer in the Washington bureau of The Times since 2002. He has covered every U. S. president since Ronald Reagan.

Richard W. Stevenson, the Washington bureau chief, has been a reporter and editor at The Times for four decades.

At the urging of President Trump, Representative Russell Fry of South Carolina has endorsed Senator Darline Graham after losing his bid in the special primary election on Tuesday to succeed her late brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

Mr. Fry announced the endorsement on Friday, throwing his weight behind Ms. Graham as she competes in a two-week runoff contest against Representative Ralph Norman, a longtime lawmaker and vice chairman of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus, in the solidly Republican state.

”President Trump needs fighters and allies in the Senate who will show up every day and get results,” Mr. Fry said in a statement. “I believe Darline Graham will be exactly that.”

Mr. Trump has been heavily involved in the race since Mr. Graham, his longtime ally, died unexpectedly in July. He endorsed Ms. Graham, a disability rights advocate who had never held political office, in the primary election after initially signaling he would support Mr. Fry. The runoff is scheduled for Aug. 25.

The president’s personal interest in the race reflects his close relationship with Mr. Graham and his focus on selecting a loyal ally to replace the late senator — especially in a year when Republicans are concerned about defending their majority in Congress. Although few see the seat at risk of flipping in the deeply red state, Mr. Trump has repeatedly dismissed the prospect of Mr. Norman, who endorsed Nikki Haley for president and is not seen as a reliable ally, filling the seat.

Since polls closed in the primary election on Tuesday, Mr. Trump has been working the phones to drum up support for Ms. Graham, according to three people familiar with the calls who were granted anonymity to discuss private conversations.

That night, Mr. Trump called Mr. Fry to encourage him to endorse Ms. Graham, one of the people said.

Mr. Trump lavished the congressman with praise and stressed that he saw a bright future for him, one of the people said.

Mr. Fry had been torn about whether to endorse Ms. Graham, in part because the bitterly fought primary left a bad taste between the two candidates and their political teams, as both sides sought to sell their alignment with the president, one of the people said.

During the primary campaign, Mr. Fry’s team cast Ms. Graham as supportive of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and sharply criticized her encouragement of building data centers in the state.

Mr. Fry ultimately decided to prioritize loyalty to the president, the person said.

We Are Living in a New Inferno

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Op-Docs

By Nita Blum-Reddick and Jonathan Pickett

Ms. Blum-Reddick and Mr. Pickett are documentary filmmakers. They embedded with the firefighters at Station 18, one of the busiest fire stations in Phoenix, during some of the city’s hottest days.

We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.

In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.

Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.

With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

What struck me most while filming was the intricate system of care in place to protect people at their most vulnerable. Much like the threats of oppressive heat, so much of that system is invisible, even for someone like me who lives in Phoenix — most of us never see the dispatchers, emergency crews, hospital teams and countless people working together behind the scenes to save lives. There was something David-and-Goliath-like about watching that network of people confront a force as immense as extreme heat. Using filmmaking as a way to make that care visible, and to show people continuing to show up for one another under almost unthinkable conditions, was incredibly meaningful.

The spark that drew me to the story was learning about The Phoenix Fire Department’s adoption of this innovative ice immersion protocol. As a non-Phoenician who had limited experience living through Arizona summers, learning about this new treatment deepened my understanding of just how deadly the heat has become in recent years. To me, the cold water immersion technique feels strangely akin to a baptism — heatstroke patients are immersed, and can sometimes “come to” quite suddenly, as if risen from the dead. For these firefighters, moments like this are just another day on the job. The privilege of bearing witness to their work has been the greatest gift of making this film.

Nita Blum-Reddick is a producer, director and professor at the Sidney Poitier New American Film School at Arizona State University. Jonathan Pickett is an Emmy-nominated producer and director.

Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Greenlight White House Ballroom

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Supreme Court

Advertisement

Supported by

The planned 90,000-square-foot ballroom is estimated to cost $400 million and is part of the president’s broader effort to remake Washington in his own style.

By Ann E. Marimow

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration on Friday asked the Supreme Court to bless the construction of President Trump’s White House ballroom to replace the demolished East Wing.

The planned 90,000-square-foot ballroom has been mired in litigation ever since the president tore down the East Wing in October as part of his plan to dramatically remake the White House campus. But the courts have let Mr. Trump build even while questioning the project’s legality, allowing the ballroom to steadily rise in recent months.

The administration’s request for intervention from the nation’s highest court comes after an appeals court said on Aug. 7 that the president had most likely exceeded his authority by moving ahead with the privately financed project without approval from Congress. The case poses a test of the limits of executive authority for a Supreme Court that has embraced some, but not all, of the president’s agenda. It also presents the justices with yet another challenge to one of Mr. Trump’s signature initiatives.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, told the justices on Friday that the project was already 65 percent complete and suggested it was too late to stop construction. A 250-person crew has been working 20 hours a day, seven days a week to build a concrete-and-steel superstructure that now stretches five stories deep and 70 feet high, he said.

“Halting the project will stall this vital construction, making this president — the subject of recurrent assassination attempts — much less safe, and risking future presidents’ safety,” he wrote in the Friday filing.

In its 2-to-1 ruling, the U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit said the Constitution gives Congress — not the president — the responsibility to decide when proposed changes to the White House may move ahead.

“Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the executive branch to dramatically redesign, reshape and reconstruct the White House — the People’s House — to fit a particular president’s desires,” the appeals court ruled.

The appeals court had paused its ruling for two weeks to give Mr. Trump time to appeal to the Supreme Court. His petition landed a week later. In the interim, work on the project continued.

Mr. Sauer asked the justices to immediately pause the appeals court ruling, which would halt construction as of Aug. 21. He said the secure ballroom space and an underground military complex were “vitally required for national security.”

Construction of the ballroom, estimated to cost $400 million, is part of Mr. Trump’s second-term effort to reshape Washington in his style. Stopping the project now, Mr. Sauer said Friday, would leave an incomplete structure in place that would be susceptible to “strong winds during extreme weather, and vulnerable to erosion, water, foundation damage” and other setbacks.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard America’s historic buildings, sued to try to stop the ballroom’s construction, asserting that the president had resisted oversight in violation of federal law.

Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who handles emergency filings from the District of Columbia Circuit, on Friday asked the trust to respond to the administration’s request by noon on Tuesday.

Mr. Trump has defended the project, insisting that congressional approval is not necessary and that his plans are no different than previous, more modest renovation projects completed at the White House without consultation with lawmakers. He has said the White House is in need of a large event facility; state dinners and other big events have long been held in tents outdoors because of the lack of such a space.

The president’s legal team has shifted its claims about the project since the litigation began, asserting in recent months that its primary purpose is to add a sprawling underground military complex to improve White House security.

In its filing on Friday, the administration’s lawyers said the trust lacks legal grounds or standing to bring the lawsuit because it does not have a “personal or financial stake” in the outcome.

After the appeals court ruling, Mr. Trump said on social media that “this unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety.” He emphasized that the project was vital for national security and military operations.

In April, Judge Richard J. Leon of the U. S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that the project exceeded the scale of the kind of minor changes presidents have traditionally made to the White House grounds and required approval from Congress. The judge, however, deferred to the president’s claims about the critical need for an upgrade of the military bunker below the White House. His ruling, upheld by the appeals court, would halt construction of the ballroom but allow renovations below ground to continue, including construction of bunkers, bomb shelters, and military and medical infrastructure.

Despite that ruling, Judge Leon permitted construction to continue temporarily both above and below ground while the litigation played out.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which reviews plans for major projects and renovations, voted to approve the project in April. The president had installed allies on the commission before announcing a design for the ballroom.

The project is being funded by private donations. Democrats and public interest groups have raised conflict-of-interest concerns about the financing because many corporate donors engage in business with the federal government.

Mr. Trump has said that the private funds give him the flexibility to pursue the project at no expense to taxpayers, and that he does not need congressional approval for the overhaul of the White House when taxpayer money is not involved.

But in June, the administration transferred roughly $350 million from the Secret Service to cover security upgrades at the White House, which appeared to be destined for the combined East Wing project.

Seven Republican senators joined Democrats in June in voting to block the construction on the project until Congress had formally authorized it, but the measure failed to secure the 60 votes needed to pass.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

The Taliban Kicked the U. S. Out of Afghanistan. Now They Want It Back.

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

In an interview, Afghanistan’s foreign minister called on the U. S. to reopen its embassy and invest in the country — a near-impossible sell for now, analysts and former diplomats say.

By Elian Peltier

Elian Peltier, the Times’s Afghanistan bureau chief, interviewed the country’s foreign minister in Kabul.

Five years after driving the United States out of Afghanistan, the Taliban are inviting it to come back — with diplomats and cash, but no military.

“We consider the chapter of war to have come to an end, and from now on, we want relations based on mutual respect and a new chapter of positive engagement,” Afghanistan’s foreign minister, Amir Khan Muttaqi, said in an interview with The New York Times in Kabul.

Mr. Muttaqi said the United States could “reopen its embassy, maintain a diplomatic presence and invest” in Afghanistan’s vast mineral wealth, dams and roads — projects that three U. S. administrations and their allies spent billions trying to develop, and that the Taliban insurgency spent two decades trying to dismantle.

The public overture, the first by such a high-ranking Taliban official in years, is the Afghan government’s latest push in a long effort to extract the country from isolation, with mixed results.

Over the past year, the Taliban administration has signed a defense partnership with Russia and secured dozens of trade agreements with Central Asian neighbors like Uzbekistan. Some of its officials regularly travel to Gulf countries and have met with Syria’s president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. It is also cooperating with European countries eager to deport Afghan migrants.

The government would see renewed engagement with the Trump administration, with its appetite for commercial diplomacy and little consideration for human rights, as the crowning achievement of its diplomatic efforts, according to five former U. S. and Afghan officials familiar with Kabul’s approach.

The Taliban argue that they have brought order and security across Afghanistan, cleaned its administration of corruption and created favorable conditions for foreign investment.

But efforts to engage with the United States have stalled.

“There is no appetite in D. C.,” said Hassan Abbas, a U. S.-based scholar and the author of a recent book on the Taliban in power. “No one wants to touch this topic. Everyone wants to forget about Afghanistan.”

In fact, the Trump administration has further distanced itself from the Taliban over the past year.

It has moved closer to one of Afghanistan’s neighbors, Pakistan, which launched dozens of airstrikes on Afghanistan earlier this year. It is embroiled in a conflict with another neighbor, Iran, one of the Taliban’s few steady partners. It has ​also designated the Taliban as a state sponsor of wrongful detention, paused issuing visas for Afghans and barred them from traveling to the United States.

The Taliban have also rebuffed President Trump on the few things he has publicly asked for, including regaining control of Bagram Air Base, which U. S. forces occupied for 20 years; the return of U. S. weapons abandoned in Afghanistan; and the release of a U. S. prisoner whom the Taliban deny holding.

“No Afghan wants or can tolerate the military presence of another country on Afghan soil, as history has demonstrated,” Mr. Muttaqi said at the foreign ministry this week, sitting in a plush armchair with the white flag of the Taliban behind him.

In a written response to questions, the U. S. State Department rejected the prospect of normalization. The response, attributed to “a department spokesperson,” said the Taliban had failed to make Afghanistan more stable and uphold counterterrorism commitments, instead allowing terrorist groups to use Afghanistan as a launchpad for attacks.

It said the United States engages with the Taliban “only when it is in the interest of the American people.”

A veteran member of the Taliban and a central figure in past negotiations between the United States and the group before it swept back to power, Mr. Muttaqi said his administration wanted to reopen diplomatic missions in the United States.

Mr. Muttaqi, 55, also confirmed that Afghanistan was negotiating migration agreements with European countries.

“We have made progress in this area, and we hope to make significant further progress in the future,” Mr. Muttaqi said, without elaborating.

In recent months, the Afghan government held several bilateral meetings on migration with countries like Germany and France. A delegation of five Afghan diplomats also met more than 20 diplomats from 15 E. U. countries in Brussels in June to discuss repatriating rejected asylum seekers and convicted criminals, according to three participants and an official briefed on the discussions.

One of the participants, an Afghan diplomat, said that in Europe, the taboo of talking to the Taliban had been broken and that Afghanistan would now engage in bilateral discussions with all interested countries to finalize agreements.

Still, no European country recognizes the Taliban administration as Afghanistan’s legitimate authority, and the government remains a pariah excluded from international bodies like the United Nations and the International Monetary Fund.

The Taliban’s ultraconservative leader, Sheikh Haibatullah Akhundzada, faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity over the persecution of Afghan women and girls. And the United States has frozen billions of dollars from the Afghan Central Bank.

And yet, a growing chorus of analysts and former diplomats in the United States is calling for renewed U. S.-Afghan dialogue beyond counterterrorism cooperation against the Islamic State and prisoner negotiations.

Mr. Trump has the opportunity to do what President Joseph R. Biden Jr. could not, said Robin Raphel, a former U. S. diplomat with extensive experience in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Moving past the current paralysis, Ms. Raphel said, could create new access to minerals, strengthen relations with Afghanistan’s Central Asian neighbors, and counter China and Russia, which do trade and have diplomats in the country.

“But that requires hands-on engagement through a U. S. presence in Kabul, which remains a hard sell in Washington,” Ms. Raphel said.

In an initial exchange with The Times earlier this year, Mr. Muttaqi highlighted Afghanistan’s mines as a potential starting point for a “new chapter for the two countries.”

“I view President Trump’s deal-making ability, pragmatic approach and decisiveness as factors that can facilitate constructive engagement with his administration,” Mr. Muttaqi said.

Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow for South Asia at the D. C.-based Atlantic Council, said minerals were the right pitch to make to the Trump administration. Afghanistan holds vast untapped reserves of lithium, copper and iron ore, as well as rare earth elements that are on the U. S. Geological Survey’s list of critical minerals.

“Values-based considerations like brutality and the Taliban’s horrific treatment of women and girls would not necessarily keep this administration from engaging with the Taliban, particularly if that could help advance U. S. economic interests,” Mr. Kugelman said.

Discussions around Afghanistan’s mineral wealth are not new.

The United States spent nearly $1 billion between 2004 and 2021 to develop Afghanistan’s extractive industry but failed to accomplish any “tangible progress,” according to a 2023 report from SIGAR, the defunct U. S. government oversight agency for Afghanistan. The Taliban administration now holds mining investment deals with companies from China, Iran and Qatar, among others.

Beyond the United States, Mr. Muttaqi called on any country to invest in Afghanistan, where the Taliban administration is in desperate need of foreign capital.

Half of its estimated 45 million people require humanitarian assistance dwindled by U. S. aid cuts last year, according to the United Nations. About four million Afghans have returned from neighboring Pakistan and Iran since early 2025, in one of the largest episodes of reverse migration in decades.

Pakistan, which used to be Afghanistan’s primary trade partner, has closed its border over security concerns, sending the Taliban scrambling for alternative avenues of trade with Central Asian states, Iran and India.

During the interview, Mr. Muttaqi brushed aside a question about whether his government’s crackdown on women and girls was a barrier to international recognition. Earlier this year, he declared the government’s move to keep them out of secondary education was “temporary” — an argument the Taliban also used during their first rule, between 1996 and 2001, when Mr. Muttaqi served as education minister, and immediately after their return to power in 2021.

Mr. Abbas, the academic, said he expected the Taliban to remain isolated as long as they refused to move on their most extreme policies — which are largely dictated out of the city of Kandahar, the group’s spiritual heartland and home to Sheikh Akhundzada.

“Without compromising, without changing anything that they stand for, it is a no-starter,” Mr. Abbas said. “Something has to happen, and the Taliban are not offering that.”

Yaqoob Akbary and Safiullah Padshah contributed reporting.

Elian Peltier is The Times’s bureau chief for Pakistan and Afghanistan, based in Islamabad.

Why Europe Keeps Being Pummeled by Heat Waves

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Extreme Heat

Advertisement

Supported by

The whole planet is warming, but changes in weather patterns could help explain why the continent is suffering so many bouts of severe heat.

By Raymond Zhong

Reporting from London

Europe is sweating through its fifth round of dangerously high temperatures since May, and for climate scientists, the only surprise is that anyone is surprised.

“We’ve said for years that the burning of fossil fuels will continue to warm the planet,” said Matt Patterson, a research fellow in climate science and machine learning at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. “It’s the fossil fuels that’s causing this,” Dr. Patterson said. “In some sense, it’s that simple.”

But he and other scientists are also trying to crack a tougher puzzle. While it’s clear that global warming is adding extra heat to heat waves, researchers are also working to figure out how the atmospheric patterns that produce heat waves might be changing, and whether human activities are to blame.

Climate change, in other words, might not just be intensifying hot weather. It may be warping it as well, with Western Europe in particular suffering the effects.

For Europeans, this summer might be remembered for heating up early and barely letting up.

In France, temperatures broke daily heat records in late May before shattering monthly records in June and July. At its peak, the country’s two-week heat wave in June was hotter than an infamous 2003 hot spell that killed nearly 15,000 people in France and tens of thousands more in other European nations. And France’s latest heat wave, which began on July 28, has now surpassed the 2003 one in duration.

In England and Wales, average daily maximum temperatures were above normal every day in July, according to Britain’s Met Office. The number of days this year when temperatures exceeded 30 degrees Celsius, or 86 degrees Fahrenheit — a daunting threshold for Britons, less so for many Americans — had already set a record by early August, with several weeks of summer still to come.

The worst of these hot spells are the result of heat domes: giant masses of high-pressure air that become stuck in place, clearing the clouds and heating the land beneath them for days or even weeks at a time. When they alight on Western Europe, these systems block cool air from flowing in from the North Atlantic and can draw in more hot air from North Africa.

The weather patterns that create heat domes aren’t new, but today they arise on top of the warming caused by greenhouse gas emissions. That makes it more likely that heat waves reach record-shattering temperatures for long stretches.

But other environmental changes — natural, human-influenced or both — might also be causing heat domes to become more frequent and longer lasting. And it’s these changes that scientists around the globe are trying to puzzle out.

One change has to do with the Arctic. The differences in temperature between the hot Equator and the frigid far north help keep weather moving around the Northern Hemisphere. But with the top of the world now warming at several times the pace of the rest of the globe, those temperature gradients are narrowing. That might be causing the movements of weather systems to become more sluggish, producing more persistent heat waves.

In Europe, reduced air pollution could be having a similar effect. Industrial emissions can contain particles called aerosols that reflect sunlight. Curbing aerosols has improved air quality, but it may also have altered the way air moves across the continent.

Scientists haven’t come to firm conclusions about how these shifts might be affecting European summers, said Antje Weisheimer, a climate scientist at the University of Oxford. The complex, fine-scale interactions in the atmosphere that drive weather dynamics are tough to capture in computer simulations, Dr. Weisheimer said. “It’s tricky,” she said. “We’re making small progress.”

Dim Coumou, a professor of climate science at the Dutch university VU Amsterdam, sees artificial intelligence as one way forward. In a recent study, he and his colleagues used an A. I. algorithm to help a weather model better predict summer temperatures in Europe. They not only improved the model’s forecasts; they also discovered why some of the model’s predictions had been off: It misrepresented the way conditions in the western Pacific Ocean influenced atmospheric patterns that eventually made their way to Europe.

With A. I., “we can also learn what the climate models are missing,” Dr. Coumou said.

Ultimately, all this research is aimed at answering a vital question for Europe’s future: How often can the continent expect to be thrashed each summer by long hot spells? And how long might they last?

“If it’s a heat wave of a few days, society can cope much, much better,” Dr. Weisheimer said. But when extreme heat drags on for week after scorching week, “it’s a problem for agriculture, for water supply, for everything you can imagine.”

Raymond Zhong reports on climate and environmental issues for The Times.

Tech Giants’ Profits Reveal Potential Vulnerability in the Stock Market

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Investment gains at Alphabet and Amazon reveal a new way in which technology companies’ fortunes are increasingly linked.

By Joe Rennison

Tech giants like Amazon and Alphabet have powered the stock market to record highs in recent years, fueled by the growth of their artificial intelligence and cloud computing businesses.

But in recent months, a big driver of those two companies’ profits came from an unusual source: The increasing value of their investment stakes in artificial intelligence companies.

Over 70 percent of Alphabet’s net quarterly income came from investments in other companies, and in particular, in Elon Musk’s SpaceX, according to a recent regulatory filing and analysis from Satori Insights, a financial markets research firm. SpaceX went public in June in the biggest initial public offering ever.

Investment gains also accounted for roughly 65 percent of Amazon’s net income, largely stemming from its stake in Anthropic, a leading A. I. start-up that is also planning to go public.

Those gains underscore a growing vulnerability in the broader stock market: The companies that keep pushing the market higher are increasingly dependent on each other’s success.

“It’s circular,” said Matt King, founder of Satori Insights. “What’s funding A. I. is now increasingly more A. I.”

Worries about the circular nature of the A. I. boom have persisted for some time, as investors have watched the dominant tech giants, chipmakers and A. I. labs invest in or loan each other money. That money is often then used to buy products or cloud services from the same companies funding them.

A. I. executives have defended these circular financing models. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has described the deals as a creative way to free up the capital needed to supercharge innovation at a time of rapid change.

But the investment gains at Alphabet and Amazon show how these companies’ fortunes are increasingly linked. They also point to the increasing interconnectedness of the stock market and the broader economy: A. I. is powering growth in both, making the threat of a stock market tumble an even greater concern for policymakers.

“The stock market was never just a reflection of the economy, but it’s now become one of the economy’s main engines,” said Mr. King.

Unrealized investment gains are added to a company’s profit for accounting purposes, according to the value of holdings at the end of each quarter. Unless the company sells any of the stakes, the gains are purely on paper. It also works in reverse: A decline in the value of investment holdings during a quarter can subtract from a company’s reported earnings.

Alphabet and Amazon did not respond to requests for comment.

They are part of a small group of closely watched technology companies, nicknamed the Magnificent 7, which also includes Microsoft, Meta, Apple, Tesla and Nvidia. This group has become a measure for the tech-driven stock market rally, and many investors like to look at the seven companies in aggregate.

Overall, the Magnificent 7 pulled in $315.6 billion in net profit for the second quarter. That covers the three months through June for all of the companies except Nvidia, which has a slightly different financial year.

Of that total, $134.6 billion, or about 42 percent, came from investment gains, according to calculations made by Mr. King, who adjusted the companies’ reported numbers to account for taxes. Other sources of net profit are typically earnings from the sale of goods and services.

Without those investment gains, profits for this group would have been roughly equal to the previous quarter — not growing — according to Mr. King. Microsoft, Meta, Apple and Tesla did not report any comparable investment income.

Nvidia reported roughly $13 billion in investment gains for its most recent quarter. The chipmaker has stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as investments in other A. I.-related companies, including CoreWeave and Applied Digital, which rent data-center access to high-powered processors for A. I. models.

The second-quarter investment gains for these seven companies were a much larger share of overall profits than the 5 percent they totaled in the previous quarter, according to Mr. King’s calculations.

Going forward, investment gains on the tech companies’ holdings could continue to fluctuate as some of the private companies they are invested in go public.

The gains announced by Alphabet, which owns Google, appear to be largely attributable to its investment in Mr. Musk’s space and A. I. company SpaceX. It reported nearly $80 billion in pretax profit stemming from investments in restricted equity securities and also disclosed holdings of $94.1 billion of SpaceX shares.

That gain is likely to change. When SpaceX started publicly trading on June 12, its shares soared. Since then, the stock has gyrated wildly, and share price is now roughly 17 percent below its level on June 30, when Google reported its stake.

Amazon said in a regulatory filing that its $50 billion investment gain came “primarily” from its stock in Anthropic.

If this interconnected A. I. boom begins to reverse — if, say, investors grow skeptical that artificial intelligence will generate big enough profits to pay for the massive infrastructure build-out underway — it will have broad consequences, analysts and economists said.

“The A. I. trade is massively important to the U. S.,” said Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays. “We are more exposed to the A. I. trade unwinding as an economy than we were even a few years ago.”

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

The Markets Have Been on a Roll. Is It Time to Hedge Your Bets?

The New York Times August 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Strategies

The S&P 500 is in position for a rare fourth year of consecutive annual gains. Risks are rising, our columnist says, yet Wall Street is doubling down.

By Jeff Sommer

Jeff Sommer writes Strategies, a weekly column on markets, finance and the economy.

The U. S. stock market has been splendid for more than three years. It has powered ahead again in 2026, putting the S&P 500 in position for a rare feat: a fourth consecutive year of double-digit gains.

That’s happened only three times since 1928 — most recently, in the late 1990s. That boom was also fueled by extravagant hopes based on a technological breakthrough. Then, it was the internet. Now, it’s artificial intelligence.

The 1990s stretch, when the S&P 500 rose more than 20 percent each year from 1995 through 1999, had another distinction: It was the only string of five consecutive years of double-digit gains in the last 98 years.

In the midst of the current rally, those glorious gains for investors in the 1990s seem bittersweet, at best, because they ended with the market crash of 2000 and were followed by an entire decade of miserable returns. During the financial crisis of 2007 to 2009, the S&P 500 dropped 56.8 percent, from top to bottom. In 2009, the S&P 500 was lower than it was in 1999.

It’s clear that doubling down on the incredible, rising stock market was not a wise move in the late 1990s.

But what about now?

Unfortunately, I don’t know where the market is heading from here. Nor does anybody else. What we do know is what happened in the past. The lessons are simple enough: Stick with the stock market for the long haul, but exercise restraint now, by diversifying with low-cost index funds and holding enough cash and bonds to survive the downturns that always come.

That’s not the message coming from many Wall Street strategists, who have become increasingly bullish as the stock market has risen and companies have churned out spectacular earnings.

A long-running Bloomberg survey found in July that the consensus forecast for the S&P 500’s year-end close had risen about 6 percent since the end of last year, to 8,000. The prevailing outlook has become more positive in the weeks since then, based on a host of higher forecasts that have shown up in my inbox in the last few days, probably reflecting the market’s surge past 7,700 this month.

Such forecasts have been wildly inaccurate for years, but I follow them closely because they reflect the mood on Wall Street. It’s red hot right now, though tempered with a dollop of worry about whether the good times can last.

A forecast on Tuesday from Capital Economics, an independent financial research service based in London, is a good example. It called the current market a bubble fueled by A. I. that will inevitably explode.

“We envisage the bubble inflating a bit more during the rest of this year before bursting: our end-2026 and end-2027 forecasts for the S&P 500 are 8,250 and 6,500, respectively,” Capital Economics said. In other words, the market is rising but will fall sharply sometime next year.

So piling into the stock market now and selling before it crashes — exactly when, the forecast doesn’t say — would be smart if that forecast was right.

It’s possible that it is, but I’m skeptical. History warns that most of us will get into trouble if we attempt to make trades based on forecasts like that.

In a recent note to clients, Sam Stovall, a market veteran who is now the chief investment strategist of CFRA, an independent financial research firm, pointed out some of the dangers of trying to move in and out of the stock market at apparently opportune times.

As a starting point, he considered the buy-and-hold approach, which requires staying in the markets, come what may, even during terrible decades. That simple strategy, which is what I try to follow, produced an 11.5 percent annualized return for the S&P 500 from the end of 1987 through the end of last year, Mr. Stovall found.

Then he illustrated some of the temptations and pitfalls of varying from this approach. First, he looked at the potential rewards of an impossible feat — timing the market perfectly. Mr. Stovall calculated what an investor’s annualized return would have been if she had been prescient enough to have missed only the market’s worst days in that period, from Dec. 31, 1987, through Dec. 31, 2025, and to have stayed in the market every other day:

Missed the 10 worst days: 14.1 percent, annualized.

Missed the 20 worst days: 15.1 percent, annualized.

Missed the 30 worst days: 16.5 percent, annualized.

Missed the 40 worst days: 17.9 percent, annualized.

All of these returns would have been wonderful. The problem, of course, is that you wouldn’t have known in advance which days to avoid. If you had abandoned the market at the wrong times, you would have missed some eye-popping gains. As I’ve observed in other columns, the best days for stocks are often clustered near the worst ones, and you can’t skip the nightmares without passing up some awesome returns.

Mr. Stovall illustrated this conundrum by computing what would have happened to your investment in the S&P 500 over that same period if you had missed only the best days:

Missed the 10 best days: 9.3 percent, annualized.

Missed the 20 best days: 7.3 percent, annualized.

Missed the 30 best days: 6.0 percent, annualized.

Missed the 40 best days: 4.8 percent, annualized.

Being absent from the market on the strong days isn’t what any investor would want, but that’s likely to happen if you stay out of the market at any time.

That said, there’s no argument about this: You would have been better off with no stock holdings at all from Dec. 31, 1999, until March 9, 2009, which marked the end of the bear market associated with the financial crisis. I ran the numbers on FactSet. For that entire period, the cumulative return for the S&P 500 was minus 46 percent, including dividends. By contrast, over the same stretch, the Bloomberg U. S. Aggregate Bond Index, a widely followed benchmark for investment grade bonds, rose 72.3 percent.

Sticking with the stock market in that decade was to experience aggravation and heartache. Holding bonds has been painful lately, but they were a balm then. That’s worth remembering now — not as a reason to flee the stock market but as a reminder to hedge your bets.

The essential problem is that it’s impossible to know what the stock market is about to do.

Certainly, right now, there are many signs that risks are rising. I listed some of them last week. They include the risks of increased inflation; wars and tariffs; questionable use of vast sums of capital for A. I.; an uncertain direction for the Federal Reserve under new leadership; mounting national debt; and broad political dysfunction. Interest rates in the bond market have increased, and that makes bonds relatively attractive, compared with stocks.

Yet Wall Street is doubling down on stocks. Enormous investments in A. I. and outstanding earnings reports from companies like Alphabet, Microsoft, Nvidia and Amazon have been propelling the market ever higher. Including dividends, an investment in the S&P 500 has doubled in value since the release of the ChatGPT in late November 2022. Market valuation measures, like the price-to-earnings ratio, which compares share prices with corporate earnings, are stretched. There are ample reasons for caution, but if earnings remain strong, it’s possible that the overall trend for the stock market will remain upward for months or years.

Valuation measures simply aren’t useful in predicting short-term moves. But it is also true that rich valuations, like those in the stock market now, do imply constrained returns over the next decade or more, as Robert J. Shiller, the Nobel laureate economist, has shown.

So what is an investor to do? There are an infinite number of answers. My own conclusion is to keep it simple and forget about market timing (and stock picking) completely. Instead, I stick with broad stock index funds at all times — and always hold bonds and cash, too, tweaking my asset allocation slightly, from time to time, depending mainly on my personal life.

I haven’t bulked up on stocks because of the latest rally. Instead, over many years, as I’ve aged, I’ve slowly ratcheted down risk by reducing my stock allocation.

There could well be another bad decade ahead. But great days for stocks will almost certainly be coming, too, and I’d hate to miss them.

Jeff Sommer writes Strategies, a weekly column on markets, finance and the economy.

The Best Photos of the Big Solar Eclipse

Wired August 12, 2026

For the first time in more than a century, Spain witnessed a total solar eclipse. The astronomical phenomenon, which was also partially visible in some regions of northern North America, much of Europe, and western Africa, offered an unusual and particularly photogenic sight due to the sun’s position just above the horizon.

The solar corona glows as the moon completely obscures the sun during the total solar eclipse on Arenal Beach in Llucmajor, Mallorca.

The path of totality traversed the northern hemisphere from west to east. Its path began in the Arctic Ocean, north of Greenland, continued west of Iceland, and crossed the North Atlantic. Later, at exactly 8:30 pm central European summer time, the shadow cast by the moon reached the Iberian Peninsula.

People gathered at El Cerro del Tío Pío Park in Madrid to observe the total solar eclipse.

Regions such as Galicia, Asturias, Castile and León, Madrid, Aragon, Catalonia, the Valencian Community, and the Balearic Islands experienced the path of totality, while the rest of the country saw a partial eclipse.

The solar corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase, as seen from San Asensio in the La Rioja region.

The event lasted about four and a half hours, while the total darkening of the sky lasted just under two minutes, allowing various space agencies to conduct scientific experiments along the path of totality.

Fans of Real Madrid watch the solar eclipse through special glasses before the Teresa Herrera Trophy match between RC Deportivo A Coruña and Real Madrid at Riazor Stadium.

One of the most notable projects involved a NASA mission tracking the moon’s shadow using a WB-57 high-altitude research aircraft that flew at 50,000 feet. A team of scientists sought to gather new data on the dynamics of the solar corona—the sun’s outermost atmosphere—which can only be studied in detail during total eclipses.

The total solar eclipse as observed from Palencia, Spain.

The space agency also brought students from various universities in the US to Iceland and Spain to launch scientific balloons before, during, and after the event. The goal was to analyze how the temporary darkening of the sky caused by the eclipse alters conditions in Earth’s atmosphere, gathering information that will help better understand the effects of these astronomical events on the environment.

Beachgoers view the eclipse in Llucmajor, Mallorca.

Later this month, a partial lunar eclipse will be visible across the Americas, offering new opportunities for researching the cosmos. In the meantime, we have the images of Wednesday’s solar spectacle to gawk at.

The moment following totality of the solar eclipse over the coastal lagoon of La Albufera in Valencia.

Several people watch the total solar eclipse from Arenal Beach in Llucmajor, Mallorca.

People prepare to watch the total solar eclipse from Arenal Beach in Llucmajor, Mallorca.

A man watches the total solar eclipse from the port of Tarragona, in eastern Spain.

A view of the solar eclipse from Segur de Calafell, Spain.

A girl watches the total solar eclipse in the port of Tarragona, in eastern Spain.

The eclipse in the moments following totality, as seen from La Zurriola Beach in San Sebastián.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

The White House Is Going to Expand Its AI Policy

Wired August 12, 2026

White House officials are almost certain to revise the Trump administration’s new artificial intelligence guidelines and expand its oversight of AI models, according to people familiar with the matter.

The White House announced this month that it had developed an AI framework, where the most powerful models created by US labs would be tested for safety by the federal government before they could be released publicly. The administration has not made the framework public, and reportedly has no plans to do so.

The AI framework currently deals only with so-called closed models developed by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI. But the framework is expected in the coming months to cover open models, too, a White House official tells Inner Loop.

In short, as soon as open models reach the same “frontier” capabilities as Anthropic’s Mythos-class models and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6, they will be added to the framework and subject to prerelease testing, the White House official says.

The move reflects the White House’s evolving approach to oversight and regulation of the AI sector that has only been increasing in power over the last few months and sparked concerns that models could autonomously hack the Pentagon or global financial markets.

This concern isn’t unfounded: Over several weeks in May and June, OpenAI recently disclosed, a group of models colluded on a secret message board on how to access the internet. After staff shut it down, the models again rebuilt the messaging board and broke out undetected in late July.

While the White House once hoped it could develop guidelines in one swoop of an executive action, the exponential development of AI models has forced officials across the Trump administration to evolve guidelines in real time, the people say.

Aside from the national security concerns, Trump officials are also grappling with the framework leading to a two-tier situation, where if only closed models start getting seals of approval, enterprises might become hesitant to use open models that don't have the same approval, even if they are cheaper.

Some Trump officials have expressed concern that it could paradoxically disincentivize US companies from developing open models. But they privately tell Inner Loop they also recognize that imposing a potential 30-day testing requirement could equally stifle development.

The AI framework remains voluntary for now, according to a White House official, in large part because President Donald Trump has been adamant that formal regulation of the industry would only help China catch up to the US in the AI race.

But the White House has been coming under pressure from other parts of the administration, Inner Loop has learned, to draw up a more robust arrangement with leading AI labs because the current framework is still vague. This, sources suggest, could even result in leading AI labs working as formal partners in testing programs.

A busy night of Democratic and GOP primaries on Tuesday revealed what might be coming down the line for the midterm elections in November.

In the closely watched Wisconsin primary for governor, the democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong lost to the more moderate candidate David Crowley.

Hong ended up with a little over 300,000 votes, which would have won nearly every previous Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor this century, as Semafor’s David Weigel noted on X. The prevailing view among political operatives is that the midterms will be won and lost on turnout, and Democratic turnout is already looking exceptionally high this year.

Meanwhile, a Trump endorsement has not meant guaranteed success for an increasing number of Republican candidates. In Minnesota, former MyPillow CEO and 2020 election conspiracy theorist Mike Lindell lost to Republican state House speaker Lisa Demuth in Minnesota’s gubernatorial primary, despite Trump’s endorsement.

In the Republican primary race to succeed Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina, Graham’s sister Darline failed to clinch a majority despite having the Trump endorsement and will go to a runoff against the hard-line conservative US representative Ralph Norman.

Without Trump at the top of the ticket, Republican turnout might be depressed, and even if Trump manages to turn out his MAGA base, the Hong result shows that Democrats are clearly animated this midterm cycle. If they remain just as energized in November, it could bode well for Democrats to take majorities in Congress.

The Safety Reckoning Inside OpenAI

Wired August 13, 2026

OpenAI’s leaders are rallying workers to respond to one of the largest crises in the company’s history—which spans across its AI safety, cybersecurity, and alignment divisions. The ChatGPT-maker says it has slowed down research, spent millions of dollars, and told several teams to drop everything to focus on investigating a set of rogue AI agents that breached the platform Hugging Face in a quest to complete an internal security test.

OpenAI is expected to release a comprehensive postmortem detailing the incident in the coming days. However, the Hugging Face incident has inspired OpenAI leaders and employees to examine how the AI lab’s culture may have enabled this incident in the first place.

Multiple current and former OpenAI employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private internal matters, tell WIRED they believe competitive pressures to quickly ship new AI models and products have made it difficult for staffers to sufficiently prioritize safety, security, and alignment.

“We’re reaching new levels of model capability that require more robust training, alignment, safety and security testing, deployment practices, and governance—as demonstrated by the work we’re doing to prepare Astra and future models,” said OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman in a statement to WIRED. “We feel the weight of deploying our models and products responsibly, and a lot of that starts with the changes we’ve made to more deeply integrate research, safety, and security into frontier-model development from the start.”

This is far from the first time OpenAI employees have raised such concerns. Back in 2024, OpenAI’s then head of alignment Jan Leike left to join Anthropic, warning on his way that safety was taking a back seat to shiny products. Two years later, the Hugging Face attack represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, demonstrating that AI agents today can cause real-world harm when safety, security, and alignment aren’t properly accounted for.

“We are responding to this with the utmost severity,” said Michael Dalton, an OpenAI security and infrastructure engineer, during a talk at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last week. “What I would internalize is that AI-orchestrated, fully automated offensive attacks are real now. The actions we have discussed today were an unintended side effect of running evaluations on frontier AI.”

Some OpenAI employees told WIRED they are optimistic this incident will inspire genuine change within the company. OpenAI has committed to slowing the release of future AI models and has been especially forthcoming about areas where its mitigations fell short. Boaz Barak, a researcher who coleads OpenAI’s safety advisory group, said in a post on X that addressing the situation “requires not just fixing some issues but also changing our culture.”

In their Black Hat talk, OpenAI security engineers Dalton and Eric Wallace said that the Hugging Face incident started in May when, unbeknownst to the company, several AI agents thought to be operating within isolated testing environments gained access to the internet and convened on a covert message board to coordinate with one another.

OpenAI would not discover the message board until July, when it learned that the AI agents had hacked into multiple services to try to achieve their larger goal of breaching Hugging Face’s platform, which they believed may contain answers to the security tests they were trying to solve.

“They were incredibly sloppy. If you’re serious about this, your AI shouldn’t be able to break out onto the internet and then do it again right afterward,” says one former OpenAI employee who requested anonymity to speak with WIRED. “This was the biggest safety incident in OpenAI's history.”

Weeks before OpenAI discovered the Hugging Face incident, WIRED reported that the company had begun a reorganization to combine its safety and core research teams, which led to the departure of its then safety leader Johannes Heidecke.

Sandhini Agarwal, who led AI safety teams at OpenAI, also left the company in July after more than six years, according to her LinkedIn. Agarwal did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

WIRED has also learned that Dylan Scandinaro is no longer serving as OpenAI’s head of preparedness—the company’s top staffer tasked with mitigating catastrophic risks from AI, including cybersecurity—though he remains at the company. OpenAI poached Scandinaro from Anthropic roughly six months ago. CEO Sam Altman announced his arrival in a social media post, noting that Scandinaro was “by far the best candidate I have met, anywhere.”

In the three years since OpenAI created the head of preparedness role, four people have held it. OpenAI tells WIRED that specific areas of preparedness have dedicated leaders across cybersecurity, biology, and recursive self-improvement who, in the interim, are reporting to the safety advisory group colead and head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.

These changes have empowered a new set of safety leaders to handle OpenAI's response to the Hugging Face incident. Chief among them is Amelia “Mia” Glaese, the company's former head of alignment, who succeeded Heidecke as OpenAI’s VP overseeing safety. She has been working closely with chief information security officer Dane Stuckey and Brockman, among other leaders, in recent weeks.

Glaese is in a long-term relationship with Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products like ChatGPT and Codex—an arrangement that multiple current and former employees tell WIRED they believe is unusual, given the often adversarial dynamic between safety and product teams.

WIRED has not identified any events where Sottiaux and Glaese’s relationship presented a conflict of interest in their previous roles as OpenAI’s head of Codex and head of alignment, respectively. Both started their new roles in recent months, after the Hugging Face incident began. Glaese and Sottiaux started dating years ago when the two worked at Google DeepMind in London, before they joined OpenAI.

An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Sottiaux and Glaese reported their relationship through appropriate company channels and that OpenAI board member and safety and security committee chair Zico Kolter has been informed. The spokesperson rejected the idea there is an adversarial dynamic between product and safety teams and says Sottiaux has exhibited a strong track record on safety in his leadership of Codex product teams.

“The entire leadership team and I stand behind Mia and Tibo as highly capable people with strong integrity, and the way they make decisions every day gives us confidence that any perceived conflict of interest is being handled responsibly,” said Brockman in a statement to WIRED.

It’s not uncommon for researchers in the AI industry to have relationships with their colleagues. Last year, for example, Anthropic hired Holden Karnofsky, husband of the company’s cofounder and president, Daniela Amodei, as a researcher.

Tim O'Brien, a Microsoft leader for more than 18 years who now consults and writes on tech policy, argued in a 2024 essay that modern AI labs have developed a version of “go fever”—a reference to the culture at NASA during the time leading up to the Apollo 1 disaster, when the agency grew so fixated on launching quickly that safety concerns fell by the wayside.

The AI labs “should make some sort of broad based announcement saying we've made a strategic business decision to slow the pace of releases in favor of rigorous products and safety testing. But nobody's gonna do that, nobody wants to go first,” says O’Brien. “They'll walk up to that line from a public relations perspective without stepping over it, because then they could be held accountable.”

OpenAI and Anthropic signed on to a letter last month saying they would support an industry-wide effort to “pace” the AI race. However, O’Brien says “it's embarrassing” that AI labs have signed this variety of open letters for years without taking any concrete action. He’s skeptical this one will be any different.

The issues raised by OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident are affecting the entire industry. In recent weeks, researchers have found that agents powered by AI models from Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI were able to escape sandboxed environments. It seems likely that even mid-tier AI models will soon be capable of significant cybersecurity damage.

The key question is whether the Hugging Face incident marks a divergence for OpenAI and the broader AI industry, prompting a long-term investment in safety, security, and alignment. Otherwise, it could just be another chaotic blip in the history of modern AI.

Like all AI, it's trained on training data. If it's never seen a whole class of attack, it won't be able to carry that out itself. So I think the lesson that I took away from Black Hat and Defcon is really that, like a lot of artificial intelligence from the past applied to things like chess or Go or whatever, the most powerful combination is humans and AI working together, and that really will start to create and hopefully patch vulnerabilities we've never seen before.
